As I have said before, I felt it was essential to understand fully what really goes on within the classroom where these students are participating. I took it upon myself to spend an hour and a half in one such classroom. I came away from that experience wanting everyone in the world to see it to understand exactly what is happening. It was fundamentally brilliant. There were ten students in that setting and two members of SEN teaching staff. On the day I randomly visited, they were doing they were doing a CPR and first aid lesson. Outside of that room, each child had a parent or both parents in some instances who had a break as a consequence of the child getting that opportunity to learn more. There were two really great things happening. Parents were getting a much-needed break – I saw the challenges of the students - and the children were getting the benefit. The teaching staff were so passionate about what they were doing.  One of the things that came up in conversation was that not enough specialist training is available for SNA teachers. In the normal scheme of things, when a teacher is going through a teaching course, it is rarely required to complete the SNA element. That is a failing. I realised that day, as I have many times in the past, the extraordinary challenges there are for all teaching staff, not just SNAs, for example with managing hot school meals and everything that goes with that. There are also school capacity issues. I do not really have a question about this but I am very passionate about it, particularly because I understand the real benefit for children who can avail of the summer programme. I really feel that, by and large, the teaching staff who are involved in SNA teaching do an absolutely compelling job. Any tampering with their job security and continuity of employment is an absolutely critical matter. I ask the witnesses’ views on the impact of the summer programme on schools, on teaching staff and, most importantly, on the students who benefit. I am sorry to cut them so tight for time. I went on a bit much.

Mr. Brendan Doody  Each year for the past number of years, we have asked the inspectorate to monitor the provision available in schools during the summer programme. Its reports are published every year and are well worth a read. Somewhat unusually for the inspectorate, perhaps, they are universally positive and strongly endorse the work of schools. The Deputy's experience of visiting a school that is providing the summer programme is shared across the board. It is a hugely important element of provision from the Department.  The issue of respite for parents, which I think is what the Deputy is referring to, was probably brought into sharpest relief during Covid, when special schools closed and we got a really deep understanding of it. Ultimately, the purpose of a school is for students to learn. However, the secondary benefit of special schools in particular is that parents are enabled to have a period when their children are cared for, looked after and taught, which is really important. As Ms Corcoran referenced, the summer programme is evolving each year. Every single year it is evolving. The inspectorate looks at it each year and we take the learning from that and try to apply it to the following year to make sure it is as good as it can be.
An Cathaoirleach  I thank the witnesses. We are going to go to a second round of questions. It is three minutes per Member, beginning with Deputy O’Meara.

Deputy Ryan O'Meara  I know Senator Curley touched on CPD in some detail in previous meetings. I will refer to the training of our special education teachers in particular. I ask the officials to outline where the Department is with work on that and how it is going to make it as accessible as possible to teachers in the system.  I understand that those going through teacher training now will have the mandatory experience. For those who have not done it, what is available to them time and cost wise? How do we make it as accessible as possible, considering the number of positions we are filling and trying to fill at all times?

Mr. Brendan Doody  I will start and other colleagues can come in. In recognising the importance of having experts in our system, we fund 388 postgraduate places annually. These are places on level 9 postgraduate programmes that are available to teachers working. Obviously, the stipulation is that they have to be working in special education settings, either in special schools or special classes. Those places are taken up every single year. We increased the number of places from 338 to 388 in the last budget, a small increase admittedly. We want to increase that again. The more specialist training we have available, the better. I will pass to Ms Walsh to talk about the much wider range of training available to teachers. It is not all about the specialist teachers. We want to enhance the capacity of all teachers to be better in their classrooms.

Ms Helen Walsh  There is quite an extensive range of training opportunities for SET teachers and class and subject teachers within the whole school community. The NCSE's professional learning programme looks at trying to work with schools in a proactive, supportive and responsible way. We have pathways for professional growth. They offer a huge suite of supports. I will come to SETs specifically in a minute.  We have responded to over 2,700 requests from teachers, including SETs, to come to their school to support them. We offer inclusion cafés, which are in-person. They provide a supportive environment to get into the nitty-gritty detail of what a specific teacher is experiencing. We have responded with 224 whole school staff sessions across the country. A total of 350 schools have responded to us for sustained support. That means we are with them all the way through for two years on the area of development they want to work through. We work with about 500 schools through the NCSE relate resource on regulation and behavioural management. We work with a further 460 schools around autism.  The Deputy is right that in order to provide a professional learning programme that hits whole school communities, it must be done in a variety of ways. We respond to that by way of coaching and in-class modelling. Our new learning management system, which we are launching in September, will offer a whole variety of learning opportunities for schools. Last year, we offered 431 seminars and webinars that reached some 28,000 teachers. We always have to improve and move forward. We are looking at what quality practice looks like into the first quarter of next year to support schools specifically in that practice space with NCSE connect. That will cover a whole range of supports, including leadership training, neurodiversity, NCSE relate, what transitions look like and inclusive pedagogy as it exists within a school context.  For SETs, we look at their areas of expertise on student support planning, creating student support files, implementing the SET guidelines and inclusive teaching. We also get into specific details, such as students with Down’s syndrome or literary or numeracy issues. We support SETs in that regard. On foot of the SET review, which the Deputy referenced, we also assign advisers to schools that have gone through a SET review and may be disappointed with the result. They may need some practice development. We ensure they have that support.

Ms Ellen Guerin  I wish to briefly mention the role of NEPS in supporting the training or, as we call it, our support and development model of service. We have a service that provides support and training for all school staff, which backs up what Ms Walsh said. It is for teachers and special needs assistants in areas such as well-being, mental health, special education inclusion and literacy.
An Cathaoirleach  I apologise; I took my eye off the clock. I will give everyone four minutes in order to be fair to everyone. I call Deputy Darren O’Rourke.

Deputy Darren O'Rourke  Sinn Féin, through a Dáil motion, proposed a special Oireachtas committee on the future of inclusive education. It would have been a Sláintecare-type committee. The Government did not disagree with it, but I do not think it agreed with it either. It has come up with this special education forum, which is the national forum. The intent of both is the same. Does the NCSE welcome the opportunity of the forum? What important things need to come out of it? The committee has an opportunity to meet with the chair of the forum. I ask that question of the Department as well.

Mr. John Kearney  No more than the committee’s work in recent times, particularly in recent weeks, when it has been considering all aspects of inclusive education and what it looks like, it is about ongoing dialogue and consultation. By its very nature, special education and by extension inclusive education keep changing and evolving. The inclusive forum is to be welcomed. Obviously, it is enshrining a shared national vision for what inclusive education looks like. A whole ambit of support structures are required to bring that vision to a practical reality for young children and families throughout the State. Underpinning all of that will be many of the issues we have discussed this morning and those the committee has been discussing in recent weeks, such as initial teacher training, access to professional development, enhancing the roles of individual teachers, SNAs within schooling communities and expanding leadership capacity within schools. Ultimately, there is the question of the wraparound supports needed at a variety of levels, with specific expertise in autism and behaviour as well as therapeutic inputs into the physical and mental well-being of students. All of those attributes will be featuring naturally in that discussion, with as many parties as possible contributing. What inclusive education looks like is an area that unites, challenges and at times divides. However, there is a collective mission and vision to be created that builds and is united by everyone contributing.
Deputy Darren O'Rourke  Will Mr. Doody comment on whether there should be an opportunity for the general public to submit to this forum, parents in particular?

Mr. Brendan Doody  The Minister has announced that the forum will run for a six-month period. As the Deputy will know, Professor Noel Purdy has been appointed as chair. There will be an opportunity for us to engage with the chair in September in this regard. It is important to note that there has been an enormous amount of consultation heretofore relating to the EPSEN Act, the roadmap for inclusion and the work of the disability committee.
Deputy Darren O'Rourke  Is that European document, which Mr. Doody previously mentioned, published?

Mr. Brendan Doody  Yes, it is published. All of these reports are coalescing around the same things, which Mr. Kearney articulated very well. First, what is the shared vision for inclusion? What are the structures that will be required in order to achieve that, such as teacher professional learning, leadership, the wraparound services, multidisciplinary team supports and, importantly, transitions? Realistically, the consultation is complete. There was a massive level of consultation involved with the EPSEN Act. The roadmap for inclusion also had a huge level of consultation. We know what everyone is saying. The question now is how we progress it. How do we make this a reality in our system? Some of it will take quite a long time, while other things can be progressed far more quickly.
Deputy Darren O'Rourke  Will the forum report in six months’ time?
Mr. Brendan Doody  Yes. The Minister has said she wants this done within six months. It will meet over a period of six months and a report will follow quickly after that.

An Cathaoirleach  I am up next. I want to go back to the parents notify portal that others have raised. It is welcome that it is open. However, I note that last year the closing date for people to submit was 1 October, whereas it is now 1 September. Many parents will engage with the portal and that is fine, but what I have seen in my years of teaching is that while some parents are geared around these things, others are not. Others rely heavily on the school to guide them in this regard. Schoolteachers are largely unavailable at this time. While we can say that some may be in and out of the school, many will not. The principals are on holiday leave and it is a big ask to think that all of this can function perfectly between now and 1 September. It is not realistic at all.  I hear that there is a desire to pull this back earlier each year. Anything administrative or orientative in a school should be wrapped up by mid-June in order to allow schools to conclude standardised testing, send out report cards and close the door for the summer. This should not be on the backs of principals, SETs and co-ordinators over the summer. Will the witnesses comment on this?  What has been the engagement on the portal so far?

Ms Angela Corcoran  The NCSE will outline the level of engagement, which has been very high. It is worth saying that, as we have mentioned before, the parents notify system is an important tool. In the first instance, parents should be contacting the SENO. That should be their first point of call. Even where the schools open, the SENO should be the first port of call.  In the first instance, the information that parents are required to provide on the parents notify system is very basic. It is the name, date of birth, address and that type of information. It is very basic in the first instance. The requirement for reports, etc., is at a later date. I will say that while they are closed we are grateful that many schools have contacted parents to remind them of the closing date of 1 September. I emphasise that parents need to engage with the SENO.

An Cathaoirleach  If I may interject, I agree with all of that. I would make the point that there are different types of parenting in this country. Some parents will be straight on it the minute the portal opens. Other parents - and I do not know a better way to say this - need their hands held. They will not engage and do not know what to do. They may not be motivated to deal with the issue. They may not have IT literacy skills. They may be unaware of what their children need in September. They may be coasting or struggling through this. It does not fit the model of parenting. Some parents lean heavily on the schools for those day-to-day things and that support. The trusted teacher who guided them through the process is not available in the summer.  I have one last question to raise. I have raised it at the committee previously and it is still a considerable concern of mine because I do not think it has been adequately addressed. So much of providing for special needs, English as an additional language, ADL, and allocations, is built on enrolment in schools that is geared around Ukrainian children who came here during the war. If a peace deal is struck there, and we all hope it will be, the EU directive allowing them to be here will be rescinded in March 2027. In some schools, that will have a minor effect but in others, in Clare and other west of Ireland counties, half of the children enrolled will leave. That will cave in the whole system. Have the witnesses models for that scenario? Allocations could change instantly if half the school leaves.

Ms Angela Corcoran  We are always looking forward and trying to anticipate what will happen. As the Deputy said, we all hope there is peace and that those children and their families are allowed to return to their homes. It is a matter we are looking at. We will provide the supports that are available. We will work with schools. There is a risk. We know that numbers in primary schools are reducing anyhow. We will work with schools to see what we can do. It is a matter of demographics. It is a challenge.

An Cathaoirleach  The number of enrolments in Kilshanny National School in Clare doubled. The Ukrainian kids there have been fantastic, but everything is built around that enrolment number. There is a whole support model. If there were to be peace, the enrolment number would halve in the middle of the school year. I do not think that has been adequately modelled for.  I am conscious that others want to come in. I will conclude. There will be time for others to close out. Our deputy chairman is calling on me to conclude. He usually makes a speech after doing that. I call Senator Scahill. I did not know he was next. I will get my hammer out.

Senator Gareth Scahill  I am sorry that I had to run up to the Chamber for a few moments. Eileen mentioned collaboration with different organisations, the Department and the NCSE. I might have to cut my contribution short because I see there is a vote in the Seanad. Where Oide is supporting teachers, what is the engagement like between it, the Department and the NCSE in terms of the planning process and how recommendations are made? That is where I would like to go.
Ms Lisa Kelly  Is the Senator addressing that to me or to Ms Guerin? I think he said "Eileen".
Senator Gareth Scahill  I was addressing you. I am sorry.
Ms Lisa Kelly  I am Lisa.
Senator Gareth Scahill  I apologise.

Ms Lisa Kelly  That is no problem at all. We in Oide work closely with the NCSE, NEPS and wider stakeholders. All of our professional learning is prepared through a high-quality design process, which involves collaboration with the organisations I have mentioned, as well as other stakeholders. As part of that design and quality assurance process, every piece of professional learning is put through a design review phase, during which stakeholders and representatives of the NCSE, NEPS, the inspectorate and other stakeholders attend to ensure that professional learning is supporting and enhancing supports to schools rather than overlapping. We work particularly closely with the NCSE around the SET training I have talked about for the post-primary level. There are level 1 and level 2 learning programmes, as has been mentioned. The wider curriculum flexibility that exists is based on a learning outcomes-based curriculum at primary and post-primary levels. We work very closely to ensure that SET training is complementary to what they are receiving from the NCSE rather than overlapping.

Senator Gareth Scahill  To follow up on the reference to collaboration, the Department would have good visibility of enrolment numbers in individual schools at a much earlier stage of the year. I know in my own home county, we had a few school closures. Those schools will not be opening again in September. That was well flagged early in the year. I was working with a few schools around their allocation of SETs and SNAs. They were not happy with their allocation and yet the schools that were closing were given allocations. I am wondering about the collaboration between the Department and the NCSE in that regard.
Mr. Kieran Rogers  The allocations were prepared last February. At that point, final decisions about the closure of schools had not been made.
Senator Gareth Scahill  For 2026?
Mr. Kieran Rogers  Yes.
Senator Gareth Scahill  The Department would have had visibility of enrolments much earlier than that.
Mr. Kieran Rogers  The allocations were prepared in February 2026 for the 2026-27 school year.
Senator Gareth Scahill  Right.
Mr. Kieran Rogers  The final decision on the closure of a school was not made at that point.
Senator Gareth Scahill  "Final" is the key word there, even though we all knew.

Mr. Kieran Rogers  A small allocation was made to those schools because it would guarantee within the model that every school would get a small allocation. There were five hours allocated to those schools. As soon as the closure happened, those hours went back into the model.

Senator Gareth Scahill  That was hard for some of the schools that were trying to appeal these allocations. Everybody knew that certain schools were closing. They were getting allocations while other schools were fighting for the few additional allocations. It comes back to clarity and communication.

Mr. Kieran Rogers  On the SET review side of things, over 80% of schools submitted reviews. They were undertaken by the NCSE. Where an additional need was identified, additional hours were allocated to those schools, ranging from 2.5 hours per week to 25 hours per week. Any school that has a concern about its allocation should submit a review. The NCSE will recommend a quantum of additional hours. In every case where there is a recommendation for an increase, that increase is granted straight away and is available before the start of the next school year.

Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh  We recently heard from a principal. Perhaps it was last week. She highlighted that schools already have a lot of detailed and relevant data to hand. She was quite convincing on this point. There are support plans, etc. The data could be used to allocate accurately and efficiently. She highlighted the need to use the data and to trust the principals that they know exactly what their school needs. There is a lot of information on the post-primary online database, P-POD. Has it been considered at all that there should be a way for the principals of the schools to share the data?

Mr. Kieran Rogers  I mentioned earlier that there is an exercise going on at the moment whereby we are undertaking visits to schools to look at the data that is available. For the further development of the model, the goal is to get greater input from schools through the feeding in of data. Work is going on in that space at the moment. The key thing is that we need to ensure there is consistent and accurate data coming in to feed into the model. That work is under way with schools.

Mr. John Kearney  The consistency piece that Mr. Rogers alludes to is important. It also picked up on the very significant work that the inspectorate had done in recent times in terms of the consistency and the quality benchmarks right across the system. As Mr. Rogers has alluded to, it is about finding out what information can be discerned from schools, but then there is the support provision to schools so there is consistency, fairness and credibility across the system in terms of resource provision.

Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh  Go raibh maith agat. Will the Department outline its position in relation to children with Down's syndrome seeking class places? I have had a couple of families contact me both last year and this year. They feel there is a lack of provision for these children. They do not feel it is appropriate for them to be in mainstream classes. There is a lot more talk now about the redesignation of the mild or general learning disability schools. Will the Department outline its position on that le do thoil?

Ms Angela Corcoran  In terms of special class provision, we have announced 584 classes this year. It is a very robust and very strong commitment from the Department to meeting the needs of children through special classes. While many of them are for autism, that is because that is where the demand is. We generally find that there is adequate supply there of places for children with other conditions. It is not something that has been expressed as a huge difficulty with us. It is all about working with parents and children to secure an appropriate place for their child. That may sometimes be in mainstream with the right support. Special classes are available there.

Ms Helen Walsh  I thank the Deputy for the question. I understand their concerns because they are probably looking at what Ms Corcoran has just described, which is so many classes for children with autism. I was getting nervous though that with the mainstream they may not see it or they may be losing confidence within that context. We have to really consider what this means for them and why they are bringing those concerns forward.  With the data we gathered this year we are looking at how to capture a child who may have Down's syndrome and very often a cognitive challenging profile for them. We are trying to capture that as best we can this year. It is not that we do not open classes for children who have that profile; it is that we do not open classes specifically for children with Down's syndrome. We look more at the cognitive profile. Hopefully in our data this year we might see a rise in that number coming forward. Parents last year may not have been as aware of it as they will be this year. We have engaged with Down Syndrome Ireland on it as well, which is a valuable stakeholders to us, to understand the needs of those parents and of those children, to have a look at what provision might look like for them, and again to work with schools to support their children in as inclusive a manner as possible.

An Cathaoirleach  That concludes members' questions. I am conscious that we are all against the clock but there may have been questions or remarks the witnesses did not get to close out. If it is okay we will go down along the row of seats if anyone wants to comment, or maybe they do not have comments to make. Witnesses may have a minute or so each if they just want to close out bits that needed a bit of closure.

Ms Lisa Kelly  The special education teacher, SET, training was brought up by Senators and Deputies today. SET teachers are involved in Oide's professional learning days at both primary and post-primary level. While our provision is curricular based, which we talked about today, a large portion of that curricular-based professional learning is around supporting teachers to support all students in their classes. As our colleague, Ms Walsh, mentioned today, every teacher needs to be upskilled and have the tools to support all of those children, including those with special educational needs. While it is not specific, the specific training is at post-primary at the moment, Oide's wider professional learning is always cognisant of the needs of those teachers within the wider teacher population.
An Cathaoirleach  Does Ms Guerin wish to make any final remarks?

Ms Ellen Guerin  The National Educational Psychological Service plans to continue to offer a comprehensive service delivery to all of the schools and to combine our model of casework with support and development work into the future for school communities.

Mr. Brendan Doody  I have nothing to add beyond welcoming the opportunity to engage with the committee and colleagues on the disability committee on the forum. I think the forum will be a really important next step in this journey towards inclusive education.
An Cathaoirleach  Absolutely.

Ms Angela Corcoran  A general point that I failed to mention is the national training programme for special needs assistants. It is really important that this gets a mention because 4,200 SNAs have completed that course over the past four to five years. This is a reflection of the commitment of SNAs to training, which I mentioned already. I thank the committee for its work and members' interest in special education. I am sure I speak for everybody here when I reiterate our commitment as a Department to progressing an inclusive education and to ensuring that every child feels supported in school and can attend and participate fully in schools. All of our work is undertaken with that objective in mind.
Mr. Kieran Rogers  I have nothing further to add other than to thank the committee for its time.
An Cathaoirleach  I thank Mr. Rogers.

Ms Helen Walsh  I just want to acknowledge the depth of the questions that always come from members of this committee. I really value the depth of those and the care for all of their constituents that triggers those type of questions. I wish to emphasise the future of professional learning for our teachers, our SET teachers and for our SNAs moving into the future. The National Council for Special Education intends to meet those professionals where they are at. Our support of them within professional learning within our service delivery model is interdisciplinary. It will be wraparound for schools. I also acknowledge the work of special schools across the State over the past year. They cater for and support our most complex children in so many ways. I just want to acknowledge their work and thank the committee.

Mr. John Kearney  I will pick up on the point the Cathaoirleach and many other committee members raised previously. I wish to reaffirm to everybody, and to parents in particular, that there are two aspects to the portal: the planning and the provision aspect itself. There were concerns this time last year in relation to the portal and timelines, but 7,860 parents came to us for 1 October and many more came after that. I concur with the Cathaoirleach's contribution in relation to the supportive role of schools in the assisting of that. There are wider communication aspects in trying to reach out to parents. We are leaving no stone unturned in that regard. We are very much co-ordinating with our Department of Education and Youth colleagues and liaising with the children's disability network teams right across the country. There is a social media campaign. We are working with the National Parents Council and the various advocacy groups, and a parental webinar is being held in relation to that. We also have enhanced the efficiency and effectiveness of the portal and it is now a very transparent process that take in the region of just five to seven minutes for parents to complete the portal entry. We are aware there are some issues in relation to parents, but again we will not leave any stone unturned in getting to them.  I concur with the comments of my colleagues here. The breadth and depth of the committee has to be commended, as well as the unique ability to look at the most challenging of systemic issues right down to the transfer of individual school operational data. I commend the level of rigour and attention to detail from the committee, under the Cathaoirleach's stewardship, in assisting the national discussion on inclusive education.

An Cathaoirleach  On behalf the committee I thank all of our witnesses. The NCSE's Oireachtas email service has been excellent of late. A few members have mentioned that. We have parliamentary questions but the Department emails have improved a lot and that is appreciated.  I thank all of the witnesses from the Department and from the different agencies represented here for what they do for education and, most importantly, what they do for inclusive education. From talking with the witnesses individually - and sometimes we google who they are - I know they have a lifelong interest in this. They do not just come in here as a clocking-in exercise. They are playing a fully invested role in each of the bodies they represent. We appreciate that they come here to drive on the agenda of special education. On behalf of students and parents, we thank all of them for that. I thank them again for being here today and for their testimony. I thank members too, as this is our final meeting of the summer. We will not be back until September, unless something profound happens in the country, but you never know.  I particularly thank the unsung heroes. We always hear the members' voices but we have Tara, Tetiana and Patricia, who do a colossal amount of work. They are the first point of engagement for all of us. The amount of work that goes into co-ordinating some of this stuff is colossal given the paperwork and the notes they prepare for us and it is massively appreciated by all members. On behalf of the committee I just want to sincerely thank them, as well as the technical team in the room who make all these meetings possible. We will start with one item that was deferred from last week's meeting. The next is No. R2026/0353, dated 2 July 2026, is correspondence received from the chief executive officer of Inland Fisheries Ireland, IFI, in response to the committee's request for further information in relation to external media communications training. Do members wish to comment on that? No. I have a brief comment to make. There was a lot of concern when got the breakdown of the figures for media training by IFI before it attended the committee. It was €53,933, which was excessive and extensive. It gave a breakdown and had provided a breakdown in relation to that previously. In this new correspondence, it gives additional costs. The additional legal costs in preparation for that meeting with us were €16,768, excluding VAT. For one appearance before the public accounts committee, it cost over €70,000. That is not including the VAT for the legal costs. It is extraordinary. Given some of the difficulties stemming from our engagements with IFI, it is excessive. There needs to be lessons learned from that. No one is saying that legal advice cannot be taken but when we take it as a whole, over €70,000 for media training and all associated costs is excessive.

Deputy James Geoghegan  I do not know why it is giving us the figure, excluding VAT. We are not its accountants. At the end of the day, this was 23%. It was €85,000 or close to €90,000 to attend the public accounts committee. Can we imagine if every single witness that came before the committee spent €90,000 to prepare to come before us? This committee would be a laughing stock in the sense that we would be increasing taxpayer spend just by scrutinising the taxpayer spend.
An Cathaoirleach  It is extraordinary.
Deputy James Geoghegan  It is farcical and frustrating. I do not know what else we can say in relation to this but it is just absolutely appalling.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  If you calculate the hours spent in preparation for a two- to three-hour meeting, it was probably ten times that in preparing for that, which, in and of itself, as a second meeting, really raises questions as to the sincerity in which IFI came before us the second time. How far are we willing to push this, though, in terms of a recommendation? Should we ask the Department of public expenditure to issue a circular to all bodies saying, "You are not permitted to spend money on training or preparing for Oireachtas committee meetings"? It is not an appropriate use of taxpayer money. It is as simple as that. When you appear before any Oireachtas committee, I am of the opinion that we could ask at least for the Department of public expenditure's opinion on this as a starting point to see if that is what we should do.
An Cathaoirleach  Yes, absolutely.

Deputy Paul McAuliffe  I refer the committee back to the correspondence we had from the Department of public expenditure - I think it was two weeks ago - in which it said training is provided for members of the public service or the Civil Service appearing before Oireachtas committees. I do not think any of us take for granted that coming before an Oireachtas committee and appearing on live TV is an onerous task that is not part of people's everyday tasks. I therefore have absolutely no problem with people preparing maybe their own training, but what is here is anything but training. What is here is an organisation trying to get its story straight before it comes before this committee, and the same systemic problems it has displayed in so many other areas appear to have been displayed in this correspondence. I just want to separate it out. This is unusual. I do not think this is something that happens for all witnesses who come before us. It is an example of the significant issues that arise in this organisation and why this committee needs to continue to examine them.

Deputy Cathy Bennett  It is an incredible waste of taxpayers' money that up to €90,000 was spent on social media or for IFI to come in here and appear before us and for everything that happened in advance of that. I want a question to go back: was there procurement? At over €25,000, there should be procurement. I want to see whether other contractors were sought in relation to this because I do not believe there could have been in haste. We want people to come in here and to give us genuine delivery when we interview them, without haste.  I also want to ask what the Government is doing about this. Has a Government circular been sent to every organisation that has government funding? Is there a policy in place for media training? I want to know whether the Government has a circular in relation to all Departments. We have seen this right across the board. I refer to the number of people who have come in here and have had media training. I want to know whether the Government has released a circular in relation to that. Maybe it could be a question that would go out to every Department from this committee asking if the Government has released a circular on media training. If we were to add it up right across every organisation that receives government funding, as to whether they have had media training, the majority have said yes. I want to see if the Government is acting on this, what action has been put in place and what is going to happen going into the future.

Deputy Séamus McGrath  A lot has been said and I just want to add my voice. It is a disturbing waste of public money, to be perfectly frank, and it brings to the fore a culture of total disregard for the appropriate use of public money, effectively. We need to condemn it in the strongest possible terms as a committee. We also need to send a message that this is going to be a question we will be asking State agencies in future when they come before us, that we will be putting a spotlight on this in terms of the use of public money for communications or other training in advance of appearances here, because we simply cannot tolerate this.

An Cathaoirleach  I agree with all those comments. It is an insult to the integrity of this committee. Previous correspondents have actually said they got media training because there was nearly an ask from this committee that they review their communications strategy following their first appearance. It was a criticism of their failure to engage the first time they were here. The question was asked, "What media training did you get? Maybe you need to question how effective that was." That was not a blank cheque for them to go out and spend this amount of money on training. It speaks of systemic issues within the organisation and is completely unacceptable. As a committee, we need to look at this issue in the whole because I do not think it is just an issue particular to IFI. I propose that we write to each Department and agencies under their bodies because, yes, we have these bodies coming before us but they also appear before other Oireachtas committees. Is there outsourcing? Is additional media training given before they appear before all those committees? We need to see the total cost to the State for appearing not just before the public accounts committee but before all the Oireachtas joint committees. I propose that we write to each Department asking for details as to what external media training they and the agencies under their remit have received before appearing before any Oireachtas committee. We should look at it. Someone mentioned recommendations. It is an issue of grave concern, and that is not criticising some organisations that do need assistance, but there is assistance given. We have written to the Department of public expenditure in the past and it has come back and provided us information on existing training and assistance that can be provided. As to why that is not being availed of, we need to ask that question.

Deputy James Geoghegan  People are looking for accountability on this issue. It is important to remember that IFI has a board, and the members of that board should really be looking at themselves if this issue did not come to the attention of the board as to the appropriateness of that spend. It is supposed to hold to account the executive of that organisation as to how it spends its money. As to how any board member sitting on a State board could think it appropriate to spend up to €90,000 to appear before a public accounts committee, they really have to look themselves in the mirror. This is a new CEO. We should write to the new CEO and ask, "Do you think this was an appropriate level of spend to appear before a public accounts committee?" We should hear from the new CEO. Let us hope that cultural change is taking place, that board members take note of this and that change is happening in IFI, because this just beggars belief.
An Cathaoirleach  This correspondence is from Dr. Eamonn Kelly.
Deputy James Geoghegan  That is right.
Deputy Cathy Bennett  To conclude-----
An Cathaoirleach  Just briefly, Deputy Bennett.

Deputy Cathy Bennett  Can we just ensure that we seek clarity on procurement and on whether circulars have gone from the Government to boards to ensure that they are not spending this amount of money on media training?
An Cathaoirleach  Okay. I think the question about procurement was answered in IFI's initial correspondence.
Deputy Cathy Bennett  So did IFI get procurement for this?

Deputy Séamus McGrath  I have a suggestion. No doubt other entities coming before us spend money on pre-session training, and we do not always ask that question because we are often discussing a lot of issues when they come before us. Would it be an idea that, as a matter of course, we ask that question in our pre-session correspondence, "Please provide information on any pre-session training, communications, legal, etc.", to everyone who comes before us prior to their coming before us to provide clarification on that issue? It is something we should consider.

An Cathaoirleach  That may be an issue when we issue the invite, that we can ask for in communication, whether it is a briefing note or whatever, which all bodies send in advance, and that they can touch on that and the cost. Deputy Grace Boland  The NTA's witness statement for today states that it is the approving authority while Irish Rail is the sponsoring authority, but I am totally confused when it comes to the buses because the NTA is acquiring the buses. R2026/0370 is correspondence received from the Secretary General of the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment in response to the committee’s request for further information following the meeting on 21 May 2026, dated 10 July 2026. Do members wish to comment? Is it agreed to note and publish the item? Agreed.  R2026/0371 is correspondence received from the Secretary General of the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation in response to the committee’s request for the attendance of a representative from the Office of the Government Chief Information Officer, OGCIO, on 16 July 2026, dated 8 July 2026. Do members wish to comment? I will make a brief comment on this because there was a request from us for a representative from the OGCIO to attend this meeting. We know the role it is supposed to play in terms of oversight of IT expenditure and programmes. It speaks volumes that it has essentially said that it does not see a role for itself in attending this critically important meeting, which will discuss a massive failure of an IT project that has led to a write down of €50 million. For the Department to come back and essentially say that it does not see a role for anyone from the OGCIO to attend here today to answer questions speaks volumes about why we are in the mess we are in.

Deputy Grace Boland  This goes back to a point I raised at our meeting in January with the NTA. This project was not classed as an IT project. It was classed as a building project notwithstanding the fact that the purpose of the building was train control. The software was actually the key part of delivering this project but, for some reason, under the various circulars, it was classed as a building project rather than an IT project. That is a point we raised with the NTA in January along with the Department. Something is seriously wrong with that. It leads us to wonder whether there are any other IT projects that are classed as something else when, in essence, the purpose of them is an IT deployment.

Deputy James Geoghegan  Deputy Boland raised a very important point. If we contrast the ICT project in the Arts Council with the ICT project in Irish Rail, as I recall, there was engagement between the OGCIO and the Arts Council as problems emerged. Admittedly, the Department and the OGCIO were very quick to make it clear that, ultimately, the responsibility lay with the Arts Council in respect of that project but there was engagement and there was some kind of formal role. As Deputy Boland said, it is that lack of clarity when it comes to State bodies as to what role, if any, is played by the OGCIO and at what the stage it has any function whatsoever. As Deputy Boland said, it appears with this project, it did not have any role or function and it is not clear why that is the case.

Deputy Paul McAuliffe  I can understand why the OGCIO is looking at the way we are examining these projects and is thinking, "We don't want to be before the public accounts committee every week," but what is clear is that we were inviting it as a representative body. The fact that it would be here and give evidence that there was no engagement or that it had not been consulted is important because many of the issues regarding these schemes result from very poor planning at the outset. I can understand the case the OGCIO is making regarding each body having its own fiduciary responsibility and so on. That was not the remit under which we sought to bring it before the Committee of Public Accounts. We sought to bring it here to provide assistance to the committee. We need to clarify the OGCIO's remit and role with it and make clear why we are inviting it here. It is disappointing that it does not have somebody present.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  This relates to our work as a committee regarding analysis of ICT projects overall.  We need to include quite a specific piece of work from the Office of the Government Chief Information Officer, OGCIO. It is a common thread in many of the cases, be those ones where, as Deputy Geoghegan said, support was sought but was not forthcoming or where, by way of miscategorisation, it was not involved in the project. We are not learning the lessons if we do not stop and look. Our work examining ICT infrastructure overall is a real opportunity to highlight that. State bodies, including Departments, do not have the intrinsic competency to get briefs right when it comes to ICT projects. That is proven across the board now. My understanding is that is where the OGCIO should step in an provide competency. If is not being utilised or offered, we have big problems here. I ask that we consider that as part of our ongoing work with ICT infrastructure.

Deputy Cathy Bennett  There is the underlying issue that no one is taking responsibility. The Department of public expenditure and the OGCIO are doing nothing to alleviate this. No action is being taken. As far as I remember, the Arts Council sought support at the time – they did not get that help. It is an underlying issue running across all Departments. The Government has to take responsibility here. This is money that taxpayers have paid into the system that Departments are giving out and for which there is no accountability. Every day we come into this committee, we see it. Ministers need to take responsibility for the Departments they are over. We cannot go around blaming the OCGIO, the Arts Council or any other entity. The Government and Departments need to take responsibility for where Government funding is going.

An Cathaoirleach  It also says in the correspondence that because Irish Rail is a commercial semi-State body, it does not see a role for itself. That adds another concern. It is an issue we will return to. I will let the Comptroller and Auditor General’s office come in.

Ms Colette Drinan  It is just to draw attention to the circular that governs the arrangements for oversight of digital and ICT-related initiatives that was issued in 2021. It sets out whom it applies to. It applies to all Votes and centrally funded public services bodies, and then to non-commercial State bodies with a turnover of more than €5 million. Maybe there is a piece there around the applicability of that.
Deputy Grace Boland  What is that?
Ms Colette Drinan  It is Circular 14/2021.

Deputy Grace Boland  I asked the NTA about that circular in January and was told it did not apply because the project was a €150 million project and it was a building, notwithstanding the fact that the ultimate aim of the project was to deliver the software for the traffic management system. The NTA said it did not fall under that because it was classifying it as a capital build.
Ms Colette Drinan  If it was classified as ICT, the fact that it is a commercial State body could create a difficulty as well. I take the point.

An Cathaoirleach  Is it agreed to note the item and follow up on the issues identified? Agreed. Deputy Joanna Byrne  I was not sure if it was in the B or C section. There has been significant public debate on whether Ireland should fulfil these fixtures against Israel. Moving on to reports, the committee is publishing its interim report on the national children’s science centre today. The report examines matters relating to the development of the proposed national children’s science centre. This interim report is being launched following a comprehensive piece of work into this debacle. It is a saga that has dragged on for more than two decades. The report lays bare a deeply concerning picture. More than €4.2 million has already been spent on planning and legal costs, with further legal costs still to be finalised. The estimated construction costs had risen to more than €70 million when last costed two years ago in 2024. This excludes the fit-out costs estimated at around €19 million in 2022 and a further €30 million in State support over ten years for operational and exhibit renewal.  Despite these escalating costs, the project still has no sponsoring Government Department and no funding allocated under the national development plan, and yet the Office of Public Works remains legally obliged to continue progressing the project, with work already under way to prepare for a tender process to be completed by the end of 2026. We know that over €22,000 has recently been paid to technical consultants as part of this process. Every day that this situation continues, more money continues to be spent, despite there being no credible pathway to delivering the project.  The committee's central conclusion is clear that an urgent political intervention is now required. The Government cannot continue, in my view, to bury its head in the sand while public funds are exposed to mounting costs and increasing legal risk. The issues at the heart of this project will not be resolved by the parties currently involved acting alone. Without decisive Government leadership and a clear political decision, the State faces continued uncertainty, further delays and even greater costs to the taxpayer.  We have examined the evidence, published our findings and made very clear recommendations, with six recommendations in total. A couple of the key recommendations include that the committee considers that the matters identified during its examination are unlikely to be resolved through engagement between the parties alone and will require consideration at an appropriate level across government. The committee recommends that the OPW and the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation and other relevant Departments engage directly and as a matter of priority with representatives of the national children's science centre, with a view to identifying a way forward for the project or a way to end any commitment to the project while minimising any cost to the State.  Another key recommendation is that the committee recommends that prior to any significant further commitment of public resources, the OPW undertakes a comprehensive assessment of the project's costs, benefits, governance arrangements, operational model, long-term funding requirements and value for money, including an assessment of the financial, legal and contractual implications of terminating or withdrawing from the project, and that issues relating to sponsorship, governance and funding be clearly identified and assessed.  It is clear that no further public money should be committed until a comprehensive assessment is completed. In my view the responsibility now rests with the Government and, in particular, with the Minister for public expenditure, Deputy Chambers, along with the Minister of State with responsibility for the OPW, Deputy Moran. Ultimately, we cannot continue to ignore this massive and growing liability to the State. Action must be taken now to protect money, bring all the parties together and finally bring this long-running saga to an end, one way or another. I will now open it up to members and invite the Leas-Chathaoirleach, Deputy McAuliffe, to come in first.

Deputy Paul McAuliffe  I thank the clerk and the staff of the committee for putting together this interim report. It is worth noting that it is unusual for the committee to issue an interim report but it was said clearly at one of our hearings that this issue demanded that somebody cry stop. In issuing this interim report this is what the committee is doing.  A number of the observations are worth highlighting. A project that initially started out as a community gain project as part of an overall development has escalated, according to observation No. 6, to a project of nearly €70 million. This has resulted in a creeping obligation which has been governed by the OPW. This was done in the absence of any sponsoring Department or authority. It was done on behalf of the OPW itself. The recommendations lay squarely on the OPW the responsibility of resolving this, although we know it will require Government action for it to happen. Two of the observations refer to the substantial costs of €1.15 million in regard to arbitration and legal fees and a total cost of nearly €4 million in regard to money spent on a project that essentially does not exist.  I have to say I think the recommendations are very strong and the one that is most compelling is recommendation No. 3, which recommends that the OPW engages directly as a matter of priority with representatives from the national children's science museum to find a way either to end the project or minimise the costs to the State. Deputy Cathy Bennett  I thank everybody for compiling the report and for their hard work on it. There are good recommendations in it. I especially feel recommendation No. 1 is particularly important as it simply states that the committee feels the matter at hand requires consideration at the appropriate level across government. I feel the appropriate level across government would be that the Cabinet and Ministers take responsibility for it. Ms Anne Shaw ( Chief Executive Officer, National Transport Authority ) called and examined.

An Cathaoirleach  This morning, we engage with the National Transport Authority, NTA, and Iarnród Éireann to resume discussion on the National Transport Authority's 2024 financial statements. On behalf of the committee I would like welcome officials from the NTA: Ms Anne Shaw, chief executive officer, and Mr. Hugh Creegan, deputy chief executive officer and director of transport, planning and investment. From Iarnród Éireann, we are joined by Ms Mary Considine, chief executive officer, and Mr. Paul Hendrick, director of capital investments. We are also joined by Mr. Tomás Campbell, principal officer at the heavy rail investments division of the Department of Transport, who is attending in a representative capacity. Finally, we are joined by officials from the Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General, including Ms Colette Drinan, secretary and director of audit, on behalf of the C and AG, who is a permanent witness to the committee, and Ms. Georgina O'Mahony, deputy director of audit. The witnesses are all very welcome.  Before we begin, I wish to explain some limitations to parliamentary privilege and the practice of the Houses as regards references you may make to other persons in your evidence. The evidence of witnesses physically present or who give evidence from within the parliamentary precincts is protected pursuant to both the Constitution and statute by absolute privilege. This means that you have an absolute defence against any defamation action for anything you say at the meeting. However, you are expected not to abuse this privilege and it is my duty as Cathaoirleach to ensure that this privilege is not abused. Therefore, if your statements are potentially defamatory in relation to an identifiable person or entity, you will be directed to discontinue your remarks. It is imperative that you comply with any such direction. Witnesses are also reminded of the long-standing parliamentary practice that they should not criticise or make charges against any person or entity, by name or in such a way as to make him, her or it identifiable, or otherwise engage in speech that might be regarded as damaging to the good name of the person or entity.  I now invite Ms Drinan to deliver her opening statement on behalf of the Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General.

Ms Colette Drinan  The National Transport Authority’s financial statements for 2024 were previously examined at a meeting of the Committee of Public Accounts on 15 January 2026. At that meeting, the Comptroller and Auditor General outlined the main features of the authority’s financial situation. He also summarised the evolution of the national train control centre project up to mid-2025, drawing attention to the ongoing delays in relation to development of the train management system and the anticipated cost overrun associated with the project, projected then to be in the order of 28%.  Further review of the train control project was undertaken in the context of the audit of the authority’s financial statements for 2025. The Comptroller and Auditor General certified the 2025 financial statements on 17 June 2026. Once the financial statements are received by the Department of Transport, the Minister has statutory responsibility for their presentation to the Oireachtas.

An Cathaoirleach  I now call invite the chief executive officer to deliver the opening statement on behalf of the NTA. Ms Shaw, as set out in the letter of invitation, you have five minutes to make your opening statement.

Ms Anne Shaw  I thank the committee for the invitation to appear before it today to continue its consideration of the National Transport Authority's 2024 financial statements. This is with particular focus on the national train control centre project and the associated traffic management system contract. I am joined by Mr. Hugh Creegan, deputy chief executive and director of transport planning at the NTA, and I also welcome representatives of Iarnród Éireann, the delivery agency for the national train control centre. Together, we will seek to address the committee's questions fully and transparently, where possible, recognising that some issues remain commercially and legally sensitive. We have provided a detailed briefing document and other information as part of our submission last Friday.  It is worth clarifying the NTA's responsibilities in relation to major transport investment projects. The NTA is the statutory body responsible for the planning, provision and funding of public transport and active travel infrastructure. We also act as the approving authority for major public transport investment programmes, including BusConnects, DART+, MetroLink and the national train control centre programme.  The Government's infrastructure guidelines clearly distinguish between the roles of the sponsoring agency and the approving authority. Under these arrangements, the sponsoring agency is responsible for the planning, procurement, contract management and delivery of a project, including the achievement of its approved scope, budget, programme and intended benefits. The approving authority is responsible for funding the project, approving key decisions at defined stages of delivery and overseeing implementation through appropriate reporting and assurance arrangements.  In its role as approving authority, the NTA provides oversight of delivery of the capital programme by the various sponsoring agencies, and reports progress to the Department of Transport through the major projects governance oversight group. We work closely with project delivery bodies to address risks, assess proposed changes and consider any implications for budgets, delivery schedules and the wider investment portfolio.  Many major transport investments continue to progress successfully, including BusConnects which continues to advance, with all 12 core bus corridors having received planning permission and construction under way on two schemes, plus the procurement of a third corridor to commence shortly. The DART+ programme also continues to advance with confirmed railway orders and construction procurement under way. MetroLink has also received planning consent and is now moving into its procurement and construction stage. Active travel investment is also delivering a large number of benefits.  The NTA is also investing in new bus depots to support service expansion, with the Jamestown depot now operational, planning consent secured for a new bus depot in Blanchardstown, a new Go-Ahead Ireland depot opening shortly in Northwest Business Park in Dublin, and the Tivoli depot in Cork due to open in quarter 3 of 2026. In the case of the National Train Control Centre programme, the NTA is the approving authority and Iarnród Éireann is the sponsoring agency. Accordingly, while the NTA is responsible for funding, oversight and approval at key decision points, responsibility for the delivery and procurement of the contract is with Iarnród Éireann. The committee is rightly concerned about the write-down reported by Iarnród Éireann and the delays affecting the traffic management system project. Let me be clear that the NTA takes these issues extremely seriously. Protecting public funds and ensuring value for money are central to our assessment of all requests and recommendations from sponsoring agencies.  Over the lifetime of the project, Iarnród Éireann, with the support of the NTA, has sought to address delivery challenges through revised programmes and alternative implementation strategies. While an alternative delivery model remained an option, no formal recommendation seeking such a change was made by the Iarnród Éireann board to the NTA until recently. Instead, Iarnród Éireann and the NTA engaged extensively with Indra to help to develop and implement revised delivery strategies to progress the project. These approaches were informed by commitments and actions by Indra to address issues on the project, recognising the risks inherent in all approaches. At the centre of these efforts was the objective of ensuring the successful delivery of a traffic management system capable of supporting both current operations and future network expansion.  Following its internal governance processes, Iarnród Éireann formally informed the NTA on 29 June of the decision by its board regarding the existing role of Indra and the proposed way forward. The NTA requested additional information on 30 June to support consideration of that decision by the NTA, including its board and capital programme committee. The NTA received this extensive supporting information, including project risks, privileged legal advice, potential liabilities, future delivery options and implications for the wider programme. As approving authority, the NTA considered the implications of Iarnród Éireann's decision for the overall project, as well as the wider capital programme. The evidence indicates that the supplier is unlikely to deliver the required system in full specification within any reasonable timeframe and an alternative delivery approach is needed. Given these ongoing costs, the matter was considered as a priority through the NTA's governance processes, and the NTA board has now accepted Iarnród Éireann's decision regarding the role of Indra going forward. This was communicated to Iarnród Éireann on 13 July.  Both organisations, together with the Department of Transport, will continue to assess the implications of this decision, including additional funding requirements for delivering the traffic management system within the overall rail investment budget envelope to achieve the best possible outcome. Separately, the NTA has commissioned an independent review of the project, which is due to report in September. The review will examine governance, delivery and project oversight arrangements within both Iarnród Éireann and the NTA, and identify lessons to strengthen the delivery of future major infrastructure projects and, in particular, technology projects. Committee members may also be aware of the next generation ticketing project, which is being delivered directly by the NTA with Indra as the supplier. I can confirm that this integrated ticketing project remains on budget and on schedule. The contracting mechanism is different from that of the NTCC contract, with payment due only to successful delivery of each of the 34 key milestones.  We understand the committee is also interested in progress in delivering bus fleet electrification and, in particular, the cost of buses in storage pending absorption into the fleet. This information is detailed in a note provided to the committee. While there have been delays in delivering charging infrastructure, accounting for these buses needing to be in storage, the costs incurred are offset by the avoidance of inflationary increases that would have arisen on later purchase of those buses. In the meantime, the buses are stored and maintained by the manufacturer to ensure they remain in optimal condition and are expected to be fully absorbed into both Dublin Bus and Bus Éireann fleets by quarter 1 of 2027. I welcome the opportunity to assist the committee today and to outline the actions being taken to protect public funds and secure the best outcome for the public.
An Cathaoirleach  I thank Ms Shaw. I will now ask Ms Considine to deliver the opening statement on behalf of Iarnród Éireann.

Ms Mary Considine  I thank the Cathaoirleach and committee members for the invitation to discuss matters relating to the National Train Control Centre, NTCC, project with the committee. Iarnród Éireann is at a time of record demand and record investment. The portfolio of projects that we are overseeing is progressing well in the main. However, the serious problems encountered with the traffic management system, TMS, contract with Indra are of deep concern to us as a management team and to our board. The project has reached a point where Iarnród Éireann has no certainty as to when the contractor will fulfil its contractual obligations, and no confidence in its ability to do so, despite the extensive and continuing efforts of Iarnród Éireann and the National Transport Authority as the approving agency.  I have detailed what the NTCC is and the progress with the other elements of that, which are all on time and on schedule. However, the delivery of the TMS, originally due to be completed in June 2024, is yet to be completed by Indra. The joint Iarnród Éireann-NTA appendix, which I have attached to this statement, details the extensive procurement process supported and advised by external subject matter specialists. Additionally, the NTA would have commissioned specialists to undertake an independent technical review of the TMS scope of services prior to providing approval to release the tender documents to the market. Ultimately, from seven pre-qualified suppliers, two bids were received in early 2019. Each bidder was required to submit a compliance matrix to demonstrate that their proposed product solution would meet a minimum of 70% of the system requirements without the need for further software development.  Indra's compliance document was assessed by our specialist consultants, which determined it would meet 96% of the contract requirements. This, together with its systems integration plan and references by it to a 15-year history of 21 successful deployments in multiple national railways, led us to believe that Indra had a mature developed product ready for deployment into Ireland with minimal additional software development required. Iarnród Éireann also engaged Turas to provide project management support services, and Ricardo Rail to provide system integration and safety assurance services to support the delivery of the contract.  Post contract award, and early in the preliminary design phase, Indra advised that its deployed TMS product would no longer be supportable over the life of the maintenance contract, and it would be upgraded to a newer version in 2021. It reassured Iarnród Éireann that the software would be developed in a manner that would support future safety certifications and that its "generic product", as it called it, would be delivered in 2021 prior to the commencement of the Irish TMS software development process. It should be noted that, as of today, to the best of our knowledge software supported by this generic product has yet to be deployed in any railway.  The timeline provided outlines how the issues impacting the TMS programme unfolded. Management ensured that our board and the NTA, as approving authority, and the Department of Transport through the major projects governance oversight group, MPGOG, were advised, and in the case of commercial resettlements that both our board and NTA approval were received. While the timeline is comprehensive, I would highlight two specific milestones. First, when the re-baselined programme requested by us in the end of 2023 and accepted in early 2024 was sliding significantly off-track by mid-2024, Iarnród Éireann advised the NTA of an increasing lack of confidence in Indra's ability to deliver the project. Indra agreed to the request of NTA and Iarnród Éireann to take steps to restore confidence, and an alternative delivery strategy was developed comprising the delivery of a minimum viable product initially, with full functionality to be delivered over eight phases. Second, by mid-2025, testing identified a number of systemic issues, and Indra's own independent safety assessor also confirmed that the software was not ready to be deployed into service.  We discussed a continuing lack of confidence in Indra with the NTA in mid-2025. The NTA, from that point, took a significantly more active role in project oversight and contract management, holding fortnightly meetings with Indra and Iarnród Éireann.  Notwithstanding that, Indra’s project delivery model was restricted to the commissioning of the Rosslare line, which the committee will see referred to as CP1. It is a relatively simple section of the network with minimal functionality representing approximately 3% of the project scope. A further 16-month delay in the CP1 commissioning milestone had been indicated by the end of 2025 and ultimately, in April 2026, Indra formally released its redeveloped CP1 software product to us for testing. It was immediately apparent, through our railway signalling principles testing, that many of the systemic issues that existed in 2025 remained and, in this context, our board took the decision to impair the carrying value of the asset in the financial statements for the year ending 31 December 2025, with the accounts submitted to the Department of Transport prior to publication.  Upon completion of the comprehensive testing process, it was concluded that the software was demonstrably not suitable for training or commissioning. Regrettably, therefore, six years on and two years after the original commissioning date, Indra still does not have a developed product fit for safe deployment on our rail network. On 22 June the Iarnród Éireann board reached decisions regarding the existing Indra contracts and the proposed way forward to deliver a necessary replacement of the existing signalling control system and we formally sought the approval of the NTA to implement those board decisions.  The committee will appreciate that, with the acceptance by the NTA of the decision relating to Indra, and as a result of sensitive commercial and legal considerations at this point, we may be unable to give absolute clarity on aspects of the decision at this time. I sincerely apologise to the committee for this in advance but I assure it that we are seeking to act in a way that can deliver the TMS component of this project in a manner that supports our wider investment programme, protects today's railway and minimises any future exposure of the taxpayer.  I am joined today by my colleague, Mr. Paul Hendrick, director of capital investment and we welcome questions from the committee.

An Cathaoirleach  Please note that we will suspend the meeting at approximately 12.30 p.m. for a short 15 minute break and resume shortly thereafter.  I open the floor to members. The lead speaker today is Deputy Paul Murphy, who has 15 minutes. All other members have ten minutes. If time permits, we will allow members in for a second round of shorter slots.

Deputy Paul Murphy  I thank the witnesses for coming before us and for the extensive briefing documents. One of the things that struck me was the diagram of a long saga, which has resulted in approximately €50 million of public money being effectively flushed down the drain and us still not being very far along on what we clearly desperately need in a new traffic management system.  My starting question is: who is responsible for this disaster? Where does responsibility lie?

Ms Anne Shaw  I will answer first. We have already clarified, in terms of the infrastructure guidelines, what the roles of each of the organisations are but both organisations continue to work together and collaborate for the successful delivery, in the same way as we work with all our sponsoring agencies on all our projects. The delivery of the project and contract that is in place sits with Irish Rail. That does not mean the NTA does not continue to support that work and provide oversight and advice as part of that. I do not know whether Ms Considine wants to add anything.

Ms Mary Considine  I thank Deputy Murphy. I can hear his frustration about where we are. There is deep regret right across Iarnród Éireann that we are in this position. However, as I outlined in my opening statement and as we detailed in the joint appendix, every opportunity has been given to the contractor to deliver. There has been significant support, including third party specialist support, to help it and we find ourselves in a very difficult position. The reality is that we now need to move at the earliest opportunity to make decisions that will allow us to put in place a traffic control system and minimise any further exposure of the Exchequer. We have a significant role to play in providing public transport and ensuring we have a reliable service and we want to future-proof the expansion of the railway. That is ultimately what we want to do in the most cost effective manner.

Deputy Paul Murphy  Sure. Effectively what the witnesses are saying is that Indra is responsible. Fine. I agree from what I have read that Indra screwed over Irish Rail, the NTA and the public but the question is why we signed such a contract that has allowed it to do so.  Let us go back to the start. There were two bidders for the contract, which seems like a small number. Who made the decision that Indra would get the contract?

Ms Mary Considine  There was an extensive procurement process, including market research, market consultation and engagement. Ultimately, seven bidders pre-qualified and two were appointed. They went through a technical review by the team and then Iarnród Éireann, in the determining of that, hired specialists, Ricardo rail, to advise it on the appointment. Separately, I understand, while I do not speak for the NTA, that the NTA hired Jacobs to review the tender. All of that was done.
Deputy Paul Murphy  Did the private company Ricardo make the decision?
Ms Mary Considine  No, it advised Iarnród Éireann.
Deputy Paul Murphy  Who made the decision?
Ms Mary Considine  Ultimately, it was Iarnród Éireann, based on a 242 page compliance document that Indra supplied, which showed it met 96% of the compliance criteria.
Deputy Paul Murphy  The board of Iarnród Éireann ultimately made the decision.
Ms Mary Considine  Yes, subject to the funding of the approving authority.

Deputy Paul Murphy  Was there appropriate technical expertise on the board to make that decision, including digital and IT expertise, to be able to make the decision that this was the correct bidder or was the board just led by what Ricardo said?

Ms Mary Considine  I believe there was appropriate experience on the board. I was not there at the time. I do not know whether my colleague can interject but we do rely on technical expertise for advice.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  I was not in the business at the time either but all the projects in this scenario go through a standard process. They go through a standard procurement evaluation and follow set criteria for the project team and any outside technical advisers the team has on the project. That leads to a recommendation based on a scoring system for that bid and the recommendation goes to the Irish Rail board for a decision.  The membership of the board changes from time to time based on tenure but there are typically one or two non-executive board directors who have technical backgrounds and then there are other business specialists. We would have to go back to check who was on the board at the time but we follow a set process.

Deputy Paul Murphy  When one reads through it, what seems to be a key factor is that, effectively, part of the contract says that the proposed product solution is to have a minimum of 70% of system requirements without the need for further software. That is part of the compliance matrix. Indra said not to worry about that, that it would do 96%. There would be 4% new but that it had this great thing, DaVinci 2.0, which is working elsewhere and that it could be used. Indra got the contract on that basis and then a few months later it said it turned out that they are not going to continue to support that product - it is Indra's product but it was not going to be able to continue to support it, which does not seem to make any sense; it seems to be a choice about obsolescence made by Indra - and that a new version, DaVinci 3.0, would be needed. Then, according to the project statement:  The project team, supported by expert consultant review from Turas and Ricardo Rail, [which designed the tender process in the first place] determined that Indra’s approach remained compliant with the TMS contract.  This seems to be at the heart of the problem. The tendering process was based on contractors having to have software already in place. Indra won the contract on the basis of having said it did and then after getting the contract, it said it would have to develop new software, yet that was found not to be a breach of the contract. Is that the core of the problem?
