Ms Mary Considine  I might refer - and then I will hand over to Mr. Hendrick for more detail - to 1.18 in our appendix document. As part of its bid, Indra outlined the technological evolution of its DaVinci 1.0 to DaVinci 2.0, that is how it evolved over the lifetime of the product. Therefore, that, with the advice our team sought from external experts, all led them to believe that Indra was still compliant with the contract. Specific advice was sought at the time from Ricardo and Turas to make sure Indra was still compliant with the original contract and that was the advice given to Iarnród Éireann.

Deputy Paul Murphy  Does that suggest there was a problem with the contract? Indra won the contract by saying it had the software and then said it would need new software and that would take a bunch of time. Iarnród Éireann still does not have it. This new software does not exist anywhere in the world according to the documents. Does that not indicate there was a problem with the contract?

Ms Mary Considine  Quite a number of assurances were given at the time that the company's generic product had already been in development since 2018. Safety assurance would have been got on that, and that feedback would have been given back.

Deputy Paul Murphy  Forget about those assurances. They are clearly worthless now so, in hindsight, was there a problem with the contract? Should we not have signed it, if it allowed the company to win it on one basis and then to say that it needed new software?

Ms Mary Considine  In reality, Indra is a multibillion-dollar company that provides systems all over the world. It pointed to its 15-year history of 21 successful redeployments all over the rail network globally. I was not there at the time but I spoke at length to our team, and there was no reason to believe that in the context of the bid put forward, which had gone through all the technical scrutiny and was passed by not only Irish Rail but also the specialists advising us, Indra was not developing its generic product, as it led us to believe, and that it was evolving situation.

Deputy Paul Murphy  Surely we should have had a contract that would not have left Irish Rail having to rely on Indra's good faith and on whether it believed things or not. We should surely have had a contract that said the company had to have the software already and could not be developing new software. Is that not a fundamental flaw here, that happened right at the start of the development of the contract? Ms Considine does not agree.
Ms Mary Considine  The advice to the company at the time did not agree with that.
Deputy Paul Murphy  Was that the advice to Irish Rail from Ricardo?
Ms Mary Considine  The advice provided to Irish Rail did not support terminating the contract.

Deputy Paul Murphy  Yes, but again, does this not go back to the point that this suggests there was a problem with the original contract? If the contract allowed Indra to win this competition on the basis that it had the software, and then the company was able to say it did not have the software, either it was in breach of the contract or there was a problem with the contract.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  We follow an open tender process, in the Official Journal of the European Union, OJEU, and have a competition open to the EU market to respond. There are a set of requirements in the contract that allows the open market to respond in the pre-qualification and bid stages. In the contract, Indra was, effectively, the designer hired. It was a design-and-build contract, so Indra was hired to deploy what is its system but to meet the client's requirements. In picking that process, we cannot overprescribe the solution we want. We have to have a set of output requirements in the contract to make it a compliant EU procurement process.  It was a surprise to the team when Indra moved from DaVinci 2.0 to DaVinci 3.0. That was not expected. I fully agree that was not expected to happen. In the discussions around it, it was seen as a normal product development process for these products, because there was previously a DaVinci 1.0. It was rolled out as part of a number of applications. Indra then moved to DaVinci 2.0, which it had been running for about ten years, and it was moving to the next version of it. The company was adamant that the next version was, effectively, going to continue to give the underlying 96% compliance and that it was going to be a better product than the previous one and the one it was going to support.  The experience we have had since that clearly shows that something has gone wrong between Indra moving from DaVinci 2.0 to DaVinci 3.0, which is where we are now, because if we got DaVinci 2.0 that other jurisdictions have, we should not be in the position we are in now. That is fully acknowledged.

Deputy Paul Murphy  Yes. In terms of lessons being learned, if we are just going to repeat the process of having these kinds of vague contracts that can be changed by companies that are just interested in maximising their own profit, we are going to repeat this experience again. Are there no lessons to be learned in terms of the type of contract signed?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  There absolutely are lessons to be learned and there is-----
Deputy Paul Murphy  Are there lessons about the contract?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  I do not see anything materially wrong with the contract itself. Going forward, I think we need to consider the process. The textbook would always say that you would do an open tendering process for major engineering and construction projects and go out and seek tenders from the open market. Those who can comply with the client requirements that have been put together would then have the ability to get into the evaluation process. If they succeed in the evaluation process, they win and you appoint them. That would be standard.  However, that is not always the right way to deliver a major engineering and construction project. An open tender process can sometimes lead to the potential issues we have experienced. A direct award approach or a direct discussion with a particular supplier who has a specific product that meets the needs of the business could be used. That is usually seen, however, as not being the default way to run a public procurement process for a major engineering project. We can definitely take on board lessons around the process. I would say that the contract, and how it was structured, was not an unusual one. I do not think there are any major-----
Deputy Paul Murphy  Is Irish Rail going to attempt to get back any of the €31 million we have given to Indra? Is there any prospect of that happening?

Ms Mary Considine  I know I am repeating what I said in my opening statement, but we are at a sensitive stage and looking at all options under legal advice. We will, however, be looking at everything to minimise the exposure for the taxpayer.

Deputy Paul Murphy  Indra has another contract, an integrated ticketing contract with the NTA. In its opening statement, the NTA said that the contracting mechanism is different from that for the NTCC contract, with payment due only following the successful delivery of each of 34 key milestones. Does that mean that the payment for this contract was not contingent on the delivery of key milestones?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  The contract we have is called a new engineering contract, NEC, target cost contract, which is quite a common contract used on major engineering projects in Ireland, the UK and the rest of Europe. It is also used for other contracts in the public transport sphere, including other schemes the NTA would oversee. The nature of this contract is such that it effectively shares any pain and gain up to a point. In other words, if a project is finished below the target price, the gain is shared between the contractor and the client, and if the project overruns against the target price, there is pain sharing, up to a cap, after which the supplier takes all the pain. It is also a contract that gives full visibility to the client team in terms of the actual resources and costs being incurred on the project. Effectively, interim progress payments are paid against those fully transparent costs.  We did, through commercial reset number two, as the Deputy might have seen in the statement, at the end of 2024, introduce additional performance milestones given our concerns. We actually had a bit of a hybrid contract at the end, where we had a combination of approaches. We did have a milestone approach in the end but, unfortunately, that milestone approach has not succeeded, obviously, in terms of how it turned out.

Deputy Paul Murphy  When we look at this, the number of private companies involved in it is quite something. A private company, Ricardo, is designing the contract. There is Turas, Indra obviously, and then this engineering company is brought in to look at it. Will Mr. Hendrick list all the private companies involved in this contract in one way or another?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  It is worth saying that in the context of the major projects we deliver, we have inside Iarnród Éireann a train operations business, which is pretty much a directly employed staff model, an infrastructure engineering business that manages the steady-state infrastructure and a mechanical rolling stock business that manages all the train fleets in terms of maintenance. Those are predominantly directly employed models where there are Irish Rail payroll staff. For major projects, though, and we must consider the cyclical nature of these, we did have a capital investments unit back in the 2000s. When the recession hit, that unit was closed. No capital was available.  We re-established the capital investments unit as a business in late 2018 as we were coming out of the austerity era. We have 200 staff on our books who work in that business, dedicated to developing and delivering major capital infrastructure projects. When the projects go to the delivery phase, we are much more market-facing, so we are reliant on the support of the supply chain in terms of the major contractors and professional advisers. We do not have the funding to be able to guarantee directly employing that level of staff because we are only funded on an annual basis. Each year, our funding could drop. We cannot guarantee that we will have any work for them.

Deputy Paul Murphy  Is this not the consequence of the hollowed-out neoliberal state, where everything is outsourced? Irish Rail is relying on one company to develop a contract and another company to fulfil it. The end result is that the public pays the price. Would it not be better value for money if Irish Rail actually had the appropriate staff to be able to do some of this management and so on?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  It is a balancing act. We have to try to strike a balance. This is a particularly niche project for the railway. It is a very complex project. The type of skill sets and people we need are not commonly available. Therefore, this type of project results in having to lean in more towards bringing in specialists temporarily because we could not guarantee that level of work for a niche, specialist project.
Deputy Paul Murphy  I thank Mr. Hendrick.

Deputy Joanna Byrne  I thank all the witnesses for joining us. I will stay with the procurement process for the moment. We have established that the board of Iarnród Éireann was responsible for awarding the contract after the procurement process. On the issue of due diligence, Iarnród Éireann's statement highlighted that Indra's system integration plan referenced a 15-year history of 21 successful deployments, which is understandable.  Iarnród Éireann sought specialist advice from Ricardo Rail before proceeding to contract stage. Am I right on that? Did Ricardo Rail do due diligence with regard to the delivery of projects that Indra claimed to have completed in other countries? Did Iarnród Éireann do that? Who was responsible for due diligence and for the reassurances that Indra was capable of doing what it had tendered for?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  The team that worked on the project right through from development to delivery was a hybrid team. There was Irish Rail staff on the team, supported or augmented by the specialist providers with expertise from Ricardo Rail. As part of the procurement process starting in 2015, they went through a market research stage to understand what suppliers were out there and what type of products and technologies were available on the market before putting the requirements together. That also involved an interested candidate who could potentially deliver the work coming to meet Irish Rail before the formal procurement process started, where it could engage in one-on-one discussions to understand what was possible. The market consultation was done once the process was started to look at the requirements and how we had set up the contract in order to make sure we got the right structure for delivering the project.

Deputy Joanna Byrne  There is a 15-year documented history that led to Indra winning the tender. It was awarded the contract in 2020. Shortly afterwards, in 2021, concerns were raised and difficulties arose with regard to commitments it was not able to fulfil in Lithuania. That is a short period, despite its supposedly long-standing history of being able to deliver. That is what I am trying to get at. Was the due diligence sufficient or were there downfalls in that regard? If there were, whose feet did they fall at?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Ultimately, Iarnród Éireann is responsible for the procurement, management and delivery of the project, irrespective of the support we have from the supply chain.

Deputy Joanna Byrne  Coming back to 2021, concerns were noticed at that stage. Iarnród Éireann was reassured in 2021 that the generic product would still be delivered, and it was not. Why did it take Iarnród Éireann until 2025 to raise concerns with the NTA and say it did not have confidence in the project being delivered?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  If we go through the whole project, there was regular interaction between Iarnród Éireann and NTA all the way through. There were monthly interactions. There were progress challenges on the project in 2022 and we put together the first commercial reset of the contract. That was done in conjunction with the NTA. As it is the approving authority, we do not make any of those arrangements without its approval. It has the right to reject any proposals and to support us if it thinks the proposal makes sense. We engaged with the NTA throughout the contract. On commercial reset number 1, where we extended the completion timeline by five months, we did it with the support of the NTA.  When we went through the delivery phase during 2023, the hardware was installed in the NTCC building, which was a positive progress milestone for Indra. It eventually completed the generic product, which its project was reliant on, in late 2023. That was another positive progress sign. However, the detailed software development, which only became visible to the project team in early 2024, is where we heard serious alarm bells as a project team. At that point, we escalated those concerns to the NTA to flag that we had done reset number 1, were four years into the project and had serious concerns about whether Indra would be able to successfully complete the project. We started that discussion in summer 2024, and then again in 2025.

Deputy Joanna Byrne  On a separate point, Spain's supreme court in May of this year upheld a €13.5 million fine against Indra for participating in a price-fixing and market-sharing cartel. This dates from an original judgment in 2023. Was Iarnród Éireann aware of that throughout 2023 to 2026?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  I am not sure.

Deputy Joanna Byrne  We are looking at a loss of tens of millions in Irish taxpayers' money to a company that engaged in cartel-like behaviour because of a decision made by Iarnród Éireann and insufficient due diligence as to the company's capability to deliver a project. What does Mr. Hendrick say to the Irish people in that regard?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  I cannot comment on the particular case. I am genuinely not familiar with it or au fait with it. Indra is an organisation with a turnover of €5 billion-plus and it is successfully delivering projects across the globe in many sectors. We went through a clear, comprehensive procurement process, as we do on all our projects. Indra was the legitimate successful applicant. We deeply regret how this project has panned out with Indra. This was not what we expected. I have 25 years of major infrastructure project experience. This is unprecedented. Every project has problems and challenges - every single project I have worked on - but you work through it and overcome it, and deliver on time and in budget. Sometimes it goes slightly over, but you always get the project delivered eventually.  Looking back on the last 25 or 30 years, Irish Rail does a lot of major engineering construction-type contracts, given the nature of the railway. We cannot point to another example of this occurring in Iarnród Éireann. I cannot point to another example of this in my career dealing with major projects. That is not to excuse it, but it is really unprecedented. We are genuinely surprised given the capability of the organisation, delivering a project probably worth €5 million per annum to it when it is turning over €5 billion per annum and has tens of thousands of people working across the globe. We were sure this would not be a problem for it and that it would eventually overcome the issues that arose. That was our expectation. Was that reasonable based on the evidence at the time? We thought it was. Our experience has led us to a different position now.

Deputy Joanna Byrne  On a more positive and parochial note, and picking up on Mr. Hendrick's line about getting there eventually, I will move on to my home town of Drogheda. It is the largest town and next emerging city in Ireland. When the NTA was with us in January, I asked about the possibility of a north Drogheda train station. I understand it falls outside the greater Dublin area and was not an issue for the NTA, but it would be remiss of me not to use the opportunity of having Irish Rail here with us. Ms Considine has said she is open to the possibility of a train station on the north side of Drogheda. Is there any light at the end of the tunnel with regard to securing that? Louth County Council has just been awarded funding for phase 3 of the port access-northern cross route, which unlocks the land that was a barrier in moving towards that. What concerns me is that a developer is seeking planning permission, which has been refused in recent weeks by Louth County Council. It was deemed an incomplete application. He is seeking to develop on land that has been earmarked, going back 20 or 25 years, for a train station. It includes land owned by Irish Rail. Concern is growing among elected officials in Drogheda, past and present, and the people of Drogheda, who are seeing a huge population burst with all the development going on. Commuters in Drogheda are getting increasingly frustrated by the lack of parking and their inability to utilise facilities on the south side of town around MacBride railway station.

Ms Mary Considine  To start on a positive note, the first fleet order will be coming into service on the new DART+. We have the charging station in Drogheda, and the new Enterprise fleet to serve Drogheda is also on order. There are many positive things happening for commuters in the area. I hear the Deputy's concerns about infrastructure. I have had discussions with Louth County Council around the new north Drogheda station. We are hearing about parking and a study completed earlier this year points to that.  To the Deputy's question on the station and parking, both of those are subject to funding. There is a constrained pot of funding. One of the discussions I had with the CEO was about whether there were other ways, such as through development levies, of funding the station.  At the moment, we do not have the funding allocated for that. It is something that will be kept under continuous review by us and the NTA, as the funding authority.

Deputy Joanna Byrne  Is that the main barrier? I am sorry, Chair, I understand I am over time. Is that the main barrier at the moment? There is consensus and a will for a train station in the north of Drogheda. That is what I am picking up. Without committing the witnesses to anything, is funding the main barrier?
Ms Mary Considine  There are funding constraints. We will always look at what is possible.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  It is good to see some of the witnesses again. I hope the feeling is mutual.
Ms Anne Shaw  Always.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  I would say that is the case. This is a "Yes" or "No" question. Was this the first project in Ireland in which Indra was involved?
Mr. Hugh Creegan  No.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  What were the other projects in which it was involved?

Mr. Hugh Creegan  It was involved with the Dublin Port tunnel when it was being built. Indra put in the control system for that tunnel. It has also been involved with some toll schemes around the country.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Have the projects in which it has been involved in Ireland always been successful and delivered on time and on budget?
Mr. Hugh Creegan  It is going back over 20 years. I have no knowledge that it has not, if I could answer in that way.

Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Is Indra the main contractor for the next generation ticketing? It is. How can the public have any faith that Indra is going to do this successfully? I know that the witnesses will point to 15 years of success and why Indra was appointed for this project in particular. I ask the witnesses to be brief. How can the public have any faith that Indra will successfully do next generation ticketing? That is not even getting into the issue of next generation ticketing itself. How can the public have any faith that it will be delivered on time and on budget with this private company?
Ms Anne Shaw  Currently, the next generation ticketing project is being delivered on time and on budget.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  It is currently.
Ms Anne Shaw  Key milestones are being achieved.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  That is not the case in Cork, but-----
Ms Anne Shaw  That gives us some confidence.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  It is not being delivered in Cork right now.
Ms Anne Shaw  The scope of the project does not yet include Cork.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  It definitely does not.

Ms Anne Shaw  Within the scope of the project that has been commissioned, Indra is delivering on time and on budget. It is fair to say that prior to engaging any contractor or vendor to deliver this system, there was quite an extensive piece of work undertaken by the NTA, again with external expertise to provide us with that. There was a pre-mortem, if you like, of all the things that needed to be covered off before we did the specification and went out to market, as well as all the market engagement. Again,-----
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Ms Shaw has full confidence that Indra will deliver next generation ticketing across the country.
Ms Anne Shaw  Given the current performance, the positive collaboration between the teams and how it is being managed within the NTA and the governance and oversight that exists-----

Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Has this project given Ms Shaw, as the person in charge of the NTA, any questions as to whether Indra will definitely deliver? Can she see herself coming before the committee in a couple of years' time to speak about Indra not delivering next generation ticketing on time and on budget? I hope that will not be the case.

Ms Anne Shaw  I hope not, too. Having reviewed where we are within this particular project, I have confidence in my own team and their expertise and the relationship they have with Indra, and the way that the contract is being managed and set up. This is a very different kind of system to rail, which has more complex considerations. That is why they are different contracts.

Deputy Eoghan Kenny  I hope so, for the benefit of the public, who have suffered on a number of occasions. On Irish Rail, who is the one person who has accountability over this project? Is it one of the witnesses?
Ms Mary Considine  Ultimately, as an executive team, we have accountability. We report to a board of directors who ultimately make decisions.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  How many are on the executive team?
Ms Mary Considine  Today, there are 11.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Are all 11 taking responsibility? Does one particular individual on the executive team that was over this project now take accountability for it?
Ms Mary Considine  There would have been a number of changes to the team since the project was initiated and-----
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Is there someone on the executive team right now who was also on the executive team when it was initiated? How many?
Ms Mary Considine  Not from a capital investment perspective, no. There has been a change at director level.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Who took over the running of this project?
Ms Mary Considine  Mr. Hendrick's area would have taken over the running of the project.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  How many people are working in Mr. Hendrick's area?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  We have 200 staff across the whole portfolio of projects, including DART+, the Cork area commuter rail programme, Ceannt Station and other projects. There is a project team from Irish Rail that was managing this particular project.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  How many are on that team?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  There are probably five or six staff and they are supported by external-----
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  What consequences have those staff members faced?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  They are still working through the project and managing the issues.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  What consequences have they faced for the loss of €50 million? Is the answer "None"?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  I am meaning to go back through the process here.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  I am asking a simple question. What consequences did those people face?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  For Indra's lack of a development of a product-----
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  For their accountability over this project and their lack of governance of the project.
Mr. Paul Hendrick  I do not think-----

Deputy Eoghan Kenny  For the loss of €50 million from the taxpayer. What consequences have those people faced? Have there been any consequences in terms of their job specification or pay, for example? I am not necessarily saying that money should be taken from them in any way, shape or form. What consequences have those people faced? The reason I ask is that if I were working in a private company, which those people are not, and lost €50 million, I would probably be sacked.

Ms Mary Considine  I will come in. Ultimately, if somebody was found to have done something wrong, we would be taking action. The reality is that our team have, through their best endeavours, done everything to support this project. They have leant in. They have tried to make up the gaps, but fundamentally, when you strip it all back, we have a contractor that has an underdeveloped project and it has not delivered for us.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Understandably-----
Ms Mary Considine  That is really disappointing.

Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Understandably, there are a lot of questions to be asked of the contractor. There were five or six individuals within Irish Rail who had accountability over this project. As well as the contractor, those individuals failed to deliver it. They ultimately lost €50 million of taxpayers' money and are now facing absolutely no consequences. They can walk away from this thinking that despite losing €50 million for the taxpayer, they do not have to face any consequences. They have faced no consequences. I am not saying they will, but what if they go again and lose another €50 million for the taxpayer? They would again face no consequences. Do the witnesses take my point on board? Do they agree with my point that if I were working for a private company and lost €50 million, I could be sacked or demoted? Those are just two options. Do the witnesses accept that, "Yes" or "No"?
Ms Mary Considine  I-----
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  I am asking for a "Yes" or a "No".
Ms Mary Considine  I understand what the Deputy is saying. The project team worked on a project that delivered a building that was brought in on time and on budget, and all the other elements.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  I am not necessarily saying that the project team did not work hard, but they failed.
Ms Mary Considine  I would-----

Deputy Eoghan Kenny  In terms of the €50 million, they failed. It is a "Yes" or "No" question. Does Ms Considine believe that if those five or six people were working for a private company they would have faced consequences?
Ms Mary Considine  If they had not done their jobs, had not reported and had not put the appropriate governance in place, there would have been consequences.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  They obviously did not put the appropriate governance-----
Ms Mary Considine  They flagged and reported-----

Deputy Eoghan Kenny  They obviously did not put the appropriate governance in place because they lost €50 million for the taxpayer. They did not lose the money to themselves. They obviously could not care less. The taxpayer lost €50 million. What consequences did those people face? Does Ms Considine accept that those people who were over this project face absolutely no consequence now for losing €50 million? That is a "Yes" or "No" question.
Ms Mary Considine  I do not accept that they face no consequences. I think-----
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  So what consequences-----
Ms Mary Considine  -----they are very disappointed and-----
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  What consequences-----
Ms Mary Considine  -----regret the decision.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Ms Considine does not accept that they did not face any consequences. That is fine and good. What consequences did they face?
Ms Mary Considine  They are working hard to try to resolve this issue.

Deputy Eoghan Kenny  There is no disputing the fact that they are working hard. I am not saying they are not. They are probably five or six very competent individuals. I do not know them. What consequences do those people face right now? I will reiterate the point. If I were working in a private company and lost €50 million for the owner of that private company, I am sure that I would be demoted, sacked, subject to a loss of pay or whatever else. What consequences do those people face? Is the answer "None"? Do they ultimately face no consequences?
Ms Mary Considine  Well----

Deputy Eoghan Kenny  They will not be demoted. They will not lose out on any pay. They will walk away at 5 p.m. or 6 p.m. I am not disputing that they work hard, but they ultimately face no consequences. We can see it from the Irish taxpayers' point of view. Ms Considine is an Irish taxpayer. All around this room are representatives of the Irish taxpayers. They are watching today and hearing that five or six individuals lost €50 million of their money and ultimately will face no consequences at all. They will not be demoted. They will not lose any pay. They obviously will not be sacked. They will ultimately face no consequences. What stops them and Irish Rail as a whole from doing something along these lines again in the future, with a lack of governance and accountability and whatever else, and facing no consequences again because they did not face any consequences for the loss of €50 million? There is nothing to stop that.  We have a systemic issue right across the State. I am not necessarily saying it is an issue that is limited to Irish Rail, but it also affects Irish Rail. A significant number of people across the State are working for the State and face absolutely zero consequences for the lack of delivery of projects or failure in respect of the spending of public money.  The witnesses spoke to Deputy Murphy in particular about lessons learned. Will the NTA and Irish Rail identify one decision that should have been taken six months before this was brought to the board's attention?

Ms Anne Shaw  We have an independent review that is ongoing and it will report in September. It will look at all of the governance and key decision points taken throughout, from the beginning of pre-procurement to where we find ourselves today.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  It is ad hoc right now, knowing the project and the delivery of-----
Ms Anne Shaw  Hindsight is something-----
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Yes, hindsight. We have heard about hindsight loads of times.

Ms Anne Shaw  With the information available and the expertise provided to the NTA and Irish Rail in making the decisions that have been made in the past, those were felt to be the right decisions in order to successfully deliver the traffic management system as well as, as Ms Considine has said, to reduce the cost exposure to the public purse.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  Very briefly, what is the relationship between the NTA and Irish Rail now? How good is it? Does the NTA ask Irish Rail what it is doing?
Ms Anne Shaw  We are both agencies of the State. We work collaboratively together on a large number of projects.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  The must be some sort of anger among staff members of the NTA, saying Irish Rail messed this up.

Ms Anne Shaw  Where things go wrong, we need to support each other to make sure we can successfully conclude and put things right, and that is the relationship we have. We continue to work together to deliver all of the other projects we are involved in together and to make sure we still deliver a traffic management system for the railway network and do it positively with both teams.
Deputy Eoghan Kenny  As a Mallow man, I can say the Cork commuter rail line is going very well, so I thank the witnesses. Well done.

Deputy Grace Boland  As Mr. Hendrick has said, sometimes things go wrong on projects and it is about how we deal with them. For me, looking at Irish Rail and the NTA, the question is how both continued to support, approve, fund and defend a failing project for years after serious warning signs emerged. Not only that, and the witnesses might clarify the figure for me, but it looks as though as much, if not more, was spent on project support as there was paid and committed to Indra. That is a serious red flag and should have been picked up well before now. Ms Considine might tell me how much we have paid in project support to prop up this fiasco.
Ms Mary Considine  In total, I believe it is €28 million or €29 million.
Deputy Grace Boland  Is Ms Considine sure it is €29 million?
Ms Mary Considine  Third-party costs and project support amount to €29 million.
Deputy Grace Boland  What about Irish Rail's internal costs?
Ms Mary Considine  They are about €2.6 million.

Deputy Grace Boland  We are over €30 million, which is a similar amount to what we paid to Indra. In terms of looking at the NTA, there is a serious oversight failure here. Irish Rail warned the NTA repeatedly, the NTA approved multiple resets, a commercial reset, budgeting increases and continuation after confidence collapsed. The NTA explicitly resisted a development of plan B last year. The NTA took a hands-on role from mid-2025. That is not oversight; it is being complicit in this whole fiasco.  I want to look at the correspondence sent to us in April. The NTA sent us correspondence in April and attached board minutes of Irish Rail. The tone of the correspondence the NTA sent to us is of a project that is delayed but progressing through testing and that has future delivery phases. Yet, the Iarnród Éireann board minutes of February, several weeks earlier, record significant concerns about the contractor's ability to deliver the programme and note that the CP1 project is only a small portion of the scope and that Irish Rail directors were deeply concerned. My question to the NTA is to ask why the picture was painted to the Committee of Public Accounts that this was a project progressing. More importantly, was it trying to paint the same picture to the major project governance and oversight group as it was to the committee or was it actually conveying Irish Rail's concerns to the oversight group?

Ms Anne Shaw  To answer the first question, I do not think we have been painting a rosy picture. We have been working on a number of key decision points with Irish Rail with, as we have already mentioned, expert advice about the different resets that have happened over the lifetime of this project. With the information available at the time, I think those were considered to be the right decisions to move forward, with the ultimate aim of delivering the traffic management system for the railway network.  The reports we gave to the committee in April were about the reset to look at CP1. CP1 was progressing well at that time. We worked with Irish Rail and Indra in terms of that.
Deputy Grace Boland  Just to note, the Irish Rail board of directors was deeply concerned and Ms Shaw is saying it was progressing well. Just to note, there is a serious difference there.

Ms Anne Shaw  We got an agreed approach in terms of what we were doing with the reset that had been done and to move forward with just CP1 and the Rosslare section of the network. That was progressing to plan and was being reported on that basis.  Just to say in terms of MPGOG, there were a number of occasions when we attended MPGOG and Irish Rail also came and gave a deep dive on the projects. MPGOG also has independent expertise that understands railway systems sitting on it. There are six independent experts on that governance and oversight group. Lots of questions are asked and there are lots of discussions, including about confidence in delivery. I do not think we have been painting a rosy picture-----
Deputy Grace Boland  I certainly feel the NTA was painting a picture to the Committee of Public Accounts that was different from the picture that Irish Rail was expressing.
Ms Anne Shaw  At that point in time when we came before the committee in April, that particular CP1 element, because that was what all the information was based on, was progressing-----

Deputy Grace Boland  I am talking about correspondence in April. It was very different in tone from what the Irish Rail board minutes were saying. I have serious issues with that and I hope Ms Shaw can confirm to me that MPGOG was fully aware of Irish Rail's concerns and did not just have the picture the NTA was painting to us. It is important.

Mr. Tomás Campbell  I will come in on MPGOG. It is worth noting that we have been very concerned about this project for a number of years and we have been kept informed on the issues. From an MPGOG perspective, at the time period in question we all knew that April would be a key milestone with delivery of the software. When the NTA was reporting into MPGOG we all knew that once the software was seen, CP1 would be viable from the timelines indicated. In the most recent meetings of MPGOG, in May and June, we had extensive discussions about how the software testing was going and the next steps. It is really important for the Department that we get the project onto a sustainable footing and go forward on the best possible basis. For MPGOG itself, we also have a mechanism in place to report to the Minister each quarter. The Minister and the management board have been kept informed of these issues. I do not think it is fair to say the NTA-----
Deputy Grace Boland  So everyone knew this was a failing project and no one stepped in to resolve it. Is that what Mr. Campbell is saying?

Mr. Tomás Campbell  I think that what MPGOG wanted to see was that Iarnród Éireann and the NTA were taking the expected steps and I believe they were. When the re-baselined programme was agreed in November 2024 it made the project more deliverable for Indra. Everyone agreed it would be easier to deliver CP1, acknowledging it was a relatively small commissioning for use.

Deputy Grace Boland  I do not accept that. We are spending as much in project support to prop up a failed project and a contractor that was failing repeatedly to deliver. Everyone from the NTA to the Department was fine with that. It is not acceptable and it is not good enough. The taxpayer is rightly annoyed.  My next question is on the correspondence between the NTA and Irish Rail this week. I noted an article in The Irish Times today that seems to indicate the NTA is pointing fingers at Irish Rail and that it is saying this is its financial problem and if it wants to terminate the contract, it should do it but it will have to pay the consequences. Is that the position? How will that affect major projects and services?
Ms Anne Shaw  I do not think that is a correct assumption from what Deputy Boland has read in The Irish Times today.
Deputy Grace Boland  Ms Shaw might please share the letter with the committee after the meeting.
Ms Anne Shaw  We will try but with the caveat that if there are any commercial sensitivities-----
Deputy Grace Boland  They can be redacted.

Ms Anne Shaw  We will try to get it to the committee. In terms of answering the question, we have considered the decision of the Irish Rail board. When we met the Oireachtas joint committee a couple of weeks ago, we said we would expeditiously deal with the matter so as to make sure things can be taken forward as swiftly as possible in the interests of the Irish taxpayer as well. We need to assess the consequences of these discussions and the continued delivery of the traffic management system. We still need to make sure we deliver the traffic management system for the railway for existing and new services planned over the investment programme. We need to consider what the financial impact requirement is and look across the wider programme to make sure we can continue to deliver that as well.  It will be a case of rephasing and reprioritising certain things over that period of time but ultimately to make sure that we deliver that.
Deputy Grace Boland  Given that Irish Rail raised concerns last year, and the NTA is now saying it is a decision for Irish Rail, why was Irish Rail not allowed terminate last year and explore plan B?
Ms Anne Shaw  I think that at that time the Irish Rail board, having reviewed the information and the proposals, did not make that request. The agreement between the organisations and the board-----

Deputy Grace Boland  Does Ms Shaw mean that Irish Rail did not make the request in writing? Is Ms Shaw saying that it is just because Irish Rail did not make the request in writing, notwithstanding that it has been raising serious red flags to the NTA since 2023, and we are now suggesting that it terminates? I assume that it was agreed between the NTA and Irish Rail that it would not be put in writing.

Ms Anne Shaw  There were discussions with various options about how this project could move forward. The decision of the Irish Rail board at that time was to move forward doing the Rosslare section and the CP1 section as well. With the information that is now available-----
Deputy Grace Boland  Was the phasing not agreed after Irish Rail suggested terminating?

Ms Anne Shaw  Does Mr. Creegan want to come in here? There were discussions around the various options, and it was agreed by all parties, including the Irish Rail board, to move forward with the option that was progressed over last year.
Mr. Hugh Creegan  The phasing proposal was developed in 2024 but what changes-----
Deputy Grace Boland  After Irish Rail had suggested terminating.

Mr. Hugh Creegan  It was after a discussion about the problems the project had and the options to deal with them. We then convened a tripartite meeting with ourselves, Indra and Irish Rail to go through the options. Out of that, Indra was required to produce a remedial plan, and it did produce a plan shortly after that. It looked a credible plan, and on that basis, we moved forward at that time. In 2025, because I think the Deputy mentioned it, we focused activity on the first phase called CP1, which she is aware of.
Deputy Grace Boland  How much has it cost us since 2024 to continue with this failed project? If we had terminated it two years ago or even last year, how much would we have saved?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Since the summer of 2025, we have probably incurred an expenditure of close to €10 million. I will have to come back to the Deputy to confirm that.
Deputy Grace Boland  Is that with Indra, all external factors and Irish Rail's costs?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  That is the total project cost and a lot of that would be in the assessment and in the financial statements in the write down.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  I thank the witnesses for being here and for their continued presence. It is clearly a project that has gone horribly wrong for both Irish Rail and the NTA but, ultimately, for the taxpayer as well. I was struck to hear from the NTA that it has commissioned an independent review of this project, to look at issues of governance, delivery and project oversight. Do the witnesses agree with me that commissioning an independent review is an offensive waste of public money? I would argue that Ms Shaw and her organisation are fully aware of what has gone wrong here. Ms Considine and her organisation are fully aware of what has gone wrong here, and Mr. Campbell and the Department are fully aware of what has gone wrong here. Given the prevalence of private involvement and consultancy, or whatever we want to call it, misguide advice, throughout, why do we need a third party to bring together all of this data that was shared with us today to tell us what has gone wrong? What is the budget for that independent review?
Mr. Hugh Creegan  I think it is €226,000.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  Some €226,000, to do what? We know the flaws and problems. Mr. Hendrick has spoken about the lessons that need to be learned. Other than to try to assuage the very taxpayer that has been robbed of this service and of this money, this makes no sense. Who is doing that review?
Ms Anne Shaw  EY is doing the review but I think it is important to have an independent report, so that neither organisation can be accused of trying to put a different picture on the information.
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  Who is paying for that report?
Ms Anne Shaw  It is coming out of the NTA budget.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  How is it independent, if the NTA is paying for it? It is an absolute offensive waste of a quarter of a million euro. I ask the NTA to reconsider whether it is necessary. I do not think it is.
Ms Anne Shaw  I still think the independent nature of the outputs and recommendations-----
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  It will not be independent. With respect Ms Shaw, there will be no independence.
Ms Anne Shaw  -----will provide us with the lessons learned.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  It appears that Indra was provided with this contract for the delivery of the project, based on its core TMS project. That is how I understood the witnesses very welcome briefing documents. It was because it had a solid and flexible logic. That is what was quoted. Indra also advised the witnesses of a 15-year history of 21 successful deployments across a number of different countries. Are the witnesses aware of anybody in their organisations who met with colleagues from any of those 21 deployments to hear from them about their experiences of working with this service provider?
Ms Mary Considine  I believe there have been discussion with Lithuania and other countries.
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  Were they prior to the contract being awarded?
Ms Mary Considine  I could not confirm that. I am not certain.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  We know what happened afterwards. I am curious about what due diligence was done before the contracts were signed. Was it simply the case that because of its size and scale we took Indra's word for it, or did we do our due diligence to make sure that we spoke to those who worked with this organisation before? From the perspective of the NTA, did anybody meet with any of those countries that signed these contracts with Indra prior to signing that agreement?
Ms Anne Shaw  No, not that I am aware of.
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  Is it industry standard for a tender brief to be 50% on cost and 50% on qualitative submission?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  It depends on the type of project.
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  Is it industry standard?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  No, because sometimes it can be 30:70 in terms of cost and quality. It can be 70:30.
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  Who made the determination that this was the appropriate ratio, 50% on cost and 50% on what has turned out to be a myth.
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Iarnród Éireann; we would have as a business.
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  What the rationale for that decision?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  As part of the market research and market consultation process that we went through before we actually started the procurement competition, we would have taken on board how important it was to ensure that we did not make it a price sensitive decision. In other words, if it was 80% price and 20% quality, there was a risk then that somebody would have a weighted opportunity to win the bid with potentially a price that did not reflect the quality of what is needed. So, the quality of what we were going to get on this really complex project was really important and that would have had a bearing on trying to get the quality up as a strong factor in the evaluations such that-----
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  Iarnród Éireann could have gone 60% or 70% with the quality then. It could have done that.
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Agreed.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  I do not know how it could have been a decent qualitative submission if it was a promise or a hope of delivery, not "This is what we do" because Iarnród Éireann was dependent on software that did not exist.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  Going back ten years ago, a lot of the criteria would have been weighted towards price but given the scale and the complexity of the projects that we are facing, we have already moved going forward to a model that is along the lines of what the Deputy just mentioned there.
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  Was Indra the cheapest bidder?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  It was.
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  By how much?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  There was a maintenance price and a capital price on the bid. There was a capital price for the works, and then there was a maintenance proposal to support the maintenance of the asset when it was built but on the capital price it was probably about 50% cheaper than the losing bidder.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  It was 50% cheaper on the price, which was worth 50% of the award criteria, and in the qualitative submission it told Iarnród Éireann that it would deliver its own internal software, which was not ready but it would have it. We agreed to sign the contract based on that promise, alongside its track record with other countries on what it delivered before, but our service that we need was dependent on new software that it did not have at that time.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  That is really good question but just to say that when Indra submitted its bid, going back to the promise, because that is what a contract is it is a promise to do versus a promise to pay, it offered us Da Vinci 2.0 in its bid submission. The way it worked-----
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  Indra did not have it to offer.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  Let us say that Indra did have Da Vinci 2.0. I just want to say that when it put in its compliance matrix, it was obviously populating and self-declaring and that looks like it was marking its own homework but we reviewed that compliance matrix. It had to be substantiated. You could not just say, "Yes, we comply". You had to show evidence of how your solution could meet those particular requirements. We had that review done also by Ricardo, which had the subject matter expertise out there on other projects. It authenticated that the bid submission was a bona fide bid submission from Indra for Da Vinci 2.0. The problem was post-contract when Indra moved away from Da Vinci 2.0 because it was moving to 3.0. That is where-----
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  In simple terms, is that not a breach of contract? Indra changed the landscape.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  It is difficult. We recognised the concern as a business but when we went through it, we were not able to identify a clear breach such that we would be able to lawfully stop the contract.  Remember that if you try to do something you are not entitled to do, the company can bring a challenge. The Deputy's question is very fair.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  Mr. Hendrick mentioned the word "slippage". I am not going to be pedantic, but slippage of 20 months on a four-year contract is more than slippage. At one point, he was notified that it would be that long. There was then a resettlement to the tune of €1.4 million. Was Indra paid €1.4 million in addition, even though it had delayed the project by 20 months? I seek a "Yes" or "No" answer.
Mr. Paul Hendrick  We reset our target price by an additional €1.4 million. There were other issues it was arguing. It was making arguments against us at that time.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  I know it was looking for €2.3 million in the resettlement.  In the time I have left, will Ms Shaw rule out, or just for the record state, what impact, if any, this has on the delivery of MetroLink?
Ms Anne Shaw  This will have no impact on the delivery of MetroLink.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  None.  With regard to the DART+ expansion and the projects that are really important, will Ms Considine state what impact the whole process will have on the delivery time of those services?

Ms Mary Considine  We have been very focused on addressing that point. We have put obsolescence provisions in place, with the support of funding from the Department of Transport, to protect the train control system in the denser part of the network around the greater Dublin area and to future-proof for the DART+ expansion. What we want to do now is move to protect the rest of the network and support the other vital capital projects that are happening around the country.
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  Can Ms Considine guarantee that there will be no delays to those programmes because of this?
Ms Mary Considine  We can say that there will be no delay to DART+, and we are working to find solutions for the other parts of the country.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  If the interim measures in place were sufficient, we would not be in this mess in the first place. We are obviously in some form of limbo now where we need to find a long-term solution. Are there any health and safety risks associated with where this whole project stands now, as regards the current rail network but also the future expansion?

Ms Mary Considine  To give assurance to the committee, the current technology, even though it is life-expired, is fail-safe technology. What that means is that something will stop running if there is an issue and we will have an outage like we had on 29 May that affects services. It is really unfortunate, but it will fail safe, so we will not be compromising safety. Safety is absolutely crucial. We will stop running services rather than compromise safety. We obviously do not want to stop running services either, so we need a solution here.
Deputy Aidan Farrelly  I thank the witnesses.

Deputy Martin Daly  I thank the witnesses for attending this morning. I do not want to rehash what has already been covered, but it really is difficult for an ordinary person, and I see myself as an ordinary person, to understand the contract situation. Reading through the submissions, I note that there were flags going up on this contract as early as 2020. If a multibillion euro corporation that was supposed to specialise in this area was failing to meet very basic requirements of a contract so early in its term, why were red flags not going up all over the place? Is there any answer to that?

Ms Mary Considine  I will hand over to Mr. Hendrick because he will be able to go into more detail, but if the Deputy reviews the correspondence that we have put before the committee, he will see that red flags were being raised. Even in the first commercial resettlement, there were assurances given by Indra that it was addressing the issue. It never raised any issue with specifications, nor did it state it could not meet the criteria. It accepted and signed up to the rebasing of the contracts, and unfortunately it did not deliver. That led to Mr. Hendrick and his team flagging very serious concerns in early 2024.
Deputy Martin Daly  As early as 2024.
Ms Mary Considine  Early, and there would have been-----

Deputy Martin Daly  It is four years. I see that Indra used things like the pandemic to explain it. The pandemic has been blamed for everything. What I cannot understand is that, for four years, these flags were going up very early on in the term of the contract. Four years is a long time.
Ms Mary Considine  Maybe Mr. Hendrick can talk about the measures that were put in place.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  The concerns that were raised related to the DaVinci 2.0 platform that Indra was advising us about post contract. It had not advised at any time going into the contract that it was going to move from version 2.0 to version 3.0. It did cause a concern. Our team went through a due diligence process with the company to ask what this meant. It reassured Irish Rail by saying that this was the next generation of the product. It has a product development history. It states it has had versions 1.0 and 2.0 and is moving to 3.0 as a business. It stated that this would be the case for TMS applications that it was involved with in other jurisdictions, so it would not have version 2.0 in one place and version 3.0 in another. Rather, the aim was to roll it out consistently. The concerns we would have had were to make sure we would still get the offering promised with version 2.0 with version 3.0. They were the undertakings that Indra gave to the business, and we worked forward on that basis.  What happened from 2022 to 2024 was that we had programme concerns. "Slippages" is the word we have used but there were significant programme concerns. The movement from version 2.0 to 3.0 has turned into a whole new process for Indra as a business. It was developing the next version of the product "outside the project", as it is called. In other words, there was an activity it was engaging in as a business that the project it had committed to doing for us was dependent on.
Deputy Martin Daly  In 2020?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  From 2020, yes.
Deputy Martin Daly  Mr. Hendrick is now saying that, between 2022 and 2024, serious slippage happened, but we are talking now about two to four years.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  Yes. It promised us that the product development process, which relates to what is called the generic product, as the Deputy might have seen in the note, would be finished. Indra guaranteed it would be finished in 2021, such that it would have no effect on the programme whatsoever. In the end, it took Indra until the end of 2023 to have the generic product process that it was engaging in as a corporate organisation outside the project completed. That was a driving factor and really delayed the project.

Deputy Martin Daly  It really feels like Indra gamed the contract. What is really interesting is that it was 50% less expensive than the next tenderer. Did that not raise concerns that it had lowballed the State on this contract? We have seen it in other big State infrastructure contracts, with lowballing and then coming back and back until the cost escalates or the contractor cannot meet the terms of the contract.
Mr. Paul Hendrick  As part of the procurement evaluation process, we would carefully examine the commercial offerings of any bid to assess them from the point of view-----

Deputy Martin Daly  Fifty percent is a huge gap. If there is a gap of 10% or 15%, someone somewhere says the company should wait a minute. I do not want to ask who the other firms that tendered were. Mr. Hendrick probably cannot tell me that. Can he? Were they reputable corporations?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Yes.
Deputy Martin Daly  International?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Yes.

Deputy Martin Daly  Okay. Fifty percent is just incredible. If a builder came in and said he could build something for 50% less, you would be expecting wet bags of concrete to be stuck in the wall. Someone would be cutting costs somewhere. It is incredible. It is just a reflection on things.  Consider the third-party advice to support Indra. Who did Irish Rail bring in to provide that third-party hand-holding advice to a multibillion-euro corporation that was supposed to deliver a huge infrastructure project? I saw in the note that Irish Rail brought in some external contractor to help it through some of its issues. Was that another contractor?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  We had two organisations, called Ricardo Rail and Turas, which provided effectively temporary staff to help us manage the project, including technically. They were helping Irish Rail, I should say. They were working for-----
Deputy Martin Daly  Helping Irish Rail.
Mr. Paul Hendrick  They were working for Irish Rail and helping Irish Rail.
Deputy Martin Daly  Was anyone brought in to help Indra or advise it? Did Indra subcontract any work?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  I am not sure, to be honest, exactly in what way Indra’s staff were contracted. It had a lot of people working for it, advising and doing the work for Indra directly.

Deputy Martin Daly  Again, I do not want to rehash what has come before. The contract is with the NTA and Irish Rail delivers it. The advice is that there is going to be a review to decide on how to terminate this contract. Am I reading that correctly, or am I misinterpreting that?

Ms Anne Shaw  The contract is between Irish Rail and Indra. Irish Rail will need to have conversations directly with Indra in terms of managing the next steps. The NTA will continue to work with Irish Rail to support any way forward.

Deputy Martin Daly  The ticketing system contract is going to Indra. Again, for the benefit of the ordinary public, how are we to understand that a corporation that has not delivered on a project is being brought in to deliver another development for the NTA, namely, the next-generation ticketing system?  How does the NTA explain that to the public?

Ms Anne Shaw  Again, there was a compliant procurement process where Indra was successful in that contract. As I mentioned earlier, there was a lot of pre-mortem, as it were, prior to developing the procurement strategy about all the things that needed to be included in the same way there was a review of all the different expertise globally, the different organisations that deliver against these projects. Indra has got that global presence in this particular field as well. It is very different technology to rail.
Deputy Martin Daly  Is Ms Shaw confident it will deliver on that contract?
Ms Anne Shaw  It is currently being delivered on time and on budget. All the milestones are being met. The teams are colocated and working successfully to deliver against those milestones.

Deputy Martin Daly  Does the NTA’s external consultants who advised on the original contract, Ricardo, culpable here in any way? What happens if I get advice and it is deficient, and obviously its advice was deficient?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Well-----
Deputy Martin Daly  Maybe "deficient" is too strong a word. Let us say it has given the NTA advice, as a specialist company, which has turned out to be erroneous.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  There will be the EY review which the NTA mentioned which will look at everything that has happened as a full look back. A lot of this happened before my time in the business. I am not here trying to defend anyone, to be clear; the facts are the facts and we will go through where all the real causes are. Based on the undertakings and representations that Indra made through the pre-call and the bid process, how Ricardo and the project team assessed it was not unreasonable based on the information they were given to review. That is just my opinion.

Deputy Martin Daly  Therefore it comes back to Indra not delivering and undervaluing what was required and a whole range of things. Low-balling, I would say.  Finally to the NTA, the State will spend a lot of money on MetroLink. Does the NTA think it is capable of delivering MetroLink?

Ms Anne Shaw  Obviously we are coming close to the next approval gate for MetroLink. There has been a lot of work to develop the project team and a lot of work to make sure we have the right design and systems in place as well. There have been thorough assessments around both the project execution and how that will be delivered. What is being delivered, all the costings, etc., are all in the process of being assured against that as well.

Deputy Martin Daly  I have run out of time here and I do not want to take anyone else’s time. Ms Shaw could accept the public has, perhaps, had its confidence shaken in the NTA and Irish Rail in the management of this particular contract
Ms Anne Shaw  Yes.
Deputy Martin Daly  That is all I can say. I cannot answer that. I thank the Cathaoirleach.

An Cathaoirleach  Before I let the next speaker in, the committee’s function here is to establish how public funds are managed. Members may refer to third parties insofar as it relates to decisions, the decisions and oversight of Irish Rail and the NTA, but the committee cannot make findings as regards the contractors’ liabilities.  Deputy Bennett is next.

Deputy Cathy Bennett  I welcome the witnesses and thank them for coming in.  I have heard numerous dates and timelines for the national train control centre project, NTCC. When did the witnesses first became concerned about the NTCC?

Ms Mary Considine  If you take the overall NTCC project itself, despite Covid and everything, the building was delivered within budget. That is quite a futuristic building that will centralise the entire control system but will also future-proof for Dublin City Council, and the gardaí are also in there. The building itself went to plan. In terms of the signalling, electrical and telecommunications elements of the project, a lot of that was delivered in conjunction with our own team, it went to plan and the hardware was installed. I know we are repeating ourselves, there were concerns about Indra and its performance from early on with the traffic management system, TMS.
Deputy Cathy Bennett  What was the first year?
Ms Mary Considine  I would say late 2020 there were initial concerns.
Deputy Cathy Bennett  So that is 2020-2026 and it has only become public now at this stage really. In the last six months, would you say?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  If I could go back, we did the first commercial reset No. 1 in late 2022. I came into my role in September-----
Deputy Cathy Bennett  Mr. Hendrick is saying 2022 then.
Mr. Paul Hendrick  We had initial-----
Deputy Cathy Bennett  This is why I am confused because everyone keeps mentioning different years and we are only finding out here in 2026.
Mr. Paul Hendrick  There was a number of programme challenges at that point.

Deputy Cathy Bennett  On target and on budget. Contactless payment was introduced to Ireland in 2011. That is the same year as the Leap cards. Deputy Cathy Bennett  Just one more thing-----
An Cathaoirleach  Very briefly, Deputy.
Deputy Cathy Bennett  Did the witnesses receive media training before attending here?
Mr. Tomás Campbell  No.

Deputy Joe Neville  I thank the witnesses for coming in. I want to get a bit granular regarding the €50 million write-off and the timeline involved. When was the first €4 million to €5 million of the €50 million spent?

Deputy Paul McAuliffe  Yes.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  In 2023, Indra, which it had a right to do under the contract, reset the programme. It moved it out twice. It moved the completion date from November 2024 to March 2025 and then, at the end of 2023, it moved it again, this time to August 2025, but that meant it was resetting to its account. In other words, we were not adjusting the target price or resetting the contract, and Indra was just advising us that it was going to be later than what we had agreed in commercial reset No. 1.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  But-----

Mr. Paul Hendrick  That was causing us concern because of slippage on it. We were obviously looking for Indra to recover and find ways to deal with it, but when we came into summer 2024 - this was before we got to commercial reset No. 2 - the serious concerns we had were that the software we had been given to test was way short of the expectation.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  This is where I want to get to. By July 2024, had Iarnród Éireann already considered replacing Indra?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Yes, as a potential solution.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  Am I correct in saying that Iarnród Éireann communicated that to the NTA?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Yes, verbally in a discussion with the NTA.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  At that time, was the NTA in contract or in tendering process in regard to the ticket management system?
Mr. Hugh Creegan  I think we would have been at the tendering stage. I cannot swear to that. Certainly, we were at the tendering stage.

Deputy Paul McAuliffe  I suppose what I am asking is whether there is an interplay here. When Irish Rail raised the concerns, was the NTA fearful of ending the relationship with Indra on the train management system because the NTA was about to embark on a relationship for the ticket management system?
Mr. Hugh Creegan  Absolutely not.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  Was that not a consideration at all?
Mr. Hugh Creegan  It was not. It never was a consideration.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  Okay.
Mr. Hugh Creegan  They were two separate projects and had to be managed appropriately in each case.

Deputy Paul McAuliffe  Does Ms Considine feel that, when she made the request to the NTA or when Iarnród Éireann started to consider replacing Indra, Iarnród Éireann had the support of the NTA on that or does she feel that the NTA was overly cautious?
Ms Mary Considine  We made decisions at our board on 22 June and we took those forward to the NTA for approval. Our understanding is we required the approval of the NTA to implement those decisions.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  If the decision had been made in 2024 to end the contract with Indra at that point, would we have saved money as a result?
Ms Mary Considine  It is very evident from the schedules here that we would have saved money if the contract had been terminated.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  Can Ms Considine quantify that for the committee?
Ms Mary Considine  I cannot comment. I was not here in 2024 but, obviously, if the contract was terminated at that stage-----
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  Can Mr. Hendrick quantify what might have been saved?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  It is hypothetical. Going back to Deputy Neville's comment on the €50 million writedown, a lot of the writedown is happening from 2021 onwards. That is where the majority of the writedown is. In summer 2024, our expenditure was probably €25 million less than the €150 million we were at at the end of December. It is a hypothetical. If you make a change at that time, you end up with a different synopsis.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  Of course. Certainly, a sum in the multiple millions of euro could have been saved.
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Potentially.

Deputy Paul McAuliffe  I will go back to the support contracts. The idea that support contracts would be of equal value to the contract itself is a mind-blowing concept. Of the €30 million, would Iarnród Éireann be able to provide us with a list of the support contracts and the value of those contracts?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Yes, we can. I suppose the principal ones were Ricardo Rail and Turas. They were in the order of €28 million, including VAT. What I should say-----
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  Then what is remaining would be-----
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Smaller ancillaries.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  Were there any other contracts that would be in the range of €1 million or €2 million?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  There might be one or two, yes. I would have to come back to the committee with the specifics.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  What role would they have held? What work would they have done?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  We brought in some extra project support staff to support us, and particularly the project director that we brought in in October 2025 to help us because of the level of challenge and difficulty.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  What was the value of the contract for the project director?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  He is a freelance organisation so he has got a couple of staff with him. There is a budget there north of €2 million but it is not expended. It is probably a few hundred grands' worth of expenditure.
Deputy Paul McAuliffe  In 2025, a project director was appointed on a contract basis with a value of more than €2 million.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  Based on a projected forecast of supporting the project for the coming years because we are not going to finish this project any time in the next two to three years on the basis of the way we are going, plus some additional support staff. It is a provisional budget. It is not expended.

Deputy Paul McAuliffe  In a project that costs €150 million and may reach €250 million, I imagine the idea that an additional €2 million was set aside only a number of months ago while Iarnród Éireann was still dealing with the other issues would be concerning to members of the committee.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  I should say he is replacing other staff. There are other staff who have been dialled out of the project, from Ricardo Rail and from Turas. We have had staff changes on our side where people have left to take up other roles in other organisations, and one or two in other roles within the business. Given the length of the project, you are always going to have a certain level of churn. Staff are moving around in the capital projects function.

Deputy Paul McAuliffe  The €50 million can be an impaired asset. It can be written off but, in reality, it is not written off because it is not available for other services. I just think of the Luas figures in my own area. There is a price tag of €600 million on that. You are talking about €50 million, and perhaps more if the impairment grows. As for the scale of this, it is one of the biggest impairments of an asset that this company has ever seen. I am sure there are bigger, but it is very rare to see this scale of impairment. Given that we have come to the last day of term in the Dáil, there is a lot more that this committee needs to do on this issue.

Deputy Séamus McGrath  I thank the witnesses for being here. At the outset, I want to start in the here and now as opposed to looking back on the project. In its opening statement, Iarnród Éireann makes reference to the decisions taken at the board meeting in June. Ms Considine mentioned that she may not be able to provide full details, but what can she tell us about those decisions taken at the recent board meeting?

Ms Mary Considine  I thank Deputy McGrath. We have real focus now and it is about moving forward. I have said that there is huge regret that we find ourselves in this position as a collective and it is about now finding a way forward to deliver a train control system that future-proofs the network and minimises further exposure to the Exchequer.  We moved to act as early as we could to bring proposals to the board to get their support as a board - the board is very focused on this as well and very conscious of its obligation for taxpayers' money - and bring those decisions to the NTA for its consideration.
Deputy Séamus McGrath  Can Ms Considine give the committee some details of those decisions?
Ms Mary Considine  I cannot go into them but they are around the contract. The NTA has considered our decisions and agreed to the decisions taken.
Deputy Séamus McGrath  However, at this time, Irish Rail is still in contract with Indra.
Ms Mary Considine  Yes, we are still in contract and working through that but we are talking about a matter of weeks to resolve it.
Deputy Séamus McGrath  What are our financial obligations to Indra at this point?
Ms Mary Considine  I will ask Mr. Hendrick to come in on that. We believe that under-----
Deputy Séamus McGrath  It was touched on in a response to Deputy Neville earlier. There was a figure of €3 million so far in 2026.
Ms Mary Considine  There is €3 million spent on the contract so far in 2026. That was not paid to Indra. They are third-party costs and our costs.
Deputy Séamus McGrath  That is not a payment to Indra. That is third-party costs.
Mr. Paul Hendrick  Mostly, yes. We stopped paying Indra in February this year because of the way the contract works. It has hit the ceiling and no more payments have been due since then.
Deputy Séamus McGrath  We are not on the hook to Indra.

Mr. Paul Hendrick  We are not paying it at the moment under the contract because we have no obligation to pay it. It is making claims under the contract, but, so far, we have not established any entitlement to those claims.
Deputy Séamus McGrath  Did the NTA agree to the decisions made at the board meeting in June?
Ms Anne Shaw  Yes.
Deputy Séamus McGrath  However, we do not know the nature of those decisions and Iarnród Éireann is not in a position to tell us about them.
Ms Mary Considine  We are not. The Deputy will appreciate that the last thing we want to do is compromise-----
Deputy Séamus McGrath  The decisions are about the contract with Indra.
Ms Mary Considine  Yes.
Deputy Séamus McGrath  Will Ms Considine give a high level breakdown of the headline figure for the writedown value of €50 million? She mentioned the €28.2 million on software.

Ms Mary Considine  Yes, I can. Some €28.2 million relates to Indra, €8.5 million of the third-party costs relate to Turas and €6.76 million relate to Ricardo, and the other €2 million is for SET and ICT enabling works. However, the majority of it is the first three items, the TMS with Indra and the €8.5 million and €6.76 million for the two specialist service providers.

Deputy Séamus McGrath  I will go back to the money spent so far this year. Is there further expenditure to come on obligations that have to be met, which will be effectively wasted? Are there still obligations to pay money to third parties or others?

Ms Mary Considine  There will be work even supporting the review the NTA is carrying out and there will be work in implementing the decisions we have taken. However, we are talking about minimising it and working at the earliest to deal-----

Deputy Séamus McGrath  Can Ms Considine give us a value? We have the value of the report. I think €230,000 roughly was mentioned. What additional funds are still to be spent to close this out as a project to meet obligations that will not result in anything other than totting up more on the €50 million writedown?
Ms Mary Considine  I believe - correct me if I am wrong - that we have moved to significantly reduce the resources involved in this and minimise the costs.
Deputy Séamus McGrath  I understand that, but will Ms Considine give us some sense of it?
Ms Mary Considine  There is still probably a couple of hundred thousand of euro per month.
Deputy Séamus McGrath  A couple of hundred thousand of euro per month.
Mr. Paul Hendrick  I will go back to the question. We still need to complete the project with whatever solution we land on and that will take a number of years.
