An Cathaoirleach  I mentioned the signalling system in Cork and the timeline that is in place. Who has the contract for delivering that signalling system?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  The main contractor for the signalling system in Cork is Alstom.
An Cathaoirleach  In fairness, time penalties were written into the contract. It is a pity the same was not done for the contract with Indra. Would you agree?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  There are liquidated damages in all of our contracts, including in the Indra contract.
An Cathaoirleach  With the Indra contract, those were not implemented until this year. Is that correct?
Mr. Paul Hendrick  They have not been levied so far.
An Cathaoirleach  Why?

Mr. Paul Hendrick  When we did the commercial reset number two we effectively reset the programme dates against which those liquidated damages would apply. In the discussions we had with Indra and the NTA in 2025 it was agreed to only focus on CP1. In the nature of what we were doing, we focused on delivering CP1. We did not forfeit our right to those liquidated damages; we just did not levy them at that time. We had agreed that approach in principle at the time. Where we are at the moment is that there are no more payments to Indra in any case, as we sit here today.
An Cathaoirleach  What was the cost quantitative breakdown for the next generation ticketing, NGT, tender?
Ms Anne Shaw  The whole cost within the business case for NGT was in the cost range. I think it has been reported to the committee before. It ranges from €240 million to €280 million.
An Cathaoirleach  How many companies put in for the tender?
Ms Anne Shaw  There were three bidders.
An Cathaoirleach  Where did Indra rank?
Ms Anne Shaw  It won the contract.
An Cathaoirleach  Was it cheaper, middle or-----
Ms Anne Shaw  It was done on the same price-quality contract. I do not have the breakdown of what the percentages were.
An Cathaoirleach  Was Indra's the cheapest tender bid?
Ms Anne Shaw  Between price and quality, yes, that is correct.
An Cathaoirleach  How much cheaper?
Ms Anne Shaw  I cannot answer that at this point. We can come back to the committee with the information.

An Cathaoirleach  Please do. Given what we know about the TMS tender, it should have set off so many different alarm bells, particularly in light of what has transpired in Spain and other jurisdictions. I ask you to come to us on that.  I would be really interested to see that.  I want to touch on the issue of electric buses. To hear that keeping the buses in storage for a lengthy time is actually saving us money and it being put forward as a justification that in some bizarre way this approach is ultimately saving us money is an insult to people's intelligence. What we see here is a continuous failure on so many different levels to plan forward. To see 98 buses, valued at €730,000 each including VAT, in storage is an absolute disgrace. As it currently stands, we have over €71 million worth of electric buses still in storage. For someone to come in and try to justify that by saying it saved us money because of inflationary measures is an insult to people's intelligence. Would you agree, Mr. Creegan?

Mr. Hugh Creegan  We are not trying for one minute to make it out to be a good idea. It was not the plan to have buses in storage. The plan was that the buses would arrive and the chargers would be in place and we would be able to deploy them into operational use.
An Cathaoirleach  I get all of that.
Mr. Hugh Creegan  We simply made the point that there was an offsetting cost, just to acknowledge that, but it was never a plan to have buses in storage.

An Cathaoirleach  Well the plan is to keep them in storage and it is going to cost us another €1.5 million by the time the 98 buses eventually come out onto the streets. What measures, if any, have been taken given the concerns this committee has expressed over the last number of months with regard to this information and the cost? Have any measures been taken to try to speed up the process to get these buses out onto the streets, or are we just content with the timeframe? Some of these buses, by the NTA's own information it has furnished, are not going to come into use until next year at some stage.

Mr. Hugh Creegan  Most of them will come in this year in quarter 3 over the next few months into Dublin Bus. The Galway ones will be in quarter 4 and quarter 1 next year. Nobody is sitting back comfortable with this. Every effort is being made to try to accelerate the installation of the required charging infrastructure in the depots. People are delivering as fast as they can but we are behind.

An Cathaoirleach  It is deeply unacceptable and concerning, to say the least, particularly when we are talking about such a waste of money here with Irish Rail and now we have the electric buses. I also want to touch on the park-and-ride facility in Fassaroe in my own constituency in Wicklow. Information the NTA has furnished the committee shows that €11 million has been spent. The NTA is nearly praising itself that it came in under budget. The expected budget was €12 million. It came in under budget, to use the witnesses' own words, but the fact that it is locked up and no one can actually use it speaks to that failure to plan forward to ensure the critical piece is put in place initially, which is to ensure there are buses and drivers to actually serve that facility. Does Ms Shaw see what is wrong there?
Ms Anne Shaw  Obviously, the intention was for the opening-----
An Cathaoirleach  I know the intention

Ms Anne Shaw  -----of Fassaroe for this year. It was planned in our budget submissions in terms of the operational costs for that park-and-ride facility as well, but we did not receive the funding we needed to do that. We are in discussions with the Department on what the budget allocations will be for 2027. As the operational costs are on an annual basis-----

An Cathaoirleach  Do the officials in the Department think it is justifiable that an investment to the tune of €11 million to provide critical public transport infrastructure is left locked up, costing €50,000 in additional security costs to ensure that no one can use it? Do they think that is justifiable?

Mr. Tomás Campbell  No. It is deeply regrettable as well. As was outlined earlier to Deputy Neville, however, it does goes back to the budget settlement with the Department of public expenditure this year for the PSO and that is what funds the services.
An Cathaoirleach  So, it is the underfunding that has facilitated this.
Mr. Tomás Campbell  We had a 43% uplift in our core PSO this year and it is now at record level. That puts us on a much more sustainable footing.
An Cathaoirleach  The expectation from the NTA was for funding levels to ensure facilities like this would become available.

Mr. Tomás Campbell  Every Government agency will ask for a budget and it will not get the entirety of the budget in a given year and that does lead to mismatches in terms of when the services will be there, but that would be-----

An Cathaoirleach  On the Fassaroe facility, some critical elements of that infrastructure have not been delivered. There were to be EV charging points and a substation on site there. I believe that was also to serve the plan, which ultimately has been put on the shelf as well, for the Ashford-Rathnew park-and-ride facilities. Will the NTA give the cost for the substation and explain why that is not included in the cost analysis it provided the committee, and will it give us the contract that it says will, ultimately, be given to a third party to provide the EV charging services?

Mr. Hugh Creegan  I thought we had this substation cost included. However, on the chargers, we recognised as we started to go through this and based upon conversations with market providers that just us installing them blindly and not having a payment system for them was the incorrect way. What we are going to do is tender for a provider to provide the charging infrastructure at various bays in the parking location. Members will have seen from the note that we have the ducting and the prerequisite engineering put in place for it. Once we get a supplier identified, we can follow through with the chargers then.  Regarding the Ashford-Rathnew park-and-ride site, the planning consent is agreed, as the committee will know, through the local authority. That is down to the funding. We are in a position to start construction next year but it is questionable whether the funding will be there to do it. It is a question of funding for that particular park-and-ride site.
An Cathaoirleach  It is questionable as to whether Ashford-Rathnew will even commence next year.
Mr. Hugh Creegan  At this stage it is, yes.

An Cathaoirleach  Okay. You might provide a note on that. There have been a lot of announcements, in my own constituency and in others, about rolling out new services. We look at new routes in Wicklow that went out to tender and the Glendalough to Bray service that people are still eagerly awaiting. Funding is not in place. We see over in west Wicklow promises made to enhance and increase the frequency of bus services there and these not being delivered. You might furnish a full note on what services had been planned that have not been able to be delivered this year because of the funding shortfall in the PSO.  The last issue I want to touch on relates to Irish Rail and company vehicles. How many company vehicles are currently in use in Irish Rail?
Ms Mary Considine  I do not have the exact figure. There would be a number of fleet vehicles on the road to support a 24-7 operation around the country. I do not have the exact number.
An Cathaoirleach  I have a figure here of 750.
Ms Mary Considine  It may be correct. I am assuming it is if the Cathaoirleach has it. I would have thought around 600.
An Cathaoirleach  Are they owned or leased?
Ms Mary Considine  They are leased.
An Cathaoirleach  They are all leased. The information I have, which you are not disputing, is that there are 750 leased vehicles in Irish Rail.
Ms Mary Considine  That could be correct. We will have to clarify that. I do not have the figure.

An Cathaoirleach  You might furnish a note to us there because that would be deeply concerning. There are more leased vehicles in Irish Rail than there are rail carriages, which says a lot. You might give us the full breakdown on those, including the costs and the nature and duration of the contracts. There was also a settlement for benefit-in-kind. You might give us some additional information in relation to that, the usage of some of those vehicles. Do you have some of that information to hand?

Ms Mary Considine  Yes. I do not have the exact figures but there was an exercise we conducted earlier on this year - a self-review - to make sure there was no BIK owing in respect of the last number of years. A thorough review was done, an assessment was made and a settlement with the Revenue based on that figure.
An Cathaoirleach  How much was that settlement?
Ms Mary Considine  I think it was around €1 million, but I will confirm that.
An Cathaoirleach  It was €1 million. You might furnish the full detail.
Ms Mary Considine  I will. I just do not have the figures to hand.
An Cathaoirleach  How many vehicles, how many individuals that related to, etc., so if you could give us the full information on that.
Ms Mary Considine  Yes.

An Cathaoirleach  That concludes our engagement today. I thank the chief executive officers and the officials from the NTA and Iarnród Éireann for attending. I also thank the representatives from the Department of Transport the Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General for their attendance once again.  Is it agreed that the clerk will seek any follow-up information required and carry out any agreed actions arising from the meeting? Agreed.  This is the final meeting of the committee until after the summer recess. We will next meet on Thursday, 17 September 2026, to discuss the business of the committee. The committee now stands adjourned. Go raibh míle maith agaibh.
The witnesses withdrew.
The committee adjourned at 2.50 p.m. until 9.30 a.m. on Thursday, 17 September 2026.

debateSection.showAs: Child Protection Matters, Special Care and Special Emergency Care Arrangements: Tusla

text.text: An Cathaoirleach  The item for consideration this morning is a discussion on child protection matters, special care and special emergency arrangements. We are joined at the meeting by representatives of Tusla, as follows: Ms Kate Duggan, CEO; Ms Rosarii Mannion, national director for people and change; Mr. Pat Smyth, national director for finance and corporate services; and Mr. Gerry Hone, national director of services and integration. They are all very welcome back to the committee. I congratulate them on the launch of their annual report yesterday.  Before we begin, I have a couple of housekeeping matters to go through. We have one member joining us on Teams. For that member, I give a reminder that the chat function should only be used to make the team on site aware of technical or urgent matters. There is a constitutional requirement for members to be present on the Leinster House complex in order to participate in public meetings.  In advance of our witnesses delivering their opening statements, I advise them of the following in respect of parliamentary privilege. They are protected by absolute privilege in respect of the presentation they make to the committee. This means that they have an absolute defence against any defamation action for anything they say at the meeting. However, they are expected not to abuse this privilege and it is my duty, as Cathaoirleach, to ensure the privilege is not abused. Therefore, if their statements are potentially defamatory in relation to an identifiable person or entity, they will be directed to discontinue their remarks. It is imperative that they comply with any such direction. I ask them to bear in mind that if we are talking about specific locations, they are sometimes easily identifiable.  Ms Duggan will be allocated five minutes to deliver her opening statement, which will be followed by a question-and-answer session with our members. I invite her to deliver her opening statement.

Ms Kate Duggan  I thank the Chair and the committee for the invitation to appear to discuss child protection matters, special care and special emergency arrangements. I am joined by my colleagues: Ms Rosarii Mannion, national director for people and change; Mr. Pat Smyth, national director for finance and corporate services; and Mr. Gerry Hone, national director of services and integration.  Tusla's mission is to support the safety and well-being of children, particularly those whose circumstances are complex or who need additional support. At the outset, it is important to highlight that staff across the country engage with tens of thousands of families every year and the majority of those interactions are positive and successful, helping people to grow up safely. As an agency, we responded to over 106,000 referrals in 2025, an increase of more than 10% since the agency was established in 2014, and almost 6,000 children and young people were in the care of Tusla. Almost nine in ten young people in the care of the State are living with loving foster carers and engaged in school and education or living in residential care homes, homes like yours or mine, where one, two, three or four young people are being looked after by caring, committed and dedicated staff.  At the end of quarter 3 of 2025, there were 2,985 young people receiving an aftercare service. Some 84% of those aged 18 to 22 in receipt of aftercare services are now in education and training. There has been a 500% increase in referrals to our separated children seeking international protection service. In 2025, there were almost 800 referrals to the service, with approximately 1,200 unaccompanied minors in care or accommodated by Tusla throughout 2025. Most of our work is preventative, supporting school attendance, ensuring childcare facilities are safe and helping families through difficult times before a crisis hits. We support thousands of families every year so that children can stay safely at home.  In relation to child safety work, we are challenged by the increasingly complex needs of a small cohort of vulnerable young people. We are seeing a marked increase in the number of children presenting with highly complex needs, including mental health challenges, substance misuse, disabilities, exploitation and behaviours linked to criminality.  In the area of special emergency arrangements, SEAs, we have acknowledged that due to our shortage of registered residential placements, we had to rely on these types of arrangements as an immediate place of safety for young people. However, we have made significant progress in how emergency placements for young people are provided and governed. From June 2026, no special emergency arrangements are used by the agency. All emergency placements instead operate as either registered private residential centres, Tusla emergency centres or private emergency placements, each with clear statutory oversight, governance and accountability.  In relation to special care, I fully acknowledge and sincerely regret the current situation where we are unable to fulfil our statutory obligations to provide timely access to special care for all young people subject to a High Court order and the impact this may have on these young people. This is because of inadequate staffing levels in special care to operate at full capacity. With the support of our parent Department, the Department of Children, Disability and Equality, we are completely focused on making every effort to increase our staffing levels in special care through expansion of qualifications, national and international recruitment campaigns, graduate sponsorship schemes, increasing third-level placements and the introduction of our social work apprenticeship and social care work-based learning programmes. We are more confident that these efforts in conjunction with the introduction of the new special care worker grade in 2025, as approved by Department of public expenditure and reform, and the new Tusla residential and special care training college, will see additional special care beds opened in 2026-27.  I have spoken publicly about the programme of reform under way across the agency since 2023. This has resulted in increased supply, recruitment and retention of staff, an increase in placement capacity, more robust oversight of third-party providers, digital transformation with the introduction of a single child and family record across all Tusla services and better access to more integrated community services for children and families across Ireland.  As an agency, we acknowledge that we continue to experience challenges in the context of such increased demand for our services and our inability to ensure that all children and families receive the right service at the right time. However, we are confident that as we continue to embed our reform programme, and with increased support, better inter-agency and intergovernmental policy commitments, that children in the care of the State should be prioritised for State services and children and families can be better supported in their communities so that all children and young people have the opportunity for better outcomes and brighter futures.  I thank the Cathaoirleach and the committee for the opportunity to engage today. I look forward to the committee's upcoming visit to our special care, residential care, separated children seeking international protection and emergency centres. I am happy to answer any questions members may have today.

An Cathaoirleach  We are also looking forward to our visit. I thank Ms Duggan for facilitating us and the members of the committee for agreeing to visit during recess. It is proposed to publish the opening statement to the Oireachtas website. Is that agreed? Agreed.  I remind members they will be allocated seven minutes speaking time. This allocation must include the response from the witnesses. I will allow a brief round of questioning, if members indicate they want that. I ask members when putting their questions to adhere strictly to the agenda item under consideration and to direct their question to the witness they wish to respond.

Deputy Daniel Ennis  This is my first time meeting Tusla and I am looking forward to working with it. I thank Ms Duggan for the opening statement. I see Tusla as a safety net for our young people. There are obvious tears in that safety net. Working together, we can hopefully mend them and provide better care and service options for our young people, especially the vulnerable and those who find themselves in precarious positions.  I have a couple of questions to get a better understanding. There was data relating to the number of children in care in the opening statement. Could Ms Duggan provide the committee with the most recent figures for children and young people in foster care, registered private residential centres, Tusla emergency centres and private emergency placements? On the ending of the special emergency arrangements, what structures, commitments and protections are we going to get to ensure that it is not just a rebranding or a changing of the jersey? I would like to get a better understanding of that.  Regarding Tusla's budget for registered placements, will Ms Duggan indicate whether the budget for capital expenditure has increased, decreased or remained constant over the years? As of 5 July, 78 young people were in temporary emergency accommodation, which was two fewer than the previous week, as was mentioned. Where are they placed? In what constituencies, cities or counties are they placed, without giving the exact address for obvious reasons?  The preventative piece is very important. I do a lot of work around preventative measures with children, including children in care, children in precarious positions and children in forced criminalisation, such as grooming by drug gangs. We know that children in care and the vulnerable children we are dealing with are more susceptible to that. Regarding Tusla's engagement with schools and services, in my constituency of Dublin Central, Young People at Risk, YPAR, do a lot of work with young people at risk. What is Tusla's engagement with YPAR and the other services like? When I say "services", I mean State bodies, national governing bodies, NGBs, and community groups in and around the Dublin Central area because we know the number of children living there who find themselves in emergency and homeless accommodation.

Ms Kate Duggan  We would be delighted to meet the Deputy separately to go through any particular issues relating to his constituency or more generally. I will provide very high-level data. At the end of May 2026, 5,948 children were in the care of the State. That is about 3% more than the same period last year so we are seeing a marginal increase in the number of children coming into care. Of those numbers, almost 86% were in foster care, which is something we are very proud of. It is the highest level in Europe. There is a real focus on continuing to increase recruitment and retention of foster carers so that children in care can be in foster care. Out of that, 626 children, or about 11%, are in residential care across the community and voluntary sector, Tusla and the private sector. There are 255 young people who would be in care but might be in a disability-specific centre, supported lodgings, a temporary emergency or emergency placement or an out-of-State placement. We can give the Deputy a full breakdown if he wants those figures. Mr. Smyth will talk the Deputy through the budget for capital expenditure.  On temporary emergency placements, in child protection there is always a need for emergency placement if a section 12 is invoked by An Garda Síochána. If there is an immediate breakdown in a home, residential or foster care placement, we have to have that available. To put it in some context, about 1% of children in care need access to an emergency placement. This week, 58 young people are in what we describe as a temporary emergency placement.  I will use a very high-level example to reassure the Deputy that it is not a changing of the narrative or a changing of the jersey. At the end of June, there were 76 young people in a special emergency arrangement and rightly so. The public, this committee, the Government and everybody wanted to make sure because the biggest concern we had was that those placements were not registered or regulated so there was no external oversight. While Tusla had internal oversight of them, there was no external oversight. What has changed now is that about one third of those young people are now in children's residential centres so those centres are registered. We have worked with those providers. New providers did enter the market and we have spent the past 12 to 18 months working with those providers to help them achieve the standards they needed to achieve to become registered centres.  One third of the young people in question are in registered centres which, like any children's residential service, are subject to inspection and monitoring by the Tusla alternative care inspection monitoring service. It is important to say that this is the service that monitors and inspects every private or voluntary centre. We would like it to be HIQA and have advocated for that function to transfer to HIQA. HIQA is aware of that and that is something we really want to push for and to happen.  The next third of young people are in centres that were unable to achieve registration. The providers were unable to achieve registration so we have taken those under the governance of Tusla and they are now subject to inspection and monitoring by HIQA like any Tusla residential centre.  Regarding the other third of young people, any newly opened centre has 45 days to register.  There may be an emergency tonight. The young person involved would need to be placed in a centre. It may not be centre that is registered today, but within 45 days it has to be registered under the Act or that child would be transferred to a Tusla-governed centre. That is the timeline of 45 days, which was not in place before and in the context of which we would engage with the provided involved in order to seek to support them to become registered. At a very high level, that is the difference. All the young people involved are in those placements. Mr. Smyth might talk about the budget capital expenditure.  We have run out of time, but one of the priorities for us, work under the reform programme, regarding the engagement is that commissioning is now devolved regionally and at network level. Every network will be working with community groups and with the community and voluntary sector to understand what the needs of the local population are and whether providers have been engaged. If it would be helpful, I would be happy to meet with the Deputy separately to discuss the matter.
An Cathaoirleach  I will let Mr. Smyth reply to Deputy Ennis in the second round.

Deputy Charles Ward  I thank the witnesses for coming in. Social care workers have raised concerns about the use of security personnel. They report that security personnel are stepping in to restrain children before a full therapeutic intervention can be carried out. The deployment of untrained security staff is having a serious effect in the context of the ability of social care workers to perform their duties. There are reports of security staff removing social care workers from rooms against their will. There are concerns that while staff need be protected, there is uncertainty among security workers as to when intervention is required in these settings. What training is given to security personnel from Tusla before they are deployed in these extremely challenging settings?

Ms Kate Duggan  I am concerned to hear what the Deputy had to say. In terms of our experience, as he rightly stated, we have an obligation to keep children. However, under the health and safety Act, we also have an obligation to keep staff safe. We have had significant incidents of violence, harassment and aggression within the service. That is not in any way to put blame on the young people involved. Those young people have experienced significant trauma. Their behaviours reflect an escalation in that trauma. Often, they act out. Injuries may be caused to staff as a result. When we looked at this, we found that there was a need to employ close protection personnel, which is how they are described. We went out to tender for the contract and the process in that regard was successful. These personnel are only used in exceptional circumstances. They do not replace staff. We have worked very hard with HIQA on a policy to ensure that they meet all the standards involved and our regulatory requirements. That was very important. HIQA is the regulator and the independent voice of safety in respect of children and young people.  What we have seen is a significant reduction in the level of violence, harassment and aggression. We only bring security personnel in on an exceptional basis. They are additional to our rota and are not counted as staff. They are there to protect staff. They receive therapeutic crisis intervention training. What we have heard is that staff are very slow to want to engage with this, but the request for it comes from the service. The service comes and says that it is concerned about the safety of staff. We went through a tender process to ensure that we had companies that were used to this work. These personnel are only deployed in line with the policy agreed with HIQA.
Deputy Charles Ward  How many incidences of physical restraint have occurred in residential areas in the past two years?
Ms Kate Duggan  I do not have the figure for that with me. I will send it to the Deputy afterwards. We will take a note of that.
Deputy Charles Ward  How many people were restrained by security personnel as opposed to registered social care workers?
Ms Kate Duggan  Again, I do not have that data with me. I will get it to the Deputy early next week.

Deputy Charles Ward  I have not been told that time is up, so I will keep on going. The Cathaoirleach can keep me straight.  Social care workers have expressed concerns about the new Tusla college. They say that those who graduate from it will be deployed to the most serious and challenging settings but that they will not even be CORU registered or regulated. Will Ms Duggan explain how this prioritises the safety of children?
Ms Kate Duggan  My colleague Ms Mannion will answer that question.

Ms Rosarii Mannion  I am happy to meet with the Deputy and to give him a tour of the college if he would like. The college was established primarily in the interests of us being self-sufficient and to facilitate us in producing our own pipeline of staff. The curriculum is vigorous. It involves three months in the college and three months in placement, followed by an assessment. If colleagues are deemed suitable to work, they are then deployed to various settings, including special care and other settings, across the agency. We have found so far that the staff coming through are of a high quality and are working very well. There have been no incidents of violence, harassment and aggression. This is broader than special care and social care; it is about a building platform to bride the gap between college and the workplace in order to ensure that, as much as possible, we are setting new graduates up for success.  Regarding the question on qualified social care workers, we have arrangements whereby we have expanded the qualifications. Anybody on expanded qualifications may work in our setting. Only somebody who is registered with CORU as a social care worker, which is a title protected in law since last year, may call themselves a social care worker. However, we are moving towards multidisciplinary team working. We want colleagues with addiction, community and youth work and, indeed, sporting qualifications. There are a broad range of qualifications there that make up the composition of effective multidisciplinary teams that can then engage and meet the holistic needs of children. It is not always a case that one single discipline can meet the needs of children who we serve. As the Deputy knows, the needs are complex and far-reaching. The best model is a fully functioning multidisciplinary team. From the evidence, we know that what colleagues want are safe places of work, safe systems and safe and effective colleagues. That is the model that we work through in terms of our people's strategy and, in particular, the use of our Tulsa internal training college.

Deputy Charles Ward  Regarding the thousands of social care workers who have gone through registering with CORU, does this mean nothing for them or will there be a distinct forward transitional period of them moving over and enhancing their qualifications?

Ms Rosarii Mannion  It may be a case of needing to enhance qualifications. Nobody is deployed to the workplace until we are happy that they meet the standard and are qualified. There is nobody who is unqualified working across our services.

Deputy John Connolly  I welcome the witnesses and thank Ms Duggan for her opening statement. Regarding some of the data in the opening statement, the agency responded to over 106,000 referrals in 2025. What proportion of those referrals met the threshold for the assignment of a social worker?

Ms Kate Duggan  I will give the Deputy very broad numbers. We know that about 60% of our referrals relate to children, young people and families who require that early intervention and support perspective. At any one time within the past year, there were about 23,000 children and young people that were open to social work and needed a social worker. In the context of allocation, what we have to do is make sure that we prioritise the allocation of social workers to those who most need them . We have spoken here before about the challenge that we have with the supply of social workers across the State. It is very clear that social workers can only do certain statutory duties. This comes back to what my colleague Ms Mannion spoke about in terms of expanded qualifications. At any one time, about 90% of our children in care have allocated social workers. Where a child does not have an allocated social worker, they may have an allocated social care worker to meet their needs, but that person will not perform the statutory duties of a social worker. In the context of our overall caseload, about 78% or 79% of children open to our safety teams would be allocated social workers. The others would be allocated social care workers to meet their needs.
Deputy John Connolly  To be clear, if a referral is made where there is a concern that a child is at risk of abuse-----
Ms Kate Duggan  They are screened within 24 hours by a social worker.
Deputy John Connolly  They are screened by a social worker.
Ms Kate Duggan  Yes.
Deputy John Connolly  That social worker will decide whether the referral requires further intervention.
Ms Kate Duggan  Yes.
Deputy John Connolly  Are all those calls screened by a social worker?
Ms Kate Duggan  Yes.

Deputy John Connolly  Okay. Very good.  The opening statement states:  Almost nine in ten young people in the care of the State are living with loving foster carers and engaged in school and education or living in residential care homes ...  Is that one in ten who is living in a residential care home?
Ms Kate Duggan  Yes, it is about that.
Deputy John Connolly  So nine in ten are with foster carers and one in ten is in a care home.
Ms Kate Duggan  At the moment it is 87%, so almost one-----

Deputy John Connolly  Yes, and the description of them is "where one, two, three or four young people are being looked after by caring, committed and dedicated staff", but the setting is a residential setting.
Ms Kate Duggan  Yes.

Deputy John Connolly  Last week we had the Children's Residential and Aftercare Voluntary Association, CRAVA, in with us. It had a number of concerns, one being that it felt a rebalance was required of preference towards the voluntary sector capacity to reduce over-reliance on for-profit care. Do we have the data as to those facilities Ms Duggan has described, "where one, two, three or four young people are being looked after by caring, committed and dedicated staff"? What proportion of those settings is run by the voluntary sector and what proportion is run by for-profit organisations?

Ms Kate Duggan  At a point in time in the year, if we took 535 young people who are in residential care, 71 of them were in community and voluntary sector placements. Then there was the percentage, which Mr. Smyth can give the Deputy, who were in Tusla centres and then the percentage who were in private centres. We set out about three years ago to seek to rebalance the provision of residential care away from private residential into community and voluntary and Tusla-led facilities, and that is a commitment we hold dear. What has been challenging for us, on one hand, is the number of separated children. I said that 1,200 had to be accommodated last year alone. As to how quickly that came upon us, the private sector was able to scale at a quicker capacity than the public sector in terms of having the infrastructure available. It is also important to say that we have engaged all the time with the community and voluntary sector to seek to increase the provision of care that it provides and it has not been able to do that. Currently, in July, it is funded for 94 beds. We fund it irrespective of whether the bed is occupied or not. That is a challenge. Within the private sector we pay only for a bed that is occupied. Out of the 94 beds it was funded for, it was able to have only 71 of those beds open, and that is a concern for us.  In addition, I listened to the hearing last week and, as I said, we are very much supportive of the community and voluntary sector, but we have seen in the past 12 months that the community and voluntary sector has discharged nine young people out of its services into a special emergency arrangement. It is very important that we work collectively to recognise the challenges that are there, both from the point of view of the sector being able to recruit staffing and in terms of capital expenditure. That is the biggest challenge it has.
Deputy John Connolly  Is staffing the reason there are 23 beds vacant?

Ms Kate Duggan  Some of it is to do with staffing and some of it is to do with the fact that the sector feels there is a risk to the health and safety of its staff who are there. All of us are challenged by the fact that we have responsibility to children and young people, that we hold them in their stable placement, that we provide wraparound supports, that we support them and that we do not discharge them into special emergency arrangements.
Deputy John Connolly  Ms Duggan said 12 were discharged.
Ms Kate Duggan  Nine.
Deputy John Connolly  Excuse me. That was in 2025.
Ms Kate Duggan  It was in the past 12 months.
Deputy John Connolly  How many are residing in Tusla centres?

Mr. Pat Smyth  We had 116 at the end of May, so between the numbers in the community and voluntary sector and in our own centres, about 35% or thereabouts are between State and voluntary placements. The balance then is private.
Deputy John Connolly  If I may ask about the 1,200 unaccompanied minors in care, are they part of the 6,000 young people in total? No. They are additional to the 6,000.
Ms Kate Duggan  Yes.
Deputy John Connolly  Tusla has responsibility for 7,200 young people.
Ms Kate Duggan  Over the whole year, there were 1,200 young people.
Deputy John Connolly  Over the course of the year. Okay.
Ms Kate Duggan  At the moment, just under 500 separated children are being accommodated or supported.
Deputy John Connolly  They are referred to Tusla from-----
Ms Kate Duggan  The International Protection Office.
Deputy John Connolly  Is that because of Tusla's remit specifically to care for the children?
Ms Kate Duggan  Yes.
Deputy John Connolly  They are not being referred over any concern for their safety or health or well-being.
Ms Kate Duggan  They are unaccompanied. They are on their own, with no known adult to support them.

Senator Nessa Cosgrove  I thank the witnesses for coming in. Last week was really important in that CRAVA was in and it outlined that if we are looking at aftercare, it is about the provision of a service rather than about money. Ms Duggan said there were young people who were moved from a voluntary and community setting into special emergency care. For that to happen, I imagine that things must have been very difficult and maybe the ratio of staff to children was at play, although I do not know. In fairness to CRAVA, it said last week that Tusla is very supportive but that it is running on a very tight budget. Money is always limiting it in developing its own capacity as regards buildings. When young people are in care, would the witnesses say that the voluntary and community sector or Tusla itself always comes ahead of the private sector?

Ms Kate Duggan  As I said, we want to expand Tusla or the community and voluntary sector over the private sector. That is our absolute commitment as a public service. It is very important to say that we pay the community and voluntary sector a grant, irrespective of the number of young people who are on placement. That is something we do not do in the private sector. In addition, the cost we give the community and voluntary sector is actually more than that which we give the private sector, not just in terms of bed occupancy levels. Mr. Smyth can give the detail if the Senator wants it. The cost of a private placement works out just slightly lower than the cost of a Tusla or a community and voluntary one. We also have a scheme in place with the community and voluntary sector whereby if there is particular damage done to a property or an instance of concern, the provider can apply for funding. I recognise the challenge the community and voluntary sector faces. We value the relationship with it and we want to support it to scale, but it is struggling, I think, to get the staffing. More important, I think the biggest challenge for the community and voluntary sector is not having the ability to fund capital investment in terms of building residential homes.

Senator Nessa Cosgrove  Whose responsibility is that, though? Surely it is not the sector's. If it gets a certain amount of money, is it for Tusla to say to the Department that it has to provide more money? If you are measuring key performance indicators or looking at outcomes, is it just based on cost-----
Ms Kate Duggan  No.
Senator Nessa Cosgrove  -----or is it based on social outcomes as well?

Ms Kate Duggan  Yes. God, it would never be a decision just around cost. We are saying the principle we have is that, as a public sector body, we want further investment. We want to rebalance the provision of care into Tusla statutory centres and community and voluntary centres. They are separate entities, and there are separate governance structures and separate boards. It is a wider discussion about whether the State will invest capital in separate entities. That is a wider discussion about the State's decision around capital investment in the community and voluntary sector.

Senator Nessa Cosgrove  If religious organisations had buildings available, would it be an option for them to work with the voluntary and community sector to increase its capacity? Is it Tusla that is looking to increase that capacity? The last thing we want to do is go down the route of private sector provision for the most vulnerable children in the State.  At all costs, we should avoid giving that over to private companies because their ultimate game is to make money. That is what a private company does. Are there ways to work around this, perhaps with other Departments, so capacity can be increased within the voluntary and community sector in terms of buildings?

Ms Kate Duggan  I suppose it is about what is within our control. We worked a lot with the voluntary sector in 2023 and 2024 in terms of the cost-of-living increase and the inflationary measures, and we secures an extra €5.2 million for the providers we work with to support them to bridge some of that funding gap. As part of the Workplace Relations Commission agreement, additional funding has been given for staffing levels. In terms of the capital infrastructure we get now, we are only starting. From 2018 to 2023, Tusla did not have the full capital investment it needed to open additional residential units. It is costly to open them. We have invested and opened our own statutory residential units over that period, which has been great. A decision will have to come, from beyond Tusla, around the State's position on capital investment in the community and voluntary sector. We will work with that, obviously. We advocate for and represent the community and voluntary sector all the time.  Where possible, particularly in our separated children service, we have put a hybrid model in place. That is a Tusla-owned building, but one of the community and voluntary providers is staffing and running it for us. We are looking at any opportunity to be able to do that. CRAVA, or any of the community and voluntary sector providers, would recognise that capital investment is the most significant barrier to being able to scale their capacity.

Senator Nessa Cosgrove  Exactly. The providers said that themselves. Should this committee be contacting the Department to ask why it is not funding this capital expenditure? Ultimately, we do not want the care of children to be given over to private providers. The question we have to raise as a committee is whether the State has a long-term plan for children in care.

Ms Kate Duggan  The first thing to say about the long-term plan is that the Department of children is finalising the whole-of-government alternative care policy, which we have contributed to. CRAVA and wider stakeholders have all contributed to that. We are really looking forward to seeing that policy and whole-of-government commitment on the provision of care to children across the State. Within that, we would hope to see prioritisation given across Government Departments to children in care, whether that involves access to housing or health services and maybe decisions around capital investment.  The community and voluntary sector is a small one in terms of the provision of residential facilities. It is about looking at what that sector's capacity is. It certainly has additional capacity in the aftercare space. We work with a huge number of community and voluntary services, almost 500, in respect of the provision of community services. It is a huge partnership for us. It is a more specific matter for the residential aspect. The cost of opening a children's residential home that is compliant with the standards expected by HIQA and under the regulations is a significant investment.
Senator Nessa Cosgrove  If we look at-----
An Cathaoirleach  I thank Senator Cosgrove. Her time is up.
Senator Nessa Cosgrove  I am sorry.

Deputy Claire Kerrane  I thank everyone for being here this morning and for the opening statement and briefing document. I will come back to the residential services provided by the voluntary and community sector in particular. The last time Ms Duggan was here the point was made that the sector has not been able to expand. With respect, it is obvious that the voluntary and community sector has not been able to expand. The providers make no profit and have no surplus. Any unspent money is returned. They physically have no way to do that. In fairness to them, they were clear when they were here last week in laying that at the Department's door and not Tusla's in terms of funding. At my request, the committee has written to the Minister asking her to look at greater funding specifically for that sector in the next budget. That is very important. The providers' hands are tied.  In terms of beds funded and beds not opened, I visited one of the homes and it is very much like walking into a family home. There is capacity for four children per house. If a child is referred to one of these homes and that child has behavioural issues, the children already in the home naturally have to be considered because the environment is so compact and its nature is different from the environment in a wider centre. It is important to make this point in respect of what Ms Duggan has said. Interestingly enough, she referred to staffing. Staffing was not raised to any great extent. I have met CRAVA separately. These providers actually hold their staff fairly well. The staff I met had 100 years of experience among them, as did many of those who were here last week.  The community and voluntary providers also raised issues with the system as it is. If they receive a referral, they cannot accept that referral, and nobody wants to be in that position. Weeks and weeks are wasted with an over-and-back process. Tusla looks and the providers look, and a system is in place, and that is fine. The providers have a bed vacant, but because it takes so long when they refuse, they are left with a vacant bed they do not really want. Perhaps the system could be looked at. It is something the providers have flagged. There should be an element of trust in cases where a provider cannot accept a child. Tusla should acknowledge that it is not doing that willy-nilly, and if it cannot accept a child, it cannot accept that child. Rather than having a bed empty for weeks when there are more children on that list, perhaps we could be a bit more efficient. I ask Ms Duggan to look at that.  Ms Duggan said that Tusla engages all the time with the community and voluntary sector. When did she last meet CRAVA? How often are these meetings? I ask because my understanding was that there were quarterly meetings at the beginning. I stand to be corrected on that, however. As far as I understand, these meetings have not been happening. Where there are issues, it would make sense to meet, sit down, discuss the fact that 70 of 90 beds are open and determine why it is the case. It would make sense to have that engagement and conversation, but I am not sure that is happening. That is to the detriment of the providers and of Tusla. If these meetings are not happening, it would be helpful to get them back on track.

Ms Kate Duggan  Regarding the four-bed unit the Deputy described, it is the same for the Tusla centres, which I hope she will get to visit in two weeks. It is the same for the private sector. That is where children live now. They do not live in centres; they live in homes. The challenge we all have is that, where we do not have placements, we have to look at what can be done. There may be a behavioural challenge, but it is about how we look at that from the point of view of the risk. We have to work with that child and the support services to allow us to say we are still going to take that young person because we are not going to put them into a temporary emergency placement. We have to look at that in the round. We all face the same challenges. Across the community and voluntary sector, the private sector and Tusla, we do not want children in temporary emergency placements. We want those homes at full occupancy, with additional supports put in around the child, if needed. It is important to say that.  In terms of the efficiency of the process, I assure the Deputy that we spend every day trying to make sure every bed is occupied. We are talking about approximately 60 young people out of the 6,000 in care who do not have a permanent home, which is what we want for them. The rounded view of the issue always needs to be looked at.  In terms of engagements, CRAVA does not represent all our community and voluntary providers. In 2026, to date, there have been three meetings with CRAVA. We have met the group three times. I have not met the group since 2025. I met it two or three times in 2025, in Portarlington and Athlone, and I cannot remember where the third visit was. We also have a children's residential services, CRS, employers' forum that we set up with the community and voluntary sector, across the community, Tusla and the private sectors. There were seven meetings in 2025 with those providers. There have been three meetings to date. The forum looks at wider staffing issues, staffing qualifications, ratios, terms and conditions, training and development, and all of that. So far in 2026, there have been 22 meetings with the 11 providers that we work with in the community and voluntary sector through our service level agreements. While CRAVA is a representative group of a small number of providers, it is also important to say that individual providers have individual issues.  We have also set up a new forum, which was very important, involving the chairs of the boards of directors of the community and voluntary sector. It considers some of the issues that existed around things like capital infrastructure and governance. The forum is headed by Tusla's director of children's residential services, who is the most appropriate person, and also includes our head of commissioning, our residential services finance manager and our commissioning lead. We had meetings with the chairs of the boards of those residential providers in November 2025, March 2026 and May 2026 and there will be another one in September 2026.  The message of non-engagement between Tusla and the sector is one that is a little bit disingenuous.

Deputy Claire Kerrane  I take all of that. That is why I wanted to put them to Ms Duggan. I appreciate that.  If a child with behavioural issues is in a private-run service and needs additional services, the private service can come to Tusla and look for a line of money to support that and put in whatever is needed. Can the voluntary sector do that?
Ms Kate Duggan  Yes. Any child in foster care.
Deputy Claire Kerrane  The voluntary and community sector can get additional money for a child beyond what their weekly----

Ms Kate Duggan  A difference is that they can also get money, which the private sector cannot, for property damage or emergency repairs. That is built into the cost of the private provision. Within the community and voluntary sector at the moment, it is approximately €1.3 million a year for four beds, irrespective of occupancy levels. For the private sector, that is approximately €1.25 million.
Deputy Claire Kerrane  There is a process that takes a number of weeks if a referral is refused. Could that be looked at?

Ms Kate Duggan  It can. A child can be refused but another child would be named very quickly. As the Deputy knows, we would never assure her that every system affecting every child was perfect on every occasion, but we have daily data now where we look at occupancy levels. I am very happy to share a report like this with the committee that sets out on a daily level all of our occupancy levels across all of the sectors. We have even advertised for another post to look at this. We want 99% or 100% of our beds filled every night because young people deserve to be in a registered residential home.

Deputy Aisling Dempsey  I thank the witnesses for being here. When we had CRAVA here last week, I spoke to it about aftercare. I believe it was Mr. Gordon Hill who said that even the word "aftercare" was not appropriate and described how inadequate some people felt aftercare was at the moment. From speaking to different people, I feel it is very inflexible. For example, a child in care who finishes education, goes to work and then wants to return to education is told that they will have to give up work for 11 months before they can access that. I wanted to ask the witnesses about this, starting with the name. Are there any plans or moves to change it and make it more descriptive and positive? To improve aftercare, is there any consultation ongoing or has any been done with foster carers and the children who are coming out of care?

Ms Kate Duggan  It is important to say that aftercare has been there traditionally because the legislation and regulations refer to aftercare post 18 years of age. We implement Government policy in terms of legislation and policy on children and young people being supported in aftercare up to the age of 23 if they are in education and training. One of the challenges, certainly when I came to the agency and just before that, was around the recognition that these young people, the same as any young person, may not have been ready to stay in education and training or to go to formal third level education. We have put a lot of supports into organisations like Way 2 Work, where young people over the age of 18 are not ready to go into what would be perceived as third level education but are engaged in training, for example, Safe Pass courses or training supporting them to work in construction. We make sure that all of those young people are considered to be in education and training and are supported. I provided some data earlier. We know that over 80% of young people in aftercare are now in education and training, which is very important. My colleague, Mr. Hone, might want to come in on aftercare.

Mr. Gerry Hone  There are approximately 3,000 young people in receipt of a leaving and aftercare service from the agency. I agree with the Deputy about the name being far from ideal. I know that is being addressed within the Department and the alternative care strategy. That has had some discussion and there is a group looking at it. However, because the title is embedded in legislation, guidance and everything else, it would mean quite a lot of change to change it. It would have to be planned very carefully and might even need some language to be changed in legislation as well. That is the difficulty. I agree that it is far from ideal in terms of the title.  From the age of 16, a leaving and aftercare plan begins to be developed for every young person who is in care. Each network has a steering group that looks at the plan for young people leaving care. When there are specific needs around health, disability or housing, there is a steering group put in place to make sure that the young person's needs are met within the plan when they leave. A lot of young people stay with their foster carers. There is a high percentage, like our own children, who will stay at home. It is their home, it is their care placement. That is supported fully by the agency.  The Deputy mentioned an anomaly in terms of somebody not being told that they were not entitled to something. Our policy is not so strict that we cannot look at individual circumstances and, given the circumstance, identify the best response to that young adult in that situation to help them move on. I regularly deal with requests that fall outside the policy on one level to actually look at such situations and see if we can do anything about them. Generally, we reach solutions. I am happy to discuss all that with the Deputy separately, no problem.

Ms Kate Duggan  The Deputy asked about engagement with foster carers. I have just finished engagements all over the country with foster carers. We fund Empowering People in Care, EPIC, and I am meeting its youth council next week. The issues that are raised from that policy perspective are on extending the age of aftercare beyond 23. That has been widely acknowledged by young people who are seeking that as a policy change. There are also the challenges they face, similar to other young people, in being able to access mental health services, if there are issues around addiction, and also the housing challenges that are facing all young people within society currently. They are probably the top three things that would be flagged to me in terms of the challenges they face.

Deputy Aisling Dempsey  Sticking with the issue of aftercare services, I have only just got to scan yesterday's report and have not read through it completely. It indicates that 43% remained with their carers. What is the breakdown of the "14% other"?

Ms Kate Duggan  I do not have that data. I can get the exact breakdown for the Deputy. When we talk about "other" in that context, for example, we fund some of the community and voluntary sector where there are dedicated supports for young people in aftercare who may be experiencing some complexities in terms of mental health or addiction. Some of them may be in an addiction service. That is just a very high-level example. I do not want to be rustling papers but I can get the breakdown of the 14% for the Deputy.
Deputy Aisling Dempsey  I thank Ms Duggan.

Mr. Gerry Hone  There is a cohort that requires specialist services, especially under the disability heading. There will be some young people in specialist disability centres as well when they turn 18 because that is seen as their need.

Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  Cuirim fáilte roimh Kate Duggan agus an fhoireann uilig. The special emergency arrangements have been completely factored out at this point. I believe everyone is glad to see that. There are 78 children and young people in temporary emergency placements. Is the difference that those placements have HIQA inspections?

Ms Kate Duggan  I explained it earlier but yes, there are 56 today in placements. When we changed SEAs, 20 of those providers or centres became registered centres so they are like any children's residential home. Of other 56 young people about half are in a centre Tusla has taken over the governance and oversight of, which means it is subject to HIQA inspection and monitoring, which is what we wanted to happen. As for the others, under the Act we can have temporary emergency centres but the young person can only be placed in that centre for a maximum time of 45 days until that centre achieves registration or else the young person moves to one of the centres that is under Tusla's governance.
Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  They are like a temporary SEA, they just cannot continue the way they did but-----
Ms Kate Duggan  They are in line with the Act.
Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  -----they are on the way to being recognised.
Ms Kate Duggan  They are engaged with us from the beginning. They have to indicate to us they are seeking to become registered centres.

Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  That is good. As much as we want these factored out, they were born from an emergency need. It has been said in general terms that at times the threshold for kids being taken into care has probably risen in the last while. I get the work Tusla is going to do from the point of view that in the best-case scenario it maintains the family unit and all the rest of it, but needs fall into this. Has that created an issue in the last while in the sense the agency did not have the SEAs as a means of dealing with more complex cases? I would like to know the number of social workers we have and by how many we are still short, the same for social care workers and then also foster carers. I am working on the basis they are still about 500 short.

Ms Kate Duggan  Mr. Hone will be happy to talk about the concern the Deputy is expressing about children coming into care. I referenced earlier we are seeing an increase in the number of children coming into care but I recognise there is an increase in the population, so we have to contextualise that. Mr. Hone can come in quickly and then Ms Mannion can talk the Deputy through the staffing numbers.  On foster carers, we have set out the numbers there. We have seen an increase for the first time in a number of years. It is a small increase of 12 but we are putting a significant amount of work into fostering. We talk about the fact 87% of children in care are in foster care and we are a European leader within that. We would like that to be higher. We would like to get back up to 90% or 91%. For that we would need about another 480 or 500 foster families. That would take us far beyond any international number. We are cognisant that is very ambitious but that is what we work to.
Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  Tusla does not have full control over selling that, because obviously there are pieces that foster carers have requested that need governmental interventions.
Ms Kate Duggan  Society is also changing in terms of-----
Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  I get that.
Ms Kate Duggan  -----people wanting to foster and open their homes to fostering. Mr. Hone will address children coming into care and Ms Mannion the staff numbers.

Mr. Gerry Hone  I thank the Deputy for his question. I think he asked whether the possibility that we might not have the special emergency arrangements could create a problem. The service has not gone away. This service is still available but we now have it in a regulated space. As such there is a process around it and for providers there are expectations around approval when they come in to a temporary emergency arrangement. It is under section 36(1)(d) of the Act. There is a set amount of time in which they have to apply for registration. There is a certain amount of time in which they have to achieve that registration. If they cannot, then it comes under Tusla governance and hence HIQA, because it has come in. All the time in the background we are trying to increase our capacity for emergency provision internally. We are in the process of buying properties, setting up emergency services and we are about to go out to tender on the provision for emergency beds in the system. On our reform programme, and Ms Mannion has already alluded to this, when a case comes in and we are looking at the needs of young person we are broadening our skills base through social care workers, social care leaders, family support workers and social workers. They are all working together and under joint protocols with the Garda and the HSE-----
Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  But we do not have enough of them.
Mr. Gerry Hone  -----to make sure needs are met.

Ms Rosarii Mannion  I thank the Deputy for his question. We have more social workers and social care workers in the agency than we ever had but of course we need more. At the end of March we had 1,713 social workers and 1,307 social care workers. At today's date we are looking to recruit in the region of 450 social workers and social care workers combined. We have an outstanding resource-----
Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  What is the breakdown of that? Is it about 300 and 150?
Ms Kate Duggan  About that, yes.

Ms Rosarii Mannion  We have an outstanding resource allocation model where we can get down to very granular detail on where we need the posts, caseload allocation, different indices on deprivation, etc. We are very conscious of course the supply of social workers is limited across the State. We have been out there. We have set up our own internal training college to be self-sufficient. We have our apprenticeship schemes in both social work and social care. At today's date we are moving towards having 193 apprentices between social work and social care combined. Over the next year or two we will have doubled the supply. That is not to say there will be enough as obviously social issues continue to grow and we are challenged, but within the agency we are doing everything possible to plug those gaps and we are funded to do so.

Senator Margaret Murphy O'Mahony  The joys of being one of the last is that a lot of what I wanted to ask has been covered by my colleagues. I thank the witnesses for coming in, for their opening statement and for the great work they do. The agency often gets bad press but I acknowledge it does a lot of good work and it certainly is doing the best it can, which is all that can be asked.  On early intervention, Tusla reports a marked increase in children presenting with complex needs, including mental health difficulties, etc. What additional supports are required to ensure these children receive appropriate care and treatment before the situation escalates into special care or an emergency placement?

Ms Kate Duggan  I referenced already the whole-of-government approach to alternative care. There are 6,000 children in the care of the State and we believe they should be prioritised across Departments for services. The State is their corporate parent and if we were the parent of a child who needed additional supports, we would be looking to get those for them and that is something we would love to see in the alternative care policy. Outside of that, obviously the responsibility for the provision of mental health, disability and addiction services lies with the HSE and we recognise it is struggling with the demand for its services and there are waiting lists for those services. We advocate for children to be able to access them but we have also started to increase the therapeutic services we can provide to children and young people coming into care. We have been funded for six of what we would call generic therapeutic teams. We want children coming into care to get a therapeutic assessment as part of their care plan to be able to support their care plan. That is not to say it replaces any access they might need to specialist disability or mental health services, so we would love to see the expansion and growth of that service, as well as funding. We have also had a huge amount of investment in our specialist therapeutic services and we have really welcomed that in relation to our Barnahus service, which members may be familiar with in terms of children who have been sexually abused, and our NIAPP service that looks at young people who are showing indicators of sexualised or harmful behaviour. We are committed and want to continue to work on the development and investment in therapeutic services more broadly across the State and in supporting us to deliver better care planning for children in care.

Senator Margaret Murphy O'Mahony  I thank Ms Duggan. I would also like the witnesses to expand on the agency's problems with recruitment and retention of staff. I am aware they have spoken about it already but I would like some more information.

Ms Rosarii Mannion  I thank the Senator. Recruitment and retention remain an ongoing challenge. We have a people strategy with eight strategic objectives and recruitment and retention are the key priorities there. In terms of recruitment, we know the supply is inadequate so we have done everything possible, as I said earlier, to become self-sufficient with our training college bursary sponsorship. In addition to that we create the conditions whereby staff want to stay in the agency. There are some things within our control and some without our control. Pay and conditions are external to our control, so we are very focused on creating an environment that is as good as it possibly can be. We provide on-site counselling, employee assistance programmes, health and well-being, coaching, mentoring and a really good induction programme, You Start.  If we think that people are getting into difficulty or they are challenged we try to get in early. We look at redeployment and rotations. We are just trying to be as proactive as we possibly can be. Every year we undertake an employee survey. Despite the sometimes negative publicity that we get, the experience of our employees, as reported by themselves, is very positive. Employees were given the option to describe in narrative terms their experience of the environment. The top three that came out from the employees themselves – from 30,000 descriptors – is that we are a learning and developing agency; we are friendly; we are supportive and; the environments are respectful, so we are doing everything we can there both in terms of recruitment and retention. We undertake exit interviews to hear from staff when they are leaving to see what we can learn and if there are things we could have done better. We find the top three themes coming through on exits are different career opportunities, the emotional impact of the work and opportunities to travel.  While our retention figures are improving all the time, they are slower than we would like. It is a very challenged market. There are plenty of opportunities out there but we are pleased that we are moving in a positive trajectory.
Senator Margaret Murphy O'Mahony  Is Ms Mannion happy with the direction of travel?
Ms Rosarii Mannion  I am happy with the direction of travel but I would like if it was better. I am confident that we are doing everything we can.

Senator Margaret Murphy O'Mahony  I thank Ms Mannion. Could I also ask her to expand please on the interim protections that are there for people waiting for special care placements? What happens if the placements are not available?

Ms Kate Duggan  Yes. Mr. Hone will probably talk to that. Currently, we have two young people waiting for a bed in special care. We certainly hope that both of those young people would have a bed before the end of July. Mr. Hone might talk to that, broadly speaking without giving specifics.

Mr. Gerry Hone  That is no problem. I chair a weekly meeting to look at the needs of the young people who are waiting for a bed in special care and have been approved through the courts for a bed. It is very important because generally those young people are not engaging very well with the services and it is very hard to get co-operation from them. The purpose of my meeting, which is attended by the regional chief officers and the area managers, as they have front-line management for those particular children, is to ensure that everything is being done to manage the risks in the community for those young people and that every agency is trying to engage with them, not just Tusla. A lot of their problems can be mental health problems or drug addiction. We try to encourage those young people to engage with the services. Getting the services to reach out to them as well while they wait is key in managing that level of risk. We do not want the situation to continue where young people who are waiting for a bed in the community are there for long periods of time because of the high risks associated with their behaviour and the challenges around their lack of co-operation with services. For example, they can go missing for long periods and that causes issues because of further concerns about their safety. Those weekly meetings make sure those risks are always on the table and we are doing everything we possibly can to manage the risks.
Senator Margaret Murphy O'Mahony  I thank the witnesses.

An Cathaoirleach  It now falls to me to ask questions. Looking at the numbers, the referrals last year were up by 10% or 106,000. That can also be a positive; it is not necessarily the case that there is an increase in negative experiences around the country. It might be that more people are finding the pathway to Tusla. There are 5,879 children in foster care and 820 or so in other places. Allowing for a small population increase of about 2%, what are the top three or four reasons for the 10% increase in referrals?

Ms Kate Duggan  We have done some work around that while trying to get insights. While it is not evidence-based research, the patterns are showing us two things. The first is the rise in complex social situations that many families find themselves in. We all recognise and acknowledge the challenges around housing and in relation to poverty indicators and domestic, sexual and gender-based violence. That creates pressure on a family and its resilience and results in an increase in the need for services like ours. The other thing is we are seeing more awareness around safeguarding and people's responsibilities – everybody's responsibilities in terms of the care and protection of children. Whether that is a mandated reporter or a member of the public, people are becoming more aware. When we look at our reform programme and why we have done the work that we have done, we also wanted to make sure that when someone is referred to us that they get more timely access to the service they need, whether that is support or welfare and that we are as efficient as we can be, and that we also make sure that we are reducing the number of re-referrals, so that people do not have to come back a second time. We are only six months into our reform programme and already we are seeing early indicators – it is too early to say definitively that it is an impact of the reform – in terms of a reduction in the number of re-referrals and more timely access to services. That is going to take time to embed. Our job as an executive is to make sure that we are managing the operational risks in front of us all of the time and working tirelessly to deliver services to children and families, but it is also about building a service for the future. I think that is what our reform programme has been about, both in terms of how we deliver services, our people strategy, our financial stewardship and our digital transformation. We are setting ourselves up. Currently, the biggest challenges are placement capacity. Over the next three years of our corporate plan it is our ambition that all of the pieces in the reform programme will come together to make sure that the services are better.

An Cathaoirleach  While Ms Duggan was taking I was thinking about a very high profile and tragic case, which I will not go into, whereby an issue was flagged in social welfare and the right reporting was followed and things like that. Even though it was a crazy, tragic circumstance it was positive that it was flagged.  We had the Children's Residential and Aftercare Voluntary Association, CRAVA, in last week. It was mentioned that there was evidence in UK reports to say that outcomes for the community, voluntary and charity, CVC, areas were better than private for-profit. Does Tusla have any data on outcomes from Tusla residential centres versus private for-profit centres?

Ms Kate Duggan  Mr. Hone might come in on this. The biggest piece of research that is under way at the moment has been commissioned by the Department on the care experiences programme, which is a long-term review of the outcomes for children in care over a period. That will be where we will see the first real evidence base in terms of the outcomes for children in care.  If we look at the measurements, up until now the agency has been established to look more at outputs in terms of the performance reports we produce: numbers leaving care; numbers in education; numbers in training; numbers going on to third level education or getting housing. We have introduced an outcomes framework within the agency where we will be able for the first time to start to look at outcome measurements for children in care and leaving care. Anecdotally, we are not seeing a difference.

An Cathaoirleach  They were quite strong on the values and vision approach. The private for-profits are there for profit versus the community and voluntary sector which is there for the child.  The main example they gave was the light-switch moment that occurs when the child turns 18 years. They spoke about how the bed becomes available immediately. We got the sense that people are turfed out of the private sector. However, Ms Duggan has spoken about an aftercare plan being developed. I would like to be more assured in that regard.
