I made the point last week that, notwithstanding the management structure or whether the vision of the company is to make profit, the people working in the private sector are still going to be caring towards a child. Can Ms Duggan confirm that there is not a light-switch moment or cliff edge?

Ms Kate Duggan  It is important to say that every child in care has an allocated social worker, whether they are in a private centre, a community and voluntary centre or a Tusla centre. Every child in care is under the jurisdiction of the courts, no matter what centre they are in. Every child in care has a care plan that is developed with the child, the staff and the social worker within it. Every child in care has a transition plan from 16 to 18 years of age. When it comes to planning for accommodation post-18 years, that is what the plan refers to.  The CSO data, which is published, gives us very clear indications. We are seeing that almost nine out of ten children in care are engaged in education and training. That is across our care system. We are seeing that 55% of children in care are being looked after by a private provider. They are being looked after by professionally qualified social care workers and other professionals. It is at the child in care review and through the care plan that any difficulties or risks are flagged.  Children in care are not a homogenous group. There are children in care who are in education and in residential services, both private and statutory, who have challenges, maybe because of underlying trauma, mental health issues or disability, and they need access to specialist services within the HSE. The CSO data is telling a much better story about the experiences of children in care. We know what the vulnerabilities of children in care are, in terms of the risk of exploitation and homelessness.
An Cathaoirleach  I am going to cut Ms Duggan off because I have been strict with everybody else's time so I had better be strict with my own.
Ms Kate Duggan  All of those services are inspected and monitored against the HIQA standards.

Deputy Daniel Ennis  To return to the budget, has capital expenditure increased, decreased or remained at the same level? On the 78 - now 56 - children in temporary emergency placements, is there information on the locations of those? Where are they? Is there a greater need in certain parts of the country? Is there engagement with young people on their experiences? Are they consulted and, if so, how is that information collected?  On the care plan, are there gaps, struggles or challenges around addiction services or mental health services for young people in terms of referrals? Is there any pushback? Are there clear pathways? If so, where are the clear pathways and challenges located? Are the witnesses seeing any trends? We are seeing kids falling into criminality a lot younger than previously. That is certainly true in my area. We are also seeing them fall into addiction at a younger age as well. Are the witnesses seeing any trends as regards location and, if so, what are those trends?  Are there any intercultural challenges around integration of people from different parts of the world who come here? I know that as regards placements, school placements, in communities and in the voluntary sector, people are seeing challenges. Could the witnesses explain some of the challenges being faced around that?

Mr. Pat Smyth  On the capital aspect, our current capital budget total is €35 million. That is split, with about €7 million for the ICT side and the rest for estates and buildings. That figure has been increased. The NDP review last year increased our total capital budget from €17 million in 2024 to €35 million now, and it is expected to be around €35 million for the next three or four years. A large part of that is dedicated to putting in place new residential houses. We have a plan to try to get around 100 new beds in place. That involves buying and refurbishing houses to bring them up to the standard we need for residential care and creating a home environment. That is the position as regards those matters.  I refer back to the question about capital going across to community and voluntary organisations. Obviously, we are in a capital programme ourselves. As Ms Duggan mentioned, one of the options is to have our own properties and get the community and voluntary organisations in to manage one of those properties for us. One of the challenges we have on the Tusla side is that, unlike disability and other areas, the size of the organisations we are dealing with is very small. Most of those organisations struggle in terms of having the quantum of resource to put the capital piece in place. A number of smaller organisations merged this year. That is something we may have to consider as we go forward, to allow those organisations to get together.

Ms Kate Duggan  I am using figures from the time when there were 78 children in emergency arrangements. In terms of the location, about one third of those were in Dublin and mid-Leinster and another third were in Dublin north-east. As such, two thirds were within the greater Dublin region. The next highest area is the south east. After that, to a much lower level, is the west, north east and mid-west. That is a broad breakdown.  In terms of access to services and trends, we would like if the 6,000 children in the care of the State were prioritised for access to services. Today, the policy is that they wait for services, the same as any other child in the care of the State, if they need access to specialist, disability, mental health or addiction services. They are not prioritised for access to those services.  In terms of trends, what we would call out are the broader societal trends. Obviously, we are seeing global movement and its impact. When I talk about cultural issues, we are seeing really good evidence of integration. We are working with families from different cultural backgrounds in terms of how they parent and looking at that in an Irish context.  Certainly, we are worried about levels of exploitation of children, and that is not just sexual exploitation. When we look at our sexual exploitation data, we are seeing higher levels of reporting of concerns around exploitation of children living in the community, at home, than we are of children in care. We are seeing a rise in addiction and drugs among parents, with the impact that has on children, but also among the children themselves. We are seeing criminal gangs and their influence on children and young people.  I saw some data just yesterday. If we look at one of our specialist services dealing with sexual abuse, Barnahus, about 50% of referrals to it involve peer-on-peer abuse. We are starting to see an increasing trend of peer-on-peer sexual abuse or allegations of sexual abuse.

Deputy Charles Ward  What is the difference between the special emergency arrangements that were contracted by Tusla in the past and those that are now registered with Tusla? How many of these companies are operating placement settings? Are these the same companies that operated in the past but now with Tusla registration? What happens if an SEA provider fails the registration process? Are the children immediately removed or is there a time period?

Ms Kate Duggan  Some of the providers are the same. It is important to recognise that in some of the provision of SEAs, private providers enter the market and we have worked with them and are satisfied they meet all of the criteria for registration.  Some of the providers are providing staffing on our behalf and are governed by Tusla. Where a service fails registration, a child is removed after 45 days if that centre has not achieved registration.
Deputy John Connolly  My question is about the 1,200 unaccompanied minors in care. Am I right to say the age verification process is undertaken by the Department of integration and IPAS services?

Ms Kate Duggan  That has always been the responsibility of the Department of justice. Now, in preparation for the EU migration pact, which went live in June, the Department of justice and the international protection office introduced a new age assessment process. While it is too early to talk about a trend, we have seen since January a reduction in the number of referrals to Tusla. It is important to say that the principle of the presumption of minority still remains. That is a principle we hold dear in terms of mitigating the risk of children being placed with adults. Internationally, the risk of every service is the risk of an adult being placed with a child. When I say a child, that child could be 16 or 17. There is also the risk of a child being placed in an adult service. We should probably use the term "young person" instead of child. That age between 17 and 19, or 17 and 20, in the absence of documentation is difficult to verify.
Deputy John Connolly  On Tusla's knowledge of the cases, what is the youngest age at which we might be providing accommodation for an unaccompanied minor.

Ms Kate Duggan  I do not have the age range here but we can certainly get it. When we talk about unaccompanied minors, there are children for whom we would have had concerns about trafficking or there are children who have come to the airport and there was a concern about the adult. It could be children as young as seven or eight. Certainly, for any unaccompanied minor under the age of 16 they are in the care of the State, and the younger young people are placed in foster care.

Deputy John Connolly  That is the point I was getting to earlier, but I was not clear enough in my commentary, on concerns about the children. There are additional concerns other than their being unaccompanied in some cases.
Ms Kate Duggan  Yes, there would be concerns about trafficking.

Deputy John Connolly  I turn to special care. Tusla has acknowledged and regrets the current situation where it is unable to fulfil the statutory obligation to provide timely access to special care for our young people. How many children are we talking about there?
Ms Kate Duggan  Today there are two, and we hope those young people will have a place in special care before the end of this month. We have two young people transitioning out.

Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  I thank the witnesses for their previous answers. I will go back to the idea of the threshold before a child is taken. I have been told that threshold has probably increased in recent years. I put that down to capacity needs. I also accept that people try to build a care plan around somebody. An issue I have been over and back on previously is the idea of caseload management. I will give part of the answer I got to a parliamentary question:  Tusla’s policy on caseload management is that there are defined manageable caseloads for all social workers, with caseloads reviewed on an ongoing basis to ensure best outcomes for children and families.  Tusla’s Social work Caseload Management system is a structured national framework designed to ensure that social work services are delivered, safely, equitably and transparently. ... Tusla has advised that the Social Work Caseload Management System has been paused in some areas. This is due to the number of Social Work vacancies being experienced by Tusla. Intensive recruitment efforts are ongoing by Tusla, and the Department is working closely with Tusla on this.  I heard this happened in County Louth, in Dundalk. It draws attention to the pressure individual social workers and social care workers could be under. Will the witnesses answer that and the question on thresholds?

Mr. Gerry Hone  On thresholds, one thing that affects them but which is not always seen is the availability of placements. Capacity for placements can affect thresholds. You might have some children at home who require a placement but they are being supported to stay at home.
Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  This might have happened when Tusla did not have SCUs.

Mr. Gerry Hone  Yes, so there is an impact there on thresholds. However, I do not think the thresholds for care have gone up because the legislation is clear on when the threshold is met, as well as our duties and responsibilities to respond when it is met. The function of front-line management is to make sure our responsibilities-----

Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  That is okay.  We will move on to caseload management from the point of view both of those to whom Tusla is providing supports and services such the vulnerable children and of the workforce, the idea being that they are not overburdened with a lot of complex cases.

Mr. Gerry Hone  No, and when you are short staffed that is always a danger. The caseload management policy is a bit out of date, particularly since we had the reform programme and are changing the approach to how we do our practice, in terms of integrated working. That caseload management process is now under review.
Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  What is the timeline on that?

Mr. Gerry Hone  We hope to have that done within the next six months, in terms of looking at it and getting it done. Even in its current format it never really covered the workload for workers at the front door. That was a gap in the system, so we have to go back to look at that caseload management system in the round and come up with something more fit for purpose based on what we have done under reform.

Ms Kate Duggan  I have some data here. When we looked in the past couple of weeks at caseloads, there is the idea of moving from 17 areas to 30 networks. The Deputy's county of Louth has separated from Meath, so it has a dedicated team. We can certainly get him the data for Louth.

Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  I was going to ask about that because I am led to believe the referral numbers are big, as are the numbers in care. That can be that action is taken as much as there is a need.

Ms Kate Duggan  We can give a simple example. If we look at the cases open in an area in December 2025 before we implemented the new structure, the average number of open cases was 1,052. Today, that is 632. Through the reform we are seeing a rebalancing. On children in care, when we had 17 areas, the average number of children in care per area was 337. That has now moved to 194. One of the objectives of our reform was reducing the numbers of children in care, the number of referrals coming to the door and the number of caseloads open to social work for the 17 areas. We have achieved that through new structures, new alignment of teams and new constructs. We are starting to see it, but I can certainly get those Louth figures for the Deputy.
Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  I would appreciate it. Can I ask one tiny question?
An Cathaoirleach  That is fine.

Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  Well, it is quite a big one. It is about the cases we have had to deal with. I am not asking about specifics. This is Kyran Durnin. It is Daniel Aruebose. It is Vadym Davydennko. It is the assault on the young girl in Citywest. Obviously, there is a review methodology Tusla operated and there were recommendations. Some of them required legislation. Where exactly are we with all of that now?

Ms Kate Duggan  The Minister published the recommendations within the Kyran Durnin review. We have implemented all of the recommendations that are within Tusla's control. Where there are recommendations outside of our control we are working with those stakeholders. The other reviews are ongoing in the context of the national review panel, but we do not wait for those reviews to change our practice. Something else I think will be back before the committee is the well-being check when it is published. That is where the Minister asked us to look at all of the cases that were closed to Tusla during Covid-19, to ensure the well-being of those children and young people. We expect that will be completed in the autumn. I think that will have great learning for the State. The Chair mentioned the DSP individual noticing something about how we use PPS numbers to collect information on children who are emigrating, in terms of educational systems and structures and on how we operate in Tusla. That will be really good, and I look forward to coming back before the committee to present the learning across State services as a result of that check.
An Cathaoirleach  The committee has reached out as well and it is very happy to engage with us once the report is published. I call Deputy Kerrane.

Deputy Claire Kerrane  I want to come back on a couple of bits. First, on the private emergency placements and the 78 children and young people who are in temporary emergency placements, are all of those special emergency arrangements, SEAs, as they were called, residential home settings now? There are no hotels, apartments, flats or anything else.
Ms Kate Duggan  Well, there may be because a residential home may be for one person in a two-bedroom apartment where the staff are there with one young person-----
Deputy Claire Kerrane  Okay, but there is no hotel or bed and breakfast accommodation.

Ms Kate Duggan  There is no hotel accommodation. Under our national out-of-hours service, there may be. I want to check my records here to give the Deputy the data as of this week. Where we have our national out-of-hours service, an example may be a Sunday night. I have to be very honest that where there is a breakdown in a placement and there may be a period of 12 or 24 hours when a placement is not available, a hotel may have to be sought. For one young person on that week in July for which I have this figure, there had to be hotel arrangement sought-----
Deputy Claire Kerrane  Short term.
Ms Kate Duggan  -----but that was just one young person for 12 to 24 hours.

Deputy Claire Kerrane  Okay, that is fine. The SEAs were previously used. Most of us and the general public, in a lot of cases, would have seen this for the first time in the "RTÉ Investigates" programme. The use of those kinds of settings - rooms in hotels and bed and breakfast accommodation - on a long-term basis has not been not a practice since June.

Ms Kate Duggan  That was never a practice, to be fair. If we looked back and got the data for a whole year for the Deputy on the number placed in hotels, we would see that the numbers really were very low.

Deputy Claire Kerrane  On that programme, another concern for the general public would have been the young person who was sleeping in the Tusla car park. Was Tusla aware that there was a young person in the car park?
Ms Kate Duggan  No, and we have no evidence-----
An Cathaoirleach  I think we will not go into that because that is a specific person and it is very-----
Deputy Claire Kerrane  No, that is fine. Obviously, it is public knowledge and I am not referencing the person but-----
Ms Kate Duggan  We have no evidence that that happened and no awareness-----

Deputy Claire Kerrane  That is fine. The other thing I want to check is if Tusla has met with Social Care Ireland and the Irish Association of Social Workers. A number of concerns have been raised around the reforms. Change is change and there will be hiccups and different parts to all of that. That is normal, but has the Tusla met with both association representative organisations?
Ms Kate Duggan  Have I personally?
Deputy Claire Kerrane  Yes.

Ms Kate Duggan  Ms Mannion and I most recently met with Social Care Ireland on issues not really related to the reform, just on wider issues in relation to Social Care Ireland. I personally have not met representatives from IASW because on the issues they were raising in terms of social work, the scope of roles and caseload allocation we felt our chief social worker would be more appropriate to meet with them. We are obviously open all of the time to meet with any representative groups, but in terms of the particular issues for which they were looking for a CEO, I would not have that information. Ms Mannion has met and also leads the discussions with CORU in relation to any of the queries that were subsequently raised. As CEO, sometimes it just is not appropriate in terms of the nature of the queries that organisations have.

Deputy Claire Kerrane  Sometimes an in-between service between special care and residential care is raised with us. Does Ms Duggan feel, as head of the organisation, that this is a missing piece, particularly for children? Obviously, there are difficulties with special care but I ask particularly in cases where there may be signposts to special care but the services and supports are not actually there for them within special care.

Ms Kate Duggan  Absolutely. I am delighted to say we are going to open three units, two before the end of this year and one in January 2027. We are calling them step-up or step-down units. I hope when the committee members come to special care and they see young people who have not committed a crime walking down around locked doors, their liberty taken away and high-wired fencing, they will understand it needs to be a measure of last resort. We are looking at having more step-up units where the environment is physically stronger. That has often been the concern we have had when we talk about the use of restraint in terms of ratios that might be needed or the strength of the environment in terms of ligature points, the windows, the doors and the layout of the environment. There are a number of environmental modifications that would have been needed and that is why we are building three purpose-built units. At the end of this year two will be opened and one will be opened next year. They have taken almost two years from the point of getting the capital approval, getting them built and up to the level of compliance in terms of HIQA, to, in this case, getting the much more robust physical environments. Three units, as I said, will be opened by January.
Deputy Claire Kerrane  I understand why security personnel are sometimes used in special care units. Do they all receive training?
Ms Kate Duggan  Yes.

Senator Margaret Murphy O'Mahony  I thank the witnesses again for coming in. Is there anything else they want to add that the time did not allow them to say? I would be particularly interested in their future plans.

Ms Kate Duggan  We are just about to write our next corporate plan, which is for the next three years. At the moment, we are going through a phase of analysis and reflection on the scale of the demand that is coming at us as an agency, the wider societal issues that are out there, and the supports that are needed for children and families generally. We want children to grow up with their families where possible. We want those families to be resilient. Where those parents have challenges around domestic violence, addiction or mental health, we want them to get the supports they need. Coming to Tusla should happen at a point after everything else has perhaps been tried and families have been supported. What we need or what we would like is the prioritisation of children in care for access to services and a whole-of-government approach to providing for the needs of children in care and families, whether that is in relation to housing, addiction or mental health services. We would like support around public confidence and trust in Tusla as an agency. We absolutely own our challenges. We recognise there are times when we are not able to provide the services that we would like to or want to provide. While we are working really hard to do that, part of it has to be about where there is a good news story, or a positive outcome where progress is being made, voices being used across society and across the political system to recognise that, while absolutely holding us to account where there is not. That is very important for us. My colleague may want to add to that.

Ms Rosarii Mannion  The only other thing I would add is that we have a social worker all-employers forum which is led by Tusla. We have made good progress there in advancing new models such as apprenticeship, etc., but a more integrated approach is probably needed, with the educational sector and other agencies really looking at getting ahead of workforce planning issues to ensure Tusla has a workforce that is reflective of the society we serve. There is a little bit of integration needed on long-term integrated workforce planning across the State among the various agencies. Tusla has really pushed the boundaries. We have done what we can and there is scope for more learning and advancement there.

Mr. Gerry Hone  Somebody asked earlier about trends and what we might be seeing for young people at the acute end. One the things that is a constant concern of mine is how we structure our addiction services in the State. You really have to be at a stage where you are co-operating with the service to actually avail of it, and a lot of the time our young people are not engaging. There is something about working across government around the structure of how we deliver addiction services, particularly to young people, and how they can access them. It is all about children going to centres to receive services if they are willing or their family is willing to co-operate with them. Whereas we actually need more outreach type of work with those young people and that type of specialism to be developed. That would be really important as a need to work better going forward.

Mr. Pat Smyth  Our challenge continues to be around ensuring that we have and we get the resources we require.  We have tried to put in place good services over the last number of years. Despite all the challenges there have been around the residential side, it is worth knowing that the average cost of looking after a child in residential is about €48 per hour, which covers nights, days and weekends. For all those kids in residential, it is not a very big cost if we compare it with everything else that we have to do. We got a plumber last week, which cost about €90 for an hour. It is a lot of money but when we boil it down to what we are trying to do here - the depth of service and what we are trying to replace - it is a big piece.  I wish to note the following. Earlier Ms Duggan referenced the CSO data and there is a very high return. The CSO has examined the data across from 2017 or 2018, in terms of the outcomes for kids who have been through Tusla services. It found that between 85% and 90% of those kids are in good prospects, education and jobs. Yes, the 10% challenge that we have is where we have to look and they consume a lot of the resources. The investment of the State has been very productive in terms of what we have tried to do over the last number of years.

Deputy Aisling Dempsey  I wish to return to our earlier conversation on the budget. As was mentioned, representatives of CRAVA were here last week. CRAVA is very much on the side of Tusla. They said that Tusla could not give them any more and it was down to the Department. I see that Tusla's budget is very structured, deals with the Department and it goes to the Department of public expenditure. In terms of what Tusla will seek for its next budget, will there be a large increase sought for this area? I know that if Tusla does not spend in one area that it is ring-fenced and would either have to be returned or applied for. Does that happen in other areas? Does the funding go into this form of care or not?

Ms Kate Duggan  Before Mr. Smyth discusses the details, I want to say that Tusla is very grateful to the Minister, Deputy Foley, and her Department for securing a 14% increase for 2026, which we did get. A significant volume of that was for normal things like pension, pay and WRC payments. However, the rest was very much around funding for ten family resource centres, which has been very welcomed by communities across the country, and then in relation to the growth in the number of separated children, those seeking the international protection service and our residential services, and money to support us in terms of opening beds in special care, if we can recruit the staff that we need. Certainly, we are starting from a good base.  Members will have received the annual report, which was published yesterday. The annual report and the data that we have given the committee today is a story of increased demand. When there is increased demand and need to that level, our first job as a public service is to demonstrate that we are doing the best we can with the money that we have. For example, there is the implementation of our reform programme and some of the differences that I have called out in terms of the work that we are doing to make sure that we are doing that. There is our digital transformation. I know that there are lots of references in the media to digital transformation programmes at the moment. We have delivered. Tusla is the only health and social care service now that has a single child record. We have delivered that in house, on time, on budget and without the use of external services. Therefore, we have demonstrated very well our ability to use the resources that we are given and get a good return on investment.  We are concerned at the potential of a levy being applied to Tusla next year as a result of the levy that has been applied, as we understand it, across a number of State Departments or agencies because of the overrun in education, as reported in the media. We are very concerned if we had to constrict our services as a result of a levy. Obviously now we are going through the process of setting out the business cases to the Department in relation to that demand. That tells its own story in the sense of, if we were able to respond fully to that demand, what that might look like in terms of additional investment. Obviously, our job is to provide this committee with the assurance that, with the available resources, we are providing services to those most in need and those at greatest risk.

An Cathaoirleach  I aim to ask four questions in five minutes. First, on the issue of 45 days for a private emergency placement. The child must either be transferred into foster care or a Tusla placement after 45 days or the placement must become registered. What happens if they do not get registered? Let us say the child is transferred somewhere else. Can another child be referred to them for another 45 days or does the placement cease altogether for any child?
Ms Kate Duggan  I will let Mr. Hone answer that. It depends on the provider and the progress they are making.

Mr. Gerry Hone  When the child is initially placed, there are 45 days to begin the registration process. During that time the social worker and the providers will work together to make sure that the care is safe during that period. When the registration process is started, there is a further 60 days to complete the registration process, which is quite in-depth in that there are loads of standards to be met, lots of paperwork to be filled out, and making sure that all policies and procedures are in place. That is the reason for the extra 60 days.
Ms Kate Duggan  And that we are confident at that point that they are going to achieve registration.

Mr. Gerry Hone  Absolutely, and that is monitored. During that time the care is monitored. If we get to a point where the service cannot register or fails to meet the standards for registration, there are several possibilities. The service can be closed and the child moved elsewhere or the service comes under section 59( a ) of the Act, which brings it in under Tusla governance completely. We take responsibility for the governance of the placement and that then brings us in under HIQA, and HIQA inspects the service in respect of the national child care standards and residential care standards.

Ms Kate Duggan  One of the other elements of progress that we have made is that young people are spending shorter periods in emergency placement because that is the solution. We want young people to be able to be placed in a centre that will be a stable placement for them. We have 45 days because it is stipulated in legislation. If we feel that they are making good progress, obviously we are happy to work with them for those 60 days because it is an administrative process. For us, it is around not having a young person in a placement beyond that 45 or 60 days, and that is what we are now measuring as an indicator.

An Cathaoirleach  In the interest of getting answers to my other questions, because we have all returned to these questions in similar ways, by the time we meet in the summer it would help us all if we received one page from Tusla that described the differences between the three new terms.
Ms Kate Duggan  We will supply that, yes.

An Cathaoirleach  On aftercare, the figures are good because 43% remained with their carers, 23% were in independent living arrangements, eight returned home and there are eight in residential care. What are supported lodgings and designated care leaver accommodation, and what is the 14% of others?

Ms Kate Duggan  Deputy Dempsey asked about the 14% of others. We will get to that breakdown. Some of that would be homeless, some of it would be addictions, and some of it would be disabilities. We will supply the Cathaoirleach with that breakdown.  A supported lodging is digs. It is a family, in the case of older young people who are in aftercare, who are willing to almost rent out a room to Tusla so that young person has their own room in a home and would live there. Tusla would have an engagement but the young person would not be in foster care.
An Cathaoirleach  What is designated care leaver accommodation?

Ms Kate Duggan  That would be an example I gave where we have worked with partners, like Peter McVerry and Focus Ireland, where we have funded or, in some cases, we have worked with the county council in a region, to have a house dedicated and it would be like a house share. It is dedicated accommodation that we fund for care leavers, and jointly fund with the councils in some cases.

An Cathaoirleach  The private sector can scale quickly, which is why we have ended up with 55%, but it is still Tusla's money that funds the private sector to scale. Why can the private sector scale quickly but Tusla cannot?  That might be a difficult question.
Mr. Pat Smyth  Some of the accommodation it is in, it may not own. It may rent. It can do that on a consistent basis and probably does that more effectively and faster than Tusla can.
An Cathaoirleach  Why is that?

Mr. Pat Smyth  The restrictions around acquisition of property for us are a bit of an issue in terms of governance. We are in a position where if we need a house tomorrow or the next day, we need board meetings, approvals and processes to take that on because that is just part of the rules of the organisation when it comes to acquiring property for the State. That is just one aspect. The alternative is that a lot of properties utilised in the State over the past number of years may be available for other services such as residential, for example, IP has been reducing, so there is a lot of availability of property coming through there at the moment. Obviously, the assurance and quality of those properties need to be-----

Ms Kate Duggan  We are also working to a capital plan. We have a defined capital budget we have to stick to. While we can pay through a contract and through a tender for the provision of a service, we have to work to a specific capital plan. We get that five years out. We now know what our capital plan is for the next five years and we have to work within that.

Deputy John Connolly  The witnesses have given various answers about the demands on resources and concerns about resources in the future. On the 1,200 unaccompanied minors Tusla provides accommodation and care for, does it get any support from the Department of justice in terms of resources?
Ms Kate Duggan  No. We do not get any funding from the Department of justice.
Deputy John Connolly  It fully comes out of Tusla's own budget.
Ms Kate Duggan  Yes, and the Department of children. About 490 separated children are in care tonight. It is 1,200 over the year. That has reduced because the number has reduced.
Deputy John Connolly  Would Ms Duggan say the migration pact has had an impact on that?

Ms Kate Duggan  It is too early to say there is a trend or correlation but certainly since the change in the age assessment, and there is now documentation verification, Eurodac checks and engagement with the IPO and the young person, we are seeing a reduction over the same period in the number referred to Tusla.
Deputy John Connolly  On the increasing number of children under threat of participation in criminal activity, what role does Tusla have with the youth diversion programme?

Ms Kate Duggan  Mr. Hone might talk about that. Where we have a concern that there is criminal activity, we report to the Garda first and foremost. On child sexual exploitation, we have had a process in place with the Garda since 2021. We have a single point of referral to a single point in the Garda whether the children live in the community or in care where we see indications perhaps a young person is being given designer clothes or has a mobile phone or has money. They are early indicators and we can report that to the Garda. Youth diversion is engagement and projects like Redtown and Greentown.

Mr. Gerry Hone  That can be part of local planning so that if a young person is involved in criminality and that is referred to us, we go to the Garda and it is whether it feels that child or young person would benefit from the youth diversion programme. I am aware of one that is funded by the Garda and Barnardos in Donegal, for example. Children are referred based on their suitability for the programme. It is generally the Garda that decides whether they are suitable or not for that programme.

Deputy Claire Kerrane  I want to go back to property upkeep and maintenance for the voluntary and community sector. As part of the service level agreement Tusla has with providers, are upkeep and maintenance costs covered?
Ms Kate Duggan  No.
Deputy Claire Kerrane  Is it just damage?
Ms Kate Duggan  Just damage. It is extenuating damage.
Deputy Claire Kerrane  Is Tusla confident that every young person is getting their aftercare plan put in place on time, in other words, as close to their 17th birthday as possible?

Ms Kate Duggan  We have seen progress in that regard. It had not been the case. We have invested in our aftercare services and appointed a national lead for aftercare who is now looking at that consistency and standards across the country. Both have made progress. I can get the numbers for the Deputy for those who have their aftercare plan in place. I will send it to her after this meeting.

An Cathaoirleach  My last question is about kinship care. The committee had correspondence recently on expanded supports for kinship care, especially financial supports. One example was a 22-year-old in continued education whose payment will cease. Are there any comments on that?

Ms Kate Duggan  Mr. Hone might give more detail on the work with the Department on developing a policy. As we said, the Department sets the policy and the legislation and we implement it. It is about working with the Department on a policy and consistency.

Mr. Gerry Hone  Work with the Department is ongoing in respect of kinship care because there is an issue about funding and what type of payments can be paid to carers in those situations. That is being looked at in the alternative care strategy in the Department. It is hoped that will get bottomed out. There is a specific group looking at it. I have staff on that group to try to bring that forward under the strategy.

An Cathaoirleach  It is probably too early to give recommendations but would it be in line with trying to give them the same benefits as children in foster care? It is obviously more beneficial if a child is kinship care but they are still taking on the duty for the State.

Ms Kate Duggan  There is entitlement to the guardianship allowance. That probably needs to be looked at in terms of consistency and the application. I met a family recently who had taken on two grandchildren. They did not need the support of Tusla in terms of needing to foster but needed some financial supports. When they applied for the guardianship payment, they were refused on the first occasion. We supported them in their second application.  There is probably something in that regard because often families do not want intervention from Tusla. They are happy to be looking after their family members and they want to do it as a private arrangement but recognising that these grandparents, for example, needed some financial assistance. Whether that is through a guardianship payment through the Department of Social Protection or it comes through Tusla, many families would want it to be separate from the care system.
An Cathaoirleach  Before I give my closing remarks, does anybody else want to give any closing remarks?

Ms Kate Duggan  I thank the committee for giving us the opportunity to come here today. I thank the committee members who have recognised the good work. We have such hard-working and dedicated staff, not just in Tusla but across the community and voluntary sector, providing services on our behalf in increasingly challenging circumstances as the years go on. I thank the committee for its support.  I hope we give the committee the assurance that what we are doing on behalf of the State is the best we can with the resources available and we will be happy to own where there are challenges and be called to account on them. We look forward to the committee's support through the implementation of the alternative care policy when it is published and in terms of funding and support not just for Tusla but for children and families in communities, which needs to be a key priority for our Government.

An Cathaoirleach  I thank the witnesses for coming in and answering the questions. I thank the committee for taking this position really seriously. We welcome when Tusla comes in and we have the difficult conversations because we are all here for the right reasons - to improve the lives and experiences of children. The staff Tusla has working on the ground do amazing work. That always has to be commended as well as addressing the challenges.  I thank the secretariat for all their hard work. Since Christmas, they have been working incredibly hard, as have all members. I wish them a happy summer break. I know they will not be having a break despite what the public might think. I know they will all be working very hard in their constituencies, whether having clinics or going to events. I know the phone will not stop ringing but I hope they get a bit of a break as well.  I look forward to seeing them when we visit the Tusla centres. I hopefully will be celebrating Mayo winning the all-Ireland.
Ms Kate Duggan  We will start with Limerick on Sunday and then go on to Mayo.
An Cathaoirleach  We live in hope. Good luck to Galway on Sunday.
The joint committee adjourned at 11.50 a.m. sine die .
Child Protection Matters, Special Care and Special Emergency Care Arrangements: Tusla

house.showAs: Joint Committee on Key Issues affecting the Traveller Community

chamber.showAs: Joint Committee on Key Issues affecting the Traveller Community

text.text: An Cathaoirleach  Apologies have been received from Senator Noonan.  This meeting is to discuss the issue of Traveller accommodation with representatives from Wexford Local Development, Wexford Local Traveller Accommodation Consultative Committee, and Ferns Diocesan Youth Service. From Wexford Local Development we are joined by Ms Marie Louise Byrne, community development co-ordinator. From Wexford Local Traveller Accommodation Consultative Committee our witnesses are Ms Elizabeth Berry from the Gorey district; Ms Kathleen Connors, Rosslare district; Ms Mary Connors, New Ross district; and Ms. Mary Mongan, Enniscorthy district. From Ferns Diocesan and Youth Service we are joined by Mr. Robbie Sludds, Traveller inclusion project worker. They are all very welcome. We do not have anyone attending remotely.  As the witnesses are within the precincts of Leinster House, they are protected by absolute privilege in respect of the presentation they make to the committee. This means they have an absolute defence against any defamation action for anything they say at the meeting. However, they are expected not to abuse this privilege and it is my duty as Cathaoirleach to ensure this privilege is not abused. Therefore, if their statements are potentially defamatory in relation to an identifiable person or entity they will be directed to discontinue their remarks. It is imperative they comply with any such direction.  Members are reminded of the long-standing parliamentary practice that they should not comment on, criticise or make charges against a person or entity outside of the Houses or an official of the Houses either by name or in such a way as to make him or her identifiable.  The witnesses are very welcome. I have known all of them quite well over many years. I invite them to make their opening statements and we will then proceed to a question and answers session.

Ms Elizabeth Berry  We thank the Chair and members for the opportunity to speak to the committee today. We are here today as the Traveller representatives on the Wexford local Traveller accommodation consultative committee, LTACC, and with our colleagues from Wexford Local Development and the FDYS Traveller inclusion project. I will introduce the LTACC representatives: my name is Elizabeth Berry and I am representing the Gorey district. I am also a Traveller community health worker for north Wexford and I work with Wexford Local Development. I am one of ten community health workers and I have worked with WLD for 16 years. I am joined by Mary Mongan, representing the Enniscorthy district who will talk about issues related to Traveller accommodation, homelessness and the real barriers Traveller families experience, such as the choice-based letting system. Kathleen Connors from Taghmon is representing the Rosslare district. Kathleen will talk about the future for young Travellers and the information available on choices available. Mary Connors, representing the New Ross district is also a nominated representative from the national Traveller organisations. Mary has been a Traveller activist and community health worker for decades and is a long-standing member of the LTACC. She will talk about the importance of reform of how the LTACCs work, if we are to see improvements.  We are also joined by Marie Louise Byrne from Wexford Local Development, who sits on the LTACC in an advisory role to the Traveller representatives in County Wexford. Robbie Sludds is from the Traveller inclusion project in FDYS. Mr. Sludds is based in a community house in Drumgoold, Enniscorthy, which is a Traveller-specific housing scheme with 14 houses. He will talk about accountability in the implementation of plans and policies and consultations Travellers participate in.  I will now pass over to Marie Louise Byrne who will provide some background information.

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  Gabhaim buíochas leis an gCathaoirleach and members for the invitation to highlight some of the issues experienced on the ground at local level. I would like to take this opportunity to provide some background information and to draw attention to the current functioning of the LTACC and the process of developing the Traveller accommodation programme, TAP, and how that happens on the ground.  In terms of numbers, the census recorded 1,441 Travellers living in County Wexford which is the eighth highest population in Ireland and the highest in the south east. However, based on Wexford County Council’s annual count, 784 Traveller families were identified at the end of 2024. This would indicate a much higher population. Services on the ground such as ourselves in FDYS estimate the figure to be closer to 3,000, which is double the number recorded in the census, which is important to note. There are two halting sites in County Wexford, Mountain View in Bunclody and Marshmeadows in New Ross. They are not transient sites and many families have lived on the sites for decades. There are approximately 46 families living in group housing schemes across the county.  WLD works in partnership with Travellers. In County Wexford there is not yet a Traveller-led organisation, so community development initiatives are shared across several stakeholders. We have a very active Traveller interagency group, which deals with education, employment, health and other issues apart from accommodation because that is left to the LTACC. WLD programmes such as the social inclusion and community activation programme, SICAP, and the empowering communities programme, which operates in Bunclody, prioritise community work with Travellers. We also host two Traveller primary healthcare projects. Ms Berry works on the north Wexford one.  In relation to the LTACC, my own role for over ten years has been to support Traveller representatives to participate in a meaningful, and not tokenistic, way. This is part of broader community development work with Travellers across the county that focuses on empowerment, leadership, equality, social justice and anti-racist practice and that uses the public sector human rights and equality duty as a tool.  The LTACC is a valuable statutory structure that allows members of the community to engage with elected representatives and officials. Despite the numerous challenges to the functioning of the LTACC, the desire is not to disband the LTACCs but to reform them – especially with regard to the mandate and purpose of LTACCs, as well as reform of how the Traveller accommodation programme is developed.  In relation to the consultation process for the TAP, my colleagues on the community development team in WLD facilitated listening groups during the summer of 2024. This involved a blend of direct outreach in Traveller-specific housing schemes, such as Drumgoold where Mr. Sludds works, and meetings with established Traveller groups in their local communities such as Clonroche, Taghmon, New Ross, Enniscorthy and Bunclody. We used community development methodologies to set a format to set the scene and explain the context for the consultation and to seek the input of Travellers on specific issues related to the provision and maintenance of accommodation. We focused on three specific issues including the different types of housing and culturally appropriate options available to Travellers and access to information about accommodation and related services. We also sought ideas as to how access to housing and accommodation services for Travellers could be improved.  A further consultation meeting was held in September to present and seek final feedback on the outcome of the consultation. The attendance and active engagement of two members of the staff of Wexford County Council housing section at this meeting was welcomed and very positively received.  The resulting submission was made by WLD in partnership with Traveller community representatives in response to the draft TAP for 2025 to 2029. A full copy of this submission has been provided to the committee clerk. There were a number of procedural recommendations including specific points in relation to consultation, representation, recognition of culture, access to information, access to related services, climate justice, health-environment and fire safety, the public sector duty and IHREC equality reviews, as well as in relation to budgets and plans and the need for more standardised reporting at a local level including numbers of new units, vacant bay or unit refurbishments, capital and current expenditure, etc. Examples of these recommendations included: a minimum of four full quorum meetings of the LTACC to take place each year; an annual schedule of LTACC meetings set out at the start of each calendar year; nomination of Traveller representatives to be carried out in collaboration with Traveller support organisations, and not via the PPN, as had been the case in the previous LTACC; the monitoring of accommodation preferences of Travellers on an ongoing basis through the LTACC; and the tracking and monitoring of data on Travellers living in emergency accommodation, that is, homeless. The TAP does not give us any numbers for Travellers in emergency accommodation yet we know Travellers were living in emergency accommodation at the time so the reporting paradoxes are hard for us to understand.  I will give one example of the failing of very basic procedures. In 2026 there has been one meeting of the LTACC, in February. A scheduled meeting in April was cancelled and we have not had a rescheduled meeting. Minutes of the February meeting have not yet been circulated. This one example of the lack of purpose and mandate and the failure of basic operational procedures. It is very difficult for Traveller representatives to remain motivated to participate on the LTACC when we are accepting this as normal.  In my opinion, the call by national organisations for a dedicated national Traveller accommodation authority with real powers to oversee delivery and monitor budgets and spending to ensure that standards and targets are met and to support local capacity must be seriously considered if anything is to change.  We have entered into a collaboration with the HSE, very much led by the HSE and ourselves, with Wexford County Council to do a piece of research into the living conditions of 50 Traveller and 50 Roma families in the Enniscorthy municipal district. That is being done with Roma families in Tipperary and Waterford. We will be the first county to look at doing it with Travellers and Roma. We will use the findings of this research as a lever to address health and related accommodation needs using the lens of the public sector duty to develop an implementation plan. This project is in procurement at the moment and should start in September.  I will now hand over to Mary Mongan who will give a brief input about culturally appropriate accommodation, homelessness and the real barriers families are experiencing.

Ms Mary Mongan  I am representing the Enniscorthy district. I will start by speaking about culturally appropriate accommodation.  From my experience of being homeless with my husband and a young family it is not nice or easy. My children miss out on so much, most importantly their education. I have experience of both homeless accommodation and emergency housing. It is difficult to understand and manage the system. When living in emergency accommodation you must stay in the property at all times, and you are not allowed to stay away for even one night. You must ask permission to visit sick relatives. I am a Traveller and as part of our culture some of us still like to go travelling when the children get their school holidays. People might ask why we travel. We travel to visit family and to keep the children rooted in their culture and traditions. It is not favouritism for Travellers to ask this. Travellers are an ethnic minority, and after years we were finally recognised as an ethnic group by the Government in March 2017.  I turn to the effects of homelessness on parents and children. For parents it is a constant worry of not knowing where you are going to live and in what area you are going to live. Children miss out on their education. They cannot start school because they are being moved around and do not have a permanent address. This is particularly difficult for children with additional needs.  Traveller families experience so many barriers in the system. Choice-based letting is just one example. It is frustrating and difficult to use. While I can read and write and am computer literate, what about people who cannot read or write or use a computer? It is a system I feel is not working and there has to be more support put in place to access the system. Eventually, I got a house through choice-based letting but I was supported by WLD. Another barrier is trying to work and build relationships with so many local authority workers including social workers, social housing liaison officers, Focus Ireland and so on. You feel obligated to work with them. I felt that I could not say no, because if I did it could affect my getting a house. I feel that Traveller families would benefit it there were a Traveller specific housing officer in every county. It should be someone from the Traveller community who understands our culture.  I thank the Chair and members for inviting me and giving me the opportunity to discuss the important topic of Traveller accommodation.

Ms Kathleen Connors  I am here to speak about supports for the younger generation coming up. I have a 17-year-old and a 15-year-old. In another few years, I will be looking forward to them getting married. Where are they going to live? When I got married, I was told I could be between ten and 15 years waiting for a house. It is known that the Travelling community get married much younger than the settled community. We have our own property with plenty of ground, so it is for them to have a mobile. The way Travellers have it now, they can have the family together and my family can stay together on my property. However, is it still the case that we are not allowed to put mobiles in our yard or have caravans in our yard? For me it is about security for my children when they grow up, and it is security for them. It is for me and them. They are quite young. When they get married, will they have the security? If they get married quite young they will not have an income. If they are expected to go out into the world to pay rent and electric and everything else like food, they cannot do that. I am going back 30 years to when my brothers got married. My family owns its own property. They brought two small caravans onto their own property and got served with fines. They had to move. It was the same with my grandfather before that. They were getting fined if they were not moving. My thing is that the next generation coming up will have some place to go where they can stay with the family so they are together and have the support of their family, and they can support one another.  There is also the issue that the information available on choice-based letting does not work, especially for the Travelling community. There are those who cannot read, do not have phones, do not have Internet or the way to get the Internet if they have phones. You have to be checking that once a week, and if you are not checking that once a week you are taken off. That does not work in the Travelling community whatsoever. If you do not know how to read and write that is definitely not going to work for you, so that definitely has to change.

Mr. Robbie Sludds  I thank the Cathaoirleach and the committee for the opportunity to speak on behalf of the Traveller community. I am the FDYS Traveller inclusion project worker for County Wexford, based in the community house in Drumgoold, Enniscorthy, which is a Traveller group housing scheme with 14 houses close to Vinegar Hill. It has a long tradition of being a place where Travellers camped before their houses were built there. I will talk about accountability in the implementation of plans, policies and consultations Travellers participate in. Travellers who take part in groups and activities with our project are often consulted with. While many are open to further consultations there is a crucial need to see action and real change on the ground as a result of these consultations. People will not engage in consultations if they do not see any change. Once consultations are done, Travellers do not often see what happens next, if anything happens. There is little accountability. There are specific issues in relation to how Travellers access accommodation and related information and services.  Many people feel that they are simply not listened to. This is a theme across all consultations or engagement with services. Calls are not returned, emails go unanswered, responses when they come are often vague or unclear and issues that have been reported go unresolved. All of this leads to mistrust and lack of faith felt by members of the community in State services. Options that are available are not clear, given the high levels of literacy difficulties and the increasing previously mentioned reliance on online platforms to access information and services, such as choice-based letting, does not work. There is also the lived experience of ongoing social exclusion within the Traveller community. A lot of work on a daily basis is helping Travellers to access services that should be accessible in the first place.  Travellers want to be listened to by officials and policymakers and to have their concerns fully heard and responded to in a timely manner. This goes well beyond anti-racism and cultural awareness training and meetings, however necessary these are, and into the impact of on how things actually work. In other words, the effectiveness of efforts should not be measured by the amount of training, meetings or consultations but rather by the impact from the perspective and lived experience of Travellers themselves.  The Traveller community has told us what it needs time and time again. What is needed now is not another consultation but accountability that turns Travellers' voices into real action and lasting change. Ultimately, the success of any policy should be measured not by the number of consultations held but by the difference it makes in the everyday lives of Travellers.  I would like to pass on the floor to Ms Mary Connors.

Ms Mary Connors  I have been a Traveller activist and community worker for what seems like forever. I have been involved in the LTACC in Waterford almost since it was established. I am a member of the National Traveller Women's Forum, the Irish Traveller Movement, Waterford Traveller CDP and most of the other Traveller groups and organisations. It is sort of embarrassing that there is no Traveller organisation in County Wexford, having the third largest population of Travellers in the country. No matter what the figures say, there are an awful lot more Travellers than are reported.  If you are in poor accommodation, you will not be interested in education, training and employment or all the other issues that come with it, or physical or mental health. You will be more interested in getting a safe, dry place for your family. If you have that, then you can work on education, training and employment and all the other issues. Therefore, for me, accommodation is the most important issue that needs to be solved.  I have sat on the LTACC in Waterford for about 20 years. For three or four of those years I was dismissed without knowing it until another person told me they were representing New Ross. I now sit on that LTACC as a representative of the National Traveller Women's Forum because I was dismissed. I rang them up when I found out I had been dismissed and said, "Thanks very much. You could have let me know." About two weeks afterwards, I got a letter: "Thanks very much for all your hard work." That is the way the council treats us. It can pick us up and throw us down and do all the rest, but the one thing about me is that I have staying power. I will keep at it and keep at it. I and other groups have brought on several Traveller reps from different areas in the county and they get fed up of it after two weeks, being talked down to and discriminated against. I have said at LTACC meetings, "I would like that to be minuted", and when I go back the next time it has not been, and I question that. It is not all about me but it is just that I am usually the only one there representing the Travellers because the reps will not stay on the committee because it is too belittling and humiliating.  There are loads of other issues but, for me, accommodation is the main one. The attitude of the council when, as they put it, "dealing with" us is, "You know what this family wants, Mary, but we, Wexford County Council, know what they need." We are the experts. We have been at this for years. Looking back on it, we were all so hopeful in 1998, when the traveller accommodation Act was released, that in five years the Traveller accommodation situation would be totally solved. We knew, as the Traveller groups in Dublin and all the Traveller groups nationally knew, that it was not going to be solved in five years but we thought there would be a strategy there and a plan for maybe the next five or ten years or whatever after that. Where are we now? We are still in the same situation. Like I said, I have sat on the LTACC for years. I sat on the NTACC as well for a couple of terms. I am also involved with a TIG. I do not see us any farther. It is a matter of the attitude of the council, and at times the HSE, education and other bodies, the lack of interest and their attitude towards Travellers. I was at one LTACC meeting when the CEO said, "All down this side of the table are very important, hard-working people." They were the council reps. I had to shout back at him, right or wrong, "You have never seen a busier small woman than me and these people", the Traveller reps on the other side of the table. That was taken as an insult and the council reps got up and walked out because we answered them back.  Is this going to improve the situation for Travellers? We have been so hopeful so many times, including of equal status. We said, "They cannot discriminate any more now", and then you get the vintners and everybody else and that just went out the window. We were the first in Europe to bring in the smoking ban. We were the first to bring in charging for plastic bags. We look brilliant in Europe. We are outstanding. In our own country, though, with our own people, we are a mess.
An Cathaoirleach  I thank all the witnesses for their opening statements. We will open the floor now to questions and answers.

Senator Joe O'Reilly  I welcome our guests. This is a great exercise in that we are focused on one area in a forensic way. Well done to you, Chair, on inviting your neighbours here. They should make sure that you treat them to some hospitality before they go home. They should not let you off without that.  To get to the questions, the third speaker, Ms Mongan, addressed my first question in that she raised the CBL issue. CBL, I know from my clinic work, and my colleagues will probably agree, is working well in a general sense. It is good for a lot of people but, as Ms Mongan says, it is an issue for Travellers. Does she want to be specific as to whether we should do it through professional workers, or what way would she say the county council should get that fairness into CBL such that Travellers can use it? I refer to the letting process.

Ms Mary Mongan  I think the older generation of Travellers - not me or my kids or whatever but people who are older than me - want that bit of communication rather than looking at a phone. I could be wrong, but my father, for instance, would rather go in to see the doctor than talk to them on the phone or look at a screen. Does the Senator know what I mean?
Senator Joe O'Reilly  I do.

Ms Mary Mongan  He is very old school. Travellers are old school. Even if it were once a week, maybe someone could come out or they could go in and be told, "This is what is available", and then someone could help them and ask, "Do you want to bid on this house?". Does the Senator know what I mean? You have to be very careful-----
Senator Joe O'Reilly  It is just to get a practical way of dealing with the difficulty.

Ms Mary Mongan  Say, for instance, I am still in emergency accommodation and I am looking for a house. If I bid on a house that I am not going to take, I am going to be taken off choice-based letting for two years, so you have to be very careful. What about people who do not know how to read or write and do not know what they are at? They might say, "Sure, look, I will chance this anyway, although maybe I do not know what I am at." They may bid on something that they may have no intention of taking and then be two years gone off the list. Does the Senator know what I mean?
Senator Joe O'Reilly  Maybe we should discuss it another day in a specific sense or the recommendation that we could make.
An Cathaoirleach  The choice-based letting was set up initially because of the large number of refusals in local authorities.
Senator Joe O'Reilly  Yes.
An Cathaoirleach  That was the case in Wexford which had a couple of them.
Senator Joe O'Reilly  It is working well outside of that difficulty.
An Cathaoirleach  If people need that extra-----
Senator Joe O'Reilly  That is my experience. I do not know what my colleagues would say.
An Cathaoirleach  There is no choice-based letting in Limerick.

Senator Joe O'Reilly  In our office it is working but I do understand the difficulty and that needs addressing.  Ms Byrne speaks to Wexford, I presume, and some of the witnesses speak nationally as well. Does she think that Traveller homelessness is under-reported and under accounted for? If so, then by how much and has she any examples? That is an important issue. Are there examples of the lack of Traveller-appropriate accommodation or homelessness?

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  The numbers we have in the current Traveller accommodation programme have no reference to any Travellers living in emergency accommodation. We work with the national organisations because we do not have the resources to analyse the data at a local level to the extent, say, the Irish Traveller Movement would. As far as I know, at the time of the TAP publication the social housing summary assessment of need recorded that nine Traveller families were living in homeless accommodation around the same period. There is an anomaly in reporting. The LTACC has never recorded the number, but we know through our work on the ground that there are Traveller families living in emergency accommodation.

Senator Joe O'Reilly  My third and fourth questions can be rolled into one. Travellers tend to marry younger than the settled population and that creates challenges with housing. I will link that to my question on the prospects of young Travellers who want accommodation. I ask the witnesses to speak a little to the experience of young Travellers. I have three young sons and they face challenges when they seek accommodation, either rental or otherwise. Will the witnesses speak to the challenges faced by young Travellers if they want to get married or otherwise?

Ms Kathleen Connors  Travellers get married at quite a young age. They want to get married. If my daughter got married in the morning, she would go with her husband's family. She would go to whatever yard or house they may be in. That is a caravan and they are not going to move into the house. If my son got married in the morning, then he will stay in my yard. Travellers get married quite young and have no way of supporting their wife or husband. If my son got a wife, he has no way of supporting her so I have to support him, his wife and their children, if they have them. It is not that we have to keep our children close. In the Traveller community, they go off travelling in the summer. When my children come back, I have their base. I can provide them with security for when they come home.

Senator Joe O'Reilly  I will hone in on one specific area and read the question as I have it here. Given the importance placed on marriage and living near family in Traveller culture, how can LGBTQI+ Travellers be accommodated both by their community and through housing policies? Will the witnesses speak to that particular cohort?

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  Both myself and Mr. Sludds work with the youth service, which has LGBT services, but neither of us works specifically in those. The Senator has asked an interesting question. There is Traveller intersectionality. There are Travellers with disabilities, Travellers who are members of the LGBTQIA+ community and Travellers who are lone parents. Overall, if the system works for everybody then it will address some of the issues. The system is so broken for every Traveller and the key is to fix it for everybody, which will include all of those groups where intersectionality is an issue.
Senator Joe O'Reilly  I thank Ms Byrne for her interesting response.

Ms Mary Connors  Ms Byrne, Ms Berry and I sit on the local Traveller accommodation consultative committee. The title may be long but it has a lot of meaning. There are also agencies and the Traveller inter-agency group, TIG, but there should not be a need for these organisations. I stand by the LTACC because as I have told them a few times, I am not here to accomplish anything because I know nothing is going to happen but I am here to see what you are at.  The TIG includes people from education, the Garda Síochána and community people. It is a group of agencies. If they were all doing their job, there would not be a need for the TIG because there would be an agency to deal with education, and others for training and employment and accommodation. They could phone or email each other but there should not be a need for these committees if the people on them did their job as they are supposed to. It is the same with the LTACC. With any of these groups, there should not be a need if everyone did their job.  There is one other thing. I have never been arrested in my life but if I did something wrong today I would know, when doing it, that it is wrong and that I can be arrested for that and sent to jail. However, there is no sanctions or comeback for these committees, the local authorities, the HSE, the Department of Education and Youth and all these agencies when they say, "All right, sure that happened. That was years ago and so-and-so was in the job at the time, not us". There is no accountability. I am sorry for giving out about it but that is the situation as we see it.

Deputy John Connolly  I agree with Senator O'Reilly that it is important for the committee to get the perspectives of the people who operate in different local authorities and ascertain how the operation of the LTACC is not standardised across all local authorities. I welcome the personal testimonies given by Mary Connors and Kathleen Connors. I compliment them on describing how they have suffered and gone through periods of homelessness. It is not easy to detail the impact of that on their families and I appreciate them doing that. It is important that we hear it.  I have a few questions on the LTACC. How many members are on the Wexford LTACC?
Ms Mary Connors  I have been a member of the LTACC for about 22 years, apart from the time that I was thrown out and brought back again.
Deputy John Connolly  I have trouble like that as well.

Ms Mary Connors  My departure was not due to an incident. I do not know what it was but it happened. Several times we have managed to get two or three more Traveller representatives to join.  Ms Berry would know more about it because she is involved with primary healthcare. Lately there have been two or three.
Ms Mary Mongan  A few of them have been cancelled.
Ms Mary Connors  They are gone off it again, are they?
An Cathaoirleach  A few of the LTACC meetings have been cancelled.
Deputy John Connolly  That was going to be my next question.
Ms Mary Connors  The representatives - the Travellers.
Ms Elizabeth Berry  There are only three of us, are there?

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  There are five Traveller reps currently. I am there as an adviser but I am not a member so I do not contribute to a quorum. I think there are five local elected representatives and then the council officials and that is it.

Deputy John Connolly  Five elected representatives from the Travelling community and local authority officials. Are there any other community representatives who are not members of the Travelling community? No.
Ms Marie Louise Byrne  Not on the LTACC.
Deputy John Connolly  How often does the LTACC meet in Wexford?
Ms Mary Connors  We met in February, I think.
Ms Mary Mongan  February was the last one.
Ms Mary Connors  It is four a year. It is meant to be every three months.
Ms Marie Louise Byrne  We requested four in a calendar year. So far we have had one.
Deputy John Connolly  That is 2026. Can Ms Byrne recall if it met four times in 2025?
Ms Marie Louise Byrne  No.
Deputy John Connolly  I believe there should be regulation around that. That should standardise how often it meets. Who is the chairperson?

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  The county chairman. It rotates on an annual basis, which is probably not ideal if it is only meeting. The chair of any committee is an important leadership role. In other counties such as Donegal, a Traveller man is the chairman of the LTACC. In having a rotating chair - in some counties it is a two-year term - some chairs show less interest and some are very active.
An Cathaoirleach  That could form one of our recommendations.
Deputy John Connolly  Is it a job the county chairperson gets along with being the chairperson of the county council? Yes.
Ms Marie Louise Byrne  It is a one-year term.

Deputy John Connolly  In Galway city, it is Niall from the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission. It only met once this year. It did not meet four times last year. There are five Travelling members of the elected representatives. The chairperson is selected by the members of the county council. It is their role to be the chairperson as well. When Ms Connors was relegated or suspended from membership, does she have any sense of how that occurred?
Ms Mary Connors  Absolutely not.
Deputy John Connolly  To go back to the five Traveller reps-----

Ms Mary Connors  There are very rarely five. It is only lately since the primary healthcare became involved with the LTACC that we have had three or four or sometimes five Traveller reps on it. Before that, it was mainly me.
Deputy John Connolly  Did I hear Ms Connors say she represented the New Ross area?
Ms Mary Connors  I did.
Deputy John Connolly  Are the five Traveller reps who are members all representing an electoral area in the county?
Ms Mary Connors  Yes, in an ideal situation they would. There would be one from north Wexford, one from south Wexford-----
An Cathaoirleach  It would follow the municipal district structure, which it is now, essentially.
Deputy John Connolly  There will be one member of the Traveller community from each electoral distinct. Is that working well?

Ms Mary Connors  No. In terms of having one from each district, you cannot keep people on it because they are humiliated, they are fed up, they see nothing coming out of it and they just say, "Ah Mary, you do it," because they know I have been involved with it for years. They say, "We have been to loads of those meetings, Mary, and nothing came out it. They said one thing and when I went to talk to them again, they said someone told you that on the phone, that was not us." They get apathetic about the whole thing. I cannot blame the people. I would be upset at first when I would say, the equal status Bill is coming out, the Traveller accommodation Act of 1998 is coming out. There is this thing and that thing and they would say, "Ah yeah, Mary, I heard it all before. You go". You cannot blame the people for that because they see nothing coming out of it.

Ms Elizabeth Berry  For one of the LTACC meetings last year, I travelled from Gorey to the meeting on the morning.
