I was just on the Wexford bridge coming from the Ballycanew direction and I got a phone call that it was cancelled. At a lot of the meetings in the past, a lot of us Travellers would turn up but there was always one or two of the representatives missing. You do not get the agenda until the morning.
Deputy John Connolly  What was the reason the meeting was cancelled that day?
Ms Elizabeth Berry  I am not sure. There was no reason. My boss rang me and said, "Elizabeth, you need to turn around. Where are you? You need to go home."
Deputy John Connolly  In terms of the council officials who attend, on the occasions it has met, was the director of housing there?
Ms Elizabeth Berry  No.
Deputy John Connolly  I assume the county manager would not be there.
Ms Elizabeth Berry  No.
Deputy John Connolly  The director of housing would not be there.
Ms Elizabeth Berry  No.
Ms Marie Louise Byrne  The SEO for housing is there. That would be the highest grade present.
Deputy John Connolly  On the Traveller accommodation plan, is an update provided at every meeting on the implementation plan?

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  No. That is what we are calling for. We are calling for oversight of delivery and monitoring of budgets and spending. The report can get quite confusing because you do not get anything in advance. For instance, my role and that of the community development team is to work in advance with the reps to prepare for the meetings, but you do not get to feed into the agenda and you do not have the minutes of the previous meeting until you are in the chamber. We have a huge list of recommendations around procedure. We were told they are all operational and they will be agreed at LTACC level. For instance, it would be to have a meeting in Drumgoold where Robbie works, which is a Traveller-specific housing scheme with 14 houses, where people can actually see the issues and Travellers can see the officials as well.

Deputy John Connolly  One purpose of the LTACC should be to build trust between the community and the local authority. If it is not operating effectively, as the experience Ms Connors relayed, it does not help. We have a focus on Wexford but what I am hearing is possibly what I would I hear in other local authorities informally as well. In our recommendations, we need to mandate local authorities to have proper structures around the operation of the LTACCS.
An Cathaoirleach  We can put that in our recommendations.

Deputy Maurice Quinlivan  I thank the witnesses especially for their personal testimonies. The meeting today is about accommodation but other issues also affect the Traveller community. I believe a lot of that goes back to accommodation - mental health, poor health outcomes, unemployment and suicide. It is all linked to the lack of adequate accommodation.  We have heard their testimonies before from different people with similar types of issues - I feel like we are going around in a loop and I am only on this committee for probably less than a year at this stage. We are frustrated that there does not seem to be any action. What change would the witnesses make tomorrow to help deliver accommodation for Travellers? What is the simplest thing they would do?

Ms Mary Connors  Make people responsible for what they are supposed to be doing, what they take on to do. Make them responsible. There have to be sanctions. Like I said a while ago, you have to be responsible for your actions or your inactions. You hear it every day of the week on the TV and radio. I am the manager or I am the director so I take full responsibility for this and I resign. People have to be responsible. I am sure people are well paid for what they do. They may do it in part but not as regards Travellers. There is always the attitude that there is a housing crisis in the country. Our answer to that is, there is a housing crisis and we are very sad about that.  It is terrible that people are living on the streets. However, why is there a Traveller interagency group? Why is there an LTACC? If they were not needed, they would not be there. Great thinking went into establishing those groups but they just never took off.
Deputy Maurice Quinlivan  The problem is there is no accountability from the group. There is no agenda in the morning.
Ms Mary Connors  They can do what they like.

Deputy Maurice Quinlivan  It is appalling to give an agenda on the morning of a meeting, for instance, when you are on the way and probably just parking your car and then the meeting is cancelled. That is no way to treat people. It shows utter contempt for people to cancel a meeting, unless it was an emergency. I do not understand and I do not understand why they are not given an agenda either.  I do not want to get bogged down on the small stuff but the LTACCs need to work properly and there has to be some accountability. Are there any other suggestions anybody would offer if the Government was to make a change of policy? For instance, I was on the Traveller committee years ago when I was on the council in Limerick. I can repeat the experiences we have heard here. The committee did not meet properly. It was never there. I think I was the only public representative who ever turned up to it. It was depressing. What would witnesses like to see happening quickly?

Ms Kathleen Connors  I would like for the council to speak to the people and listen to what they want because there is no point in saying they have got somebody a house and where it is, when the person does not want to be there or there are no family members there or it is not where they are from. The council says, "This is your house, there is your key, that is it. Good luck. We sorted you out." We have heard many times about the council giving someone a house, saying they are going to fix this, that and the other thing and do stuff to it, but then that is it. There is no more communication from the council. They have phoned you and that is it, good night. The council needs to sit and talk to Travellers and ask what they want and, if they could do anything for the Travellers, how they could help.  There is no point in putting people somewhere and saying that person is then sorted, they are out of the way and that it is grand when they are not happy there, they do not want to be there or they are in the wrong place. The council can put someone who needs special care or has disability needs in the wrong place, in the wrong house and then the council does not come back or does not have any communication with those people again.

Mr. Robbie Sludds  Success should be measured by outcomes. After all is said and done, there is a lot more said than done. Travellers, from where I am based at the heart of the community, listening to them, day in and day out, are tired. They do not care about the acronym that hangs over someone's head. They want to see people who can actually make a difference in their lives. I hope today is not in vain because I have to go back and talk to those people to let them know something valuable is going to be done for them. At the end of the day, 20-odd years Ms Connors has been sitting on this and the rest of those sitting here are showing up all the time for the people they represent, every single day, including me. I would love to see something of value come out of the LTACC or some change that is going to make a difference in the Traveller community. They were recognised as an ethnic minority in 2017 but I feel they are not respected as a culture going forward.

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  On the question of something that could change on a national policy level, I know we will not see quick change on the ground but we really have to look at a change at structural level. National oversight is needed. I am a community worker. We always want power at the lowest level and the principle of subsidiarity. However, in this case, it is not working. It is 25 years of something not working. Without national oversight, I cannot see it changing.

Deputy Maurice Quinlivan  That was going to be my next question, believe it or not. The Department will come in here, the County and City Management Association, CCMA, will come in and other local authorities will come in here and tell us that they spend their Traveller accommodation money every year. Anybody I speak to or whom my colleagues speak to does not see anything being done in their area. Where is that money going? We do not know where that money is going. I do not ever believe in taking away powers from local government, but in this case I think we have to. In this case, there has to be a national authority that makes sure Traveller accommodation is implemented, and without that, we are on a hiding to nothing. A number of people would agree with me on that. I do not know of any new Traveller site built in Limerick in years. I imagine that is replicated across the country. I hope our recommendations include some sort of national authority that makes sure Traveller accommodation money is spent properly. I thank everyone for coming here today and I appreciate their comments.
An Cathaoirleach  I am conscious there is a vote in the Seanad.

Senator Anne Rabbitte  That is okay. While everybody was talking, I was doing a little bit of googling. Believe it or not, in 2019, the Traveller accommodation expert review was commissioned and one of the main recommendations was that there be an independent chair. We should lean back into this because, if there is an independent chair, their function is to ensure the meetings happen and that everybody is getting their agenda and minutes on time. There is a structure. There is accountability. It is transparent. That is one of the first recommendations I would be putting forward.
An Cathaoirleach  It should be for a fixed five-year term at least.
Senator Anne Rabbitte  It absolutely should. I certainly think that. We do not need to reinvent the wheel. It was done in 2019. We actually just need to see it operationalised.
An Cathaoirleach  It appears it is done in other areas as well.

Senator Anne Rabbitte  Absolutely. That is the inequity of it all. When we talk about transparency, we need to have a barometer of every one of the local authorities to see how many meetings are happening. In my local authority, their meetings have not gone up online since 2019. That just shows the inefficiencies around the transparency of Traveller accommodation. I am from Galway. Deputy Connolly is from the city and I am from the county.  That speaks to the part about culture and the changing culture. We went into that a few times and Ms Mongan spoke about culture. Everybody has talked about culture. It is the cultural piece of the system not recognising. Would Ms Mongan like to speak to that? She talked about homelessness and overcrowding. I know there is a big issue within the Traveller community that overcrowding is not seen as being a homelessness issue. I might have to run out the door to the Seanad in a minute, but I just wanted to get in that.

Ms Mary Mongan  I cannot speak for every Traveller; I can only speak for myself and my family. I am one of three. I have only two sisters. My mother and father are in a small three-bedroom bungalow. I had a mobile home in their yard. It is still there but it is not liveable in. There is no heating. There is no proper running water. It just was not habitable. I have children with additional needs. I have five children. My sister has three. She and her husband live with my mother and father. My other sister, who is not married, my mother and father, my sister who is married and her three children are all living in the house. When the mobile home was not habitable for me, I did live with my mother and father for a few weeks. It was not working. It was very hectic. Seven of us and eight of them made 15 people in the one small bungalow. Nobody plans to become homeless. I found myself travelling back and forth so I had a bed to sleep in. I was sofa surfing. My husband is from Offaly. I did not want to stay too long on top of anyone. I was back and forward. The children missed out on so much. They really did, and I felt guilty for that because I am all for education.  My mother taught me to read and write and I did what I could with them so they would not fall behind and stuff, but the overcrowding is not talked about enough. Where would I go? Take for instance my mum and dad's yard. Where else would I go? You are not going to get a housing assistance payment, HAP, house. Nobody is going to rent to Travellers. If they think you are a Traveller they are not going to rent you a property so you have to try to get social housing. That is the only way out. I was not a priority when I lived in the yard, even though I had children with disabilities. I had a social worker from the council come out to me and say I was not a priority because I was practically housed when I was living in a yard and even though, as I said, there was no proper running water. I would have to go into the house to wash myself and use mum's house for washing clothing. There was no proper heating except maybe an electric heater, which is not good. It is dangerous to be plugging in an electric heater when you have to unplug the kettle first and unplug the heater if want to boil the kettle. It is so dangerous as well. A couple of times the plug nearly melted. I am sorry, I am probably rambling a bit so I will leave it there.

Senator Anne Rabbitte  No, not at all. While we talk about homelessness, there is a hidden group experiencing overcrowding within the Traveller community and it would be great if we could focus on that. I thank Ms Mongan for sharing her story but it is a widespread story among the Traveller community that needs to be understood. In the cultural response from officialdom she was not recognised as having a priority need, even though she did not have access to running water.

Ms Mary Mongan  Yes. It is just basic human rights. Everyone should be entitled to it. You take for granted that at the flick of a switch you can have electricity and heating. I am housed now anyway and that is the main thing.

Ms Elizabeth Berry  When the younger generation, who have just married and are doubling up in the backs of yards and so on, try to move out and get rented accommodation their surnames can be an issue. Connors is a very big surname in Wexford and when they know that the family has the Connors name it is a "No" straight away. They say the accommodation has been given out or whatever. It is the same with the halting sites. I can only talk about Bunclody but I assume New Ross is the same. They are meant to be temporary but people are just pushed in there and never given houses. For the next generation coming up who want houses there is no movement. People are just stuck there for years. There is no moving on whatsoever. That is their forever home but they were not promised that going in.

Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  I thank everybody for coming in. I want to come back to the organisation of the LTACC. Who do the witnesses think would be the right chair? Clearly there is an issue with having a new chair every year in terms of continuity. What is best for the LTACC? Do the witnesses have any strong views? I do not mean about a particular individual. We talk about an independent chair but the trade-off there is we want to put the onus squarely on Wexford County Council to get itself in gear. What is the best route?
An Cathaoirleach  Does it have to be member of the Travelling community or does it have to be-----
Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  I have an open mind. I want to hear.

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  I will quickly speak to that because I have a view of the national picture, as Mary does too, from talking to the national organisations. There are different situations across the country. It is not always the cathaoirleach of the county council. I was told initially that is the way it is and I, no more than anyone else, will accept that until you hear different and you wonder. Obviously, I have never seen the terms of reference.
Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  That was my next question.

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  I was thinking about it over the last couple of days and I am not sure I asked for it either. That speaks to the procedure and whether there is an induction process or any sense of training. Training and development is an ongoing thing. Ms Berry is a trained trainer and does the Traveller cultural awareness training and the anti-racism training. That would have to be scheduled in. Procedural things may sound boring and irrelevant but they are incredibly important for a functioning entity. If you do not have the basics right then-----
Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  Yes, 100%. What is the view on the issue of the chair?

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  The people who are on the LTACC are best placed to decide. It has to be looked at on a national level as to whether it is an independent chair or from the body of members. I am pretty sure the current rotating chair system is not the most effective.
Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  Okay.

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  I do not know what everybody else thinks, but I am reluctant to offer a view because there are different situations in different areas. An independent chair would be difficult if there is nobody but the elected representatives and the Traveller representatives, based on the current structures. The Housing Agency is doing research on the functioning of the LTACCs at the moment.

Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  Ms Byrne mentioned terms of reference. Did anybody ever get terms of reference for the operation of the LTACC in Wexford? The witnesses are saying "No". There were no terms of reference agreed or circulated.  Who would be the most senior Wexford County Council official, not by name but by level, who has participated in the LTACC? Has the county manager or director of services ever shown up? I do not want names, but what is the witnesses' sense of it?

Ms Mary Connors  There was a senior housing officer. I have seen a lot of SHOs in my years involved with the council but it is generally somebody who is going to retire in a year or two and they are shoved in there until they are gone. They last a year or two.

Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  Okay. It is a committee set up by statute so it is a legal committee and its job is to advise the county council on planning for Traveller accommodation, its management, etc. The representatives got a phone call to say the meeting was cancelled at very short notice when the agenda had just arrived, or they did not even get an agenda.
Ms Elizabeth Berry  There was no explanation.
Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  There was no explanation. I know the answer to this but it is kind of depressing. Do the representatives get plans around-----
Ms Elizabeth Berry  No.
Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  -----financial budgets or other plans? Are they coming into the LTACC in relation to what Wexford County Council has planned in years one, two and so on?
Ms Elizabeth Berry  No.
Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  Is any of that information brought to the LTACC?
Ms Elizabeth Berry  No.

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  Not on a regular basis. Sometimes one of the elected representatives will specifically ask for numbers. You get the annual count. I do not think we have seen the 2025 one yet. It is difficult when there has only been one meeting. That goes back to the fundamentals.
Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  Yes, but that is the whole point in terms of-----

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  It is about that consistent reporting of targets. I work on a programme that is monitored to the nth degree twice a year. Our funding comes through the local community development committee, LCDC, and the social inclusion and community activation programme, SICAP, and is monitored with respect to targets, financials and everything twice a year in person. We have audits on top of that. There is a huge contrast.
Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  That is not uncommon.
Ms Mary Connors  And Ms Byrne is responsible for her decisions and actions.
Ms Marie Louise Byrne  Yes.

Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  I agree with what the Cathaoirleach said earlier. Regarding terms of reference, we need to smarten up here. Professionalisation is required. There needs to be terms of reference, clarity on a chair, clarity on regular meetings, no cancelling of meetings at short notice, a clear agenda and that senior officials from the city council are committed.

An Cathaoirleach  I totally agree with the Deputy. The structure suits many county councils at the minute because one meeting a year and cancellation of stuff suits the agenda. There is no focus. They do not necessarily want a focus. That is why this meeting has been vital in providing us with the reality on the ground, which is replicated time and time again. Galway City Council appears to be the outlier. I could be wrong. There could be other councils.
Deputy John Connolly  It quite possibly is. In fairness to Mr. Niall Crowley, my experience of his role in organising the committee was very positive.
Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí  The kind of professional-----

Deputy John Connolly  He was not a councillor. He is not a member of the Traveller community. It was a decision that council management took to appoint someone of his stature to try to make sure that it worked well.
An Cathaoirleach  Does anybody else wish to contribute?

Ms Marie Louise Byrne  If there is to be a restructuring on a national basis, the mandate would be important and it is about the purpose of the LTACC. In the acronym LTACC, one of the C's is for consultative. Is it consultative? There is a bit of ambiguity there. If we go back to the very basics - and sometimes we can overcomplicate things - about what is the purpose and what is this committee's mandate.

An Cathaoirleach  There are a number of issues that we will put into our recommendations. On foot of that, we will invite the relevant Ministers in to issue our recommendations and demand that we see change in this. One of the things we are talking strongly is a national body to oversee Traveller accommodation. While none of us want to see the dilution of local government, the jobs are not being done. We want to remove the whole box-ticking exercise aspect from the LTACCs. For example, it is there, tick the box and we did it. Ms Byrne is right about the consultative piece. What does that mean in the context of delivering results?  The independent chair would be a vital component to our recommendations and to the success of LTACCs going forward for a statutory five-year period. I was cathaoirleach of Wexford County Council. I was chair of the LTACC. You were only getting used to the whole set up when you were gone again. I do not have to tell Ms Mary Connors this, but these things take time. A one-year stint is a waste of time when there are two-, three-, four- and five-year plans. Accountability is crucial as well, as are the mandatory meetings. I would not say the treatment meted out to Ms Berry was an isolated incident. If we went across the country, we would find similar. What we have gleaned from this meeting is that the entire structure of the LTACC has to be changed nationally with a piece in place that we can point to and say, "That is the way the structure should be." This is obviously with consultation. We are not going to be dictatorial in the way we go about it. If we can make recommendations that are informed from having the likes of this meeting, it will go a long way towards improving the situation and being very definite about the direction we want to take it.
Ms Elizabeth Berry  There are all the knocks that we had of going to them. I like going to them to bring back the information. It is just a knock every time and there are not enough of them.

An Cathaoirleach  We will certainly do all we can to improve and change the situation for the better. I thank the witnesses for coming along. We look forward to, perhaps, interacting with some of them again in the future.
The joint committee adjourned at 2.14 p.m. sine die .
Traveller Accommodation: Discussion (Resumed)

text.text: Deputy Darren O'Rourke  I wish the staff and the Minister all the best for the summer. I know it will be a busy summer but I hope that everyone gets a break. I ask the Minister to state the number of children with additional needs who require but have yet to receive an offer of an appropriate school place for September 2026, based on her most recent meeting with the NCSE; the date of that meeting; and the measures she has taken to ensure that every child with additional needs has an appropriate school for September.

Minister for Education and Youth (Deputy Hildegarde Naughton)  I thank the Deputy for his comments and I too wish everyone well over the next couple of weeks.  An estimated 25% of students, or approximately 240,000 children and young people, have special educational needs. While the majority are supported successfully in mainstream settings by their class teacher, special education teachers, SET, and special needs assistants, SNA, as necessary, there remains an increasing need for special class and special school places for children with more complex needs.  The parents notify process has played a key role in forward planning, supporting the delivery of 584 new special classes, the establishment of four new special schools for the coming 2026-27 school year and expanded capacity in existing special schools. The National Council for Special Education has verified that some 7,860 children and young people who were notified to them by 1 October 2025 are eligible for a specialist place for the 2026-27 school year. The NCSE continues to work with families where children have come forward since then, to secure appropriate placements. NCSE data indicates there is sufficient overall capacity to meet identified demand. However, the Department recognises that places may not always arise in a preferred school or locality. The NCSE is actively engaging with these families to identify suitable placements. Approximately 7,000 of the 7,860 students have a diagnosis of autism and, given there are generally adequate places for students with other diagnoses, the focus is on new places for children with autism. NCSE data shows that approximately 75% of those who came forward by 1 October are already enrolled in school.  As in previous years, students without a school place are prioritised for access to specialist placements. My Department receives regular updates on placements and the Minister of State, Deputy Moynihan, meets the NCSE every week. I have regular engagement with the NCSE and the Minister of State met its representatives as recently as yesterday to monitor progress.

Deputy Darren O'Rourke  The Minister finished on the bit I am interested in and that I specifically asked about,. What was the latest weekly update? The information the Minister has just given me was previously provided to the House on 23 April. It is now 16 July. Does the Minister have any additional information to provide to the House as of this week?

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  There is weekly engagement with the NCSE. Since January, 584 special classes have been sanctioned for the upcoming school year. That includes 68 inclusive classes. Of the 584 new special classes, 378 are being established in primary schools and 206 in post-primary schools. This brings the total number of special classes sanctioned to date to over 4,300. The NCSE continues to work with families and schools on this. As we know, there may be more children throughout the year who will need specialist placements. The NCSE is working proactively with them in relation to that.

Deputy Darren O'Rourke  Again, we have those figures from a briefing we had with the Department as recently as yesterday. It is all welcome progress but the question I am asking today is what is the unmet need as things stand? How many children do not have an offer of a school place? How many children have an offer of a school place but it will not be ready for September, in terms of advancing of works? It has been reported in the media this week that an extremely high number of children will not have a place for September. Many of them are taking legal cases. The Minister can confirm or deny that. I am providing her with the opportunity but she has not done it so far.

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  A huge amount of work is being done on securing specialist places, be it in special classes or special schools. We are far ahead of where we were this time last year. We had a budget for 400 special classes. I got increased funding in March of this year. We are ahead in relation to forward planning. There are now 584 special classes allocated. This is far more than any previous years because of the parent notify system, on 1 October. I brought that forward again this year. This enabled the Department to forward plan even better for when I go into budget negotiations for September 2027. A huge amount of work is happening with the Minister of State, Deputy Moynihan, and me. There is sufficient overall capacity to meet identified demand. There is a pathway for children to receive a specialist place or supports within mainstream settings. As I have said, about 25% or approximately 240,000 children and young people have special educational needs and the majority of them are supported in mainstream settings but the focus and priority will be on children who do not have a place and are coming into the primary school system or moving from primary to post-primary, for example.
Special Educational Needs

text.text: Deputy Aidan Farrelly  I ask the Minister to provide the House with an update on the commitment with regards to Opportunities for Youth: National Strategy for Youth Work and Related Services 2024-2028.

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  As Minister for Education and Youth I am committed to supporting the workforce in the youth sector to deliver high-quality youth work and non-formal developmental opportunities for young people. Action 7 in Opportunities for Youth: National Strategy for Youth Work and Related Services 2024-2028, commits to developing a workforce development strategy in respect of the youth sector. This is to include consideration of training needs and the requirement for high-quality, accessible and inclusive youth work services and opportunities.  The Department has engaged extensively with youth workers and managers in youth organisations and is aware of the recruitment and retention challenges being experienced in the sector. This engagement included completion of a workforce survey and employer questionnaire. These were followed by 11 regional, in person and online consultations. The data captured from the consultation period will inform the development of the strategy. Important data from the consultation include: the high level of job satisfaction in the sector; learning and development opportunities; the challenging recruitment and retention environment; the varying youth worker pay scales; different contract types; and details on average and median youth worker pay. Profile data on youth workers was also captured, including their qualifications, length of employment, age range, gender and ethnicity. It is important to highlight that this is the first time this information has been sought and received from the youth work sector.  It is important to highlight that this is the first time this information has been sought and received from the youth work sector and that will establish critical baseline information for us for the development of the strategy. To support the development of the workforce development strategy, a workforce advisory group will be established. My Department is working in partnership with the National Youth Council of Ireland to agree the role of this group, including its membership. It is intended for the advisory group to have its first meeting in September.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  I thank the Minister. If she will indulge me, it is very rare I get the opportunity to speak about my life experience prior to being in here but I have been a youth worker for about 16 years or the guts of three Dáil terms. The day before the general election I submitted my PhD thesis, which was on professional youth work. It asked youth workers many of the same questions that were asked afterwards by the Department. I will happily share the findings with the Minister.  Youth workers, in the main, are very satisfied but equally they are very concerned about what the future looks like because we are losing good youth worker after good youth worker to other sectors who can offer more. They can offer more in terms of pay and remuneration but also the burnout associated with the occupation is really difficult.  When the Minister says that advisory group is going to meet in September, who makes up the membership of that? The information the Minister's Department has collected is golden with regard to the sector. Will the Minister publish the findings of that survey? It would be really useful information.

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  I thank Deputy Farrelly. I would be very happy to receive that information. It would help our data collection and make sure we are getting a really good picture of the youth work sector across the country. The work that has been under way within the Department is to try to get that profile, to really understand our youth work sector and to get feedback from them.  The first advisory group will have its first meeting in September and the terms of reference of that group will be finalised once the group is established. My Department is working in consultation with the National Youth Council of Ireland to agree the role of that group. The workforce survey data will be shared with the workforce advisory group in the first instance to inform its work in overseeing the development of the strategy. The workforce data will also accompany the strategy in the publication. So, it will be published.  While the subject of the pay and conditions of the sector has been raised through consultations, they will not directly form part of the strategy. As the Deputy knows, youth workers are not employed by my Department. They are not public servants and funding is allocated on the provision of service spaces to meet the needs of the youth population in an area. The employment of the staff, including youth workers, is a matter relevant for youth organisations and services.

Deputy Aidan Farrelly  It is acceptable that data will be shared with the task force in September but I ask that it be shared more widely once the terms of reference have been agreed. It would be really useful for the academic sector and for those who are in the market of training and professionally qualifying youth workers in the field.  I have been around long enough to have seen youth work move from Department to Department. The only conclusion I can come to in terms of analysis is that the Minister has a real opportunity in her Department to map out what the future of youth work looks like, and not just for the young people. We are consistently talking about the issues facing young people and how youth work is often a response to those issues. Actually, youth work is an occupation and profession that is one of the best jobs to have but we need to make sure the landscape is there for budding youth workers to go through appropriate professional qualification programmes and that the job will fulfil them not just from a rewarding job perspective but also from a financial perspective and from the perspective of promotions and so on, right through their 20s, 30s and 40s.  I wish that group the best. I also wish the Minister's Department the best in its endeavours with that and I thank her again.

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  It is very fitting that youth has moved into the Department of education. It is a good fit. I have met with many youth organisations across the country since I was appointed and they seem very happy with the formal education and the informal education. I have witnessed the huge expertise on the ground. This is the data we want to collect and there is a willingness there and an appetite for training as well. As the Deputy knows very well, it is so important we have the right skill set in our youth services across the country, dealing with children and young people and with trauma, and making sure we have the best, which we do, and that workers are accessing the training they require.  For example, in response to some of the calls from the sector, a bursary initiative was established in June to support eligible youth workers and youth work managers to undertake the three-year MA qualification in community and youth work, part-time, in-service programme in Maynooth University. Also, the workforce advisory group will regularly update the nation youth sector reference group, which is also currently being established. That group will include representatives from across the youth sector, including academics and youth representatives, and will support a balanced and transparent input from across the wider sector.
Youth Work Supports

text.text: Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  This Government is committed to improving staffing levels in primary schools and supporting the recruitment and retention of teachers. According to the latest published data from November 2025, there were more than 97% of allocated primary teaching posts filled. Teacher numbers at primary level have increased by almost 6,000 since 2019 and now stand at the highest level ever recorded at over 43,400.  The Government is investing a record €14.1 billion in education and schools through budget 2026. This record level of investment has enabled significant progress in tackling educational disadvantage and supporting children and young people with special educational needs to achieve their full potential. Funding has been provided for 860 additional special education teachers across special schools and mainstream settings, together with more than 1,700 additional special needs assistants.  Budget 2026 also includes an additional €48 million full-year investment across both the DEIS strategy and the DEIS plus scheme. That provides more teaching positions and more staffing and supports for schools as well. That DEIS programme will benefit approximately 30,000 children and young people attending DEIS plus schools as well as one in four children across schools in the DES programme.  Under the programme for Government, there is a commitment to reduce the general primary pupil-teacher ratio to 19:1 over the lifetime of the Government and to introduce targeted measures for schools with very large class sizes. This builds on substantial progress already made. The primary staffing schedule has improved from an average allocation ratio of 26:1, five years ago, to 23:1 for the current school year, which is the lowest ever at primary level. Average class sizes have fallen from 24.1 to 22.2 pupils, while the overall pupil-teacher ratio improved from 15:1 in 2019-2020 to 12.8:1 in 2023-2024, which is comparing favourably with the OECD average levels.

Deputy Darren O'Rourke  I thank the Minister. She said from November that 97% of posts were filled. In real terms at the same time, 996 teaching posts were unfilled, which is almost 1,000. Figures as recent as last week tell us that over 39,000 primary school students were in classes of 30 pupils or more in the past school year. A figure of 36,805 were in classes of 30 to 34 pupils and 2,237 were in classes of between 35 and 39 pupils. That is simply incredible in 2026 in Ireland and it has a direct impact on the type of attention children can get in the classroom. It is as simple as that. It is also contributing to the burnout for teachers.  I did not hear the answer in her initial response and maybe the Minister will provide it in her next response. Is it her ambition to move on the pupil-teacher ratio in this budget cycle and will she provide for 1,000 primary school teachers?

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  It is an absolute commitment in the programme for Government to reduce the pupil-teacher ratio over the lifetime of the Government. The Deputy will appreciate I cannot announce anything here in the Dáil. I have to go into negotiations in relation to the upcoming budget.  In the past ten years there has been a five-point improvement to the primary staffing schedule. In 2015, teachers were allocated to primary schools at a general average of 28 pupils for every one teacher. This is now reduced to 23:1.  Lower thresholds are in place for DEIS urban band 1. That includes DEIS plus schools. We have 17:1, 21:1 and 19:1 for junior, senior and vertical schools respectively. A three-point reduction in retention thresholds assists schools in retaining existing staff. As the Deputy knows, there are over 43,000 teachers employed in our primary schools. This is an increase of over 9,000 teachers at primary level in ten years. I understand the importance of ensuring that every child gets access to their special education teacher and all of the supports required. That is obviously ongoing work with me and the Minister of State, Deputy Moynihan, in the context of this upcoming budget. I hope to put in place more measures to support our schools right across the education sector.

Deputy Darren O'Rourke  It is a statement of fact that in recent years we have seen a reduced number of classroom teachers. Budget 2026 led to the removal of 498 classroom teachers, a net reduction of 381 when one looks at the gains. The year 2025-26 saw a reduction of 290 and 2024-25 a reduction of 237. That has a real impact.  I can give the example of Lismullen National School. I hope to correspond with the Minister directly in relation to Lismullen National School, if she is agreeable. Parents have written to me. Next year, there will be a class of 36 and parents, as the Minister would herself, are identifying the challenge that will present as regards the type of support that is going to be available for their children, the type of attention and schooling opportunity, and also for the teachers involved. I would appreciate the Minister considering this issue.  It is my ambition to have 1,000 extra primary school teachers and I will strongly be making the case for that in the Sinn Féin budget. I ask the Minister to do the same in her own negotiations.

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  There is a number of issues here, such as the staffing appeals criteria. The numbers going into primary schools are reducing and our population bulge is in post-primary. That is a reality of the way trends are going. There is a staffing appeals circular, set out in Circular 0025/2026, and it includes specific appeals for small-school enrolments in the previous October, involving projected enrolments, accommodation difficulties and where there may be language support. The primary staffing appeals board operates independently of myself and the Department.  Mainstream appeals posts are allocated provisionally on the basis of the school achieving the required appointment and retention figures in the coming September rather than the previous September. The appeals board considers the circumstances of the school in deciding if a teaching post is warranted a year ahead of the normal staffing arrangements. The appeals board held meetings in May and June and it will meet again in October. Schools will be notified of the closing date for applications to appeals boards in early September but I take the Deputy's overall point in regard to the pupil-teacher ratio.
Question No. 4 taken with Written Answers
School Staff

text.text: Deputy Paul Lawless  What arrangements are in place for parents and parents' representative organisations to raise concerns directly with the Department regarding the national education curriculum and the provision of resources such as books, etc.? How frequently does the Minister meet with these organisations, stakeholders and parental bodies?

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  The National Parents Council, NPC, is the representative body for parents of children in primary and post-primary education. It serves as an important channel of communication between parents and my Department. Annual funding is provided to support its work, including €765,782 in 2025. The National Parents Council represents parents’ views on education policy, curriculum reform and educational resources, ensuring that parental perspectives are reflected in policy development, implementation and decision-making.  The NPC is on the primary and post-primary education forums, which support the planning and sequencing of change across the school sector. The National Parents Council is also a key stakeholder of the National Council for Curriculum and Assessment, NCCA, and its advisory structures, ensuring that parents’ perspectives inform curriculum development and related resources across early childhood, primary and post-primary education. In addition, the NCCA facilitates parental participation through surveys, written submissions, consultation events and focus groups. It represents parents on a wide range of Department-led groups, including those relating to special education, senior cycle redevelopment, DEIS, anti-bullying procedures, student and parent supports and disability participation and consultation.  The NPC is also on the convention on education, ensuring that parents’ views are reflected in national discussions on the future direction of education in this country. My Department has also engaged with the National Parents Council on the development of the Education (Student and Parent Charter) Bill.  I met with the National Parents Council in March of this year. In addition, both the parents council and individual parents may raise concerns directly with me and my Department regarding the curriculum, educational resources and other education matters. This direct engagement helps ensure that parental views inform policy development and decision-making at national level.

Deputy Paul Lawless  Confidence in our education system depends on quality resources but parents remain seriously concerned about inappropriate material that is being promoted in our schools, libraries, etc. Concerns have been raised in relation to the book What's the T? by Juno Dawson, which contains sexually explicit material and was promoted to children by Children's Books Ireland and RTÉ. It received significant publish backlash, and rightly so. It has been reported that a teacher raised concerns with the Department in an email back in March 2023, and indeed the former Minister for justice, Charlie Flanagan, raised this personally with the Minister's predecessor in December 2023. Despite those concerns being raised, the book remained recommended as a good resource for children.  Very plainly, what has the Department done since this controversy broke? What review has happened? Can the Minister outline to the House the results of that review, if it took place at all?

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  I do not know exactly what the Deputy is asking me in relation to the Department of education. I do not know if it is a book used in schools but, so the Deputy understands how it works, in regard to schools that use textbooks or other teaching and learning resources, that is a matter for the individual school. Decisions around materials are made at a whole-school level. Textbooks are commercially produced and my Department does not endorse publications, products or services from individual, commercial or other providers. Any concerns regarding material included in specific textbooks should be raised with relevant publishers.  From an education point of view, I have absolute confidence in our teachers. There is a huge amount of training and supports. We have Oide, which has in-service days. We have curriculum reform and a huge amount of consultation and training happens around that. It is always age-appropriate and I think schools are very well aware of any issues that parents may have and parents may come and talk to schools directly. We have a very good track record in relation to that.

Deputy Paul Lawless  Is the Minister aware of the controversy surrounding the What's the T? book by Juno Dawson? Is she aware that the book was promoted by Children's Books Ireland? That is very important.  The idea that the Minister would say she is basically not responsible is, I believe, questionable. She is the Minister for education; the buck stops with her. For her to say she is not responsible is unacceptable, in my view. The Minister has such an enormous responsibility for the children of this country and if it is the case that there is inappropriate material being promoted to children, she actually is responsible and it is her job, I believe, to make sure that never happens again and that there are robust processes in place to make sure no child will be subjected to sexually explicit, age-inappropriate material in our schools and libraries and promoted by Children's Books Ireland and RTÉ.

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  I will repeat it for the Deputy. In regard to our schools, I come from a teaching background myself. I do not know exactly what the Deputy is inferring in relation to the education system.
Deputy Paul Lawless  Is the Minister aware of the What's the T? book?

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  I have not read that book but what I can tell the Deputy in relation to our education system is that, be it social, personal and health education, SPHE, or relationships and sexuality education, RSE, there is a huge amount of consultation between schools and parents.  With regard to the NCCA as our curriculum is developed, there is huge amount of consultation. Our teachers are so well trained in this country to make sure that when they are engaging in SPHE, for example, they are ensuring that all of our children are in a safe and supported environment within our schools and that any lessons are age appropriate. Where parents have concerns, they can approach and contact their schools. I know of cases where parents will reach out to schools and where schools will actually hold information nights for parents in advance of, for example, a SPHE lesson so that they were very aware of what their children are going to be taught in relation to any particular sensitive area but it is always age appropriate. We always have to make sure that our schools are inclusive, that we support our young people and that they feel safe and supported.
School Curriculum

text.text: Deputy Ryan O'Meara  What does the Government intend to do to meet the programme for Government commitment to reduce the pupil-teacher ratio in our schools to 19:1?

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  The Government is investing a record €14.1 billion into education and schools through budget 2026. This record level of investment has allowed the Government to invest in tackling educational disadvantage and supporting those with special educational needs to achieve their full potential. It has enabled huge investment in the school buildings programme, in curriculum reform, in school leadership and in continuous professional development for teachers.  Under the programme for Government, there is a commitment to aim to reduce the general pupil-teacher ratio at primary level to 19:1 over the term of this Government and introduce targeted measures in schools with very large classes. This will build on the progress that has been made by the previous Government. The general average of pupils to teachers in the primary staffing schedule improved from 26:1 five years ago to 23:1 for the current school year. Average class sizes in primary schools have improved from 24.1 to 22.2 through the investment we are making in schools.  The Department’s primary staffing schedule is the key factor for determining the level of staffing resources provided at individual school level. This school year, the primary staffing schedule operates on a general average of 23 pupils to every one teacher, which is historically the lowest ever ratio of pupils to teachers at primary level. More favourable ratios are implemented for DEIS urban band 1 schools.  The numbers employed in our schools have now reached the highest ever level. Teacher numbers at primary level have increased by almost 6,000 between 2019 and 2025. This has led to a steady improvement in both the pupil-teacher ratio and in average class size statistics during this period. I am very conscious of the primary staffing schedule and the need to prioritise teacher allocations in primary schools. I am considering how best to make further progress as part of the annual budgetary process in reducing the primary pupil-teacher ratio in the context of that programme for Government implementation.

Deputy Ryan O'Meara  I acknowledge the work that was done by the previous Government in reducing the pupil-teacher ratio. Good work was done and, to be fair, in the last budget, good work was done in respect of the capitation grants to schools and that needs to be recognised. It was a huge issue this time last year, particularly at the Oireachtas education committee. The pupil-teacher ratio is key and we have committed very clearly to 19:1 by the end of this Government. I will highlight some data that has come out of the Department in recent days. A total of 39,000 students in the country were in classes of over 30 students for the 2025-2026 academic year. One school in particular in Tipperary - St. Peter and Paul's CBS in Clonmel - actually had 38 students in one class in the academic year just gone, which realistically is twice what the programme for Government says it wants class sizes to be, so I reiterate that very important call for the reduction to 19:1 over the course of this Government.

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  Where we can, we give guidance and I know schools are very well aware of this. They do this well themselves so that where possible, the more junior classes would have a lower class size. Where there are higher numbers in some classes in many schools, one will find other classes within the school that would have lower numbers to accommodate for that earlier, so that the junior classes would have lower class sizes where possible but I hear the concerns highlighted by the Deputy.  I am very aware of our commitment in the programme for Government on this. Prior to 2016, teachers were allocated to primary schools at a general average of 28 pupils for every one teacher. In budget 2016, we improved that ratio by one point at 27:1. In budget 2018, we further improved it by one point to 26:1 and in 2021, we improved it by a further point to 25:1. In addition, there has been a three-point reduction in the retention schedule and that schedule assists schools that would otherwise be at risk of losing teaching posts, so this measure helps to better ensure teacher retention in primary schools while also ensuring that fewer pupils are required to retain or to recruit a teacher.

Deputy Ryan O'Meara  The ask from this budget from the INTO is very important - 1,000 additional teachers - to help us reduce class sizes for every child to give him or her more attention, to support inclusive education, to meet growing pupil needs, to ease the workload pressure and potential burnout for teachers facing those very high numbers within the classroom and to bring stability to school and strengthen leadership. Coming from a rural constituency, I acknowledge a lot of those rural schools that are struggling at the moment to maintain their two, three or four teachers because they are always faced with the threat of losing one because they are just barely over the number at the moment. Those additional teachers will help with that. We need to fill the posts that are there, of course. However, hiring those additional 1,000 teachers will certainly help with our key commitment. It has been done step by step but this year's budget will be very important step towards that key figure of 19:1.

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  We have more favourable ratios as part of our DEIS urban band 1 schools. The Deputy heard me announce the DEIS schools earlier this year, so there are measures for children and students who are most at risk of educational disadvantage. We have been reducing the pupil-teacher ratio incrementally over the years and that is something I want to continue over the lifetime of this Government but, as the Deputy can appreciate, I cannot go into detail on any budgetary decisions because I have yet to have my meetings with the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation. I have to look at the whole of the education budget, making sure that we are supporting children with educational needs, reducing the burden on our leadership teams within our schools, because I hear those concerns around burnout very clearly, and looking at ways of listening to the stakeholders on what we could do to ease the pressure on our schools so they can focus more on teaching and learning, which is what they are all there to do, notwithstanding the administrative necessities required in our schools.
Pupil-Teacher Ratio
Ceisteanna Eile - Other Questions

Deputy Noel McCarthy  Will further consideration be given by the Department to a decision to refuse an application for the additional school accommodation scheme from a school in light of the school's projected increase in enrolment numbers?

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  The school referred to by the Deputy submitted an application under the additional school accommodation, ASA, scheme for an additional temporary classroom in 2025. This school had previously been approved for a permanent extension under the ASA scheme in 2021 for a two-classroom special education needs unit and one mainstream classroom. The project is devolved to the school for delivery and my Department is currently awaiting a submission of the stage 1 design report from the school. The school subsequently applied in 2024 for reconfiguration of an existing classroom to cater for a second special class pending completion of the permanent extension project. The Department approved this application and it has already been delivered. The NDP implementation plan for the education and youth sector 2026 to 2030 was published in January 2026. This NDP implementation plan includes a strong focus on maximising existing school capacity across the school estate and also ensuring that schools' admissions policies and processes are targeted at meeting local mainstream and special class requirements. Available funding must be prioritised where local capacity across schools in the area is insufficient along with ensuring delivery that is affordable, offers value for money and meets functional needs.  The school's application for interim classroom accommodation is parallel to the delivery of its traditional building project that has been assessed, including in the context of available capacity in the local area. It is the Department's position that the school has sufficient accommodation within the existing school buildings to cater for its local demand through the management of its enrolments, in line with its current capacity. In the Youghal school planning area, where the school referenced is located, there are 23% fewer junior infants than there were in 2020. All 14 primary schools in the school planning area indicate capacity to enrol more pupils. The proposal for interim accommodation in this context is not therefore an effective prioritisation of NDP funding. This position has been explained to the school.

Deputy Noel McCarthy  I thank the Minister for her response. I am unsure if she is familiar with the history of Kilcredan National School. It has been the central point of three smaller parish schools - Ladysbridge, Kilcredan and Ballyburden - since they merged in the 1970s. Kilcredan is a popular rural school catering for the families of several local parishes. The population of these parishes continues to increase, with recent development of many new housing estates and more planned. Due to the increased enrolment, an extra teacher but not an extra classroom was sanctioned last September. As a result, 14 children were accommodated in a learning support room which had a knock-on effect on the school's SEN provision. This summer, 31 children finished in the school, with 48 expected to start in September.  An additional school accommodation scheme application was refused on the basis that Kilcredan national school has sufficient accommodation within the existing school buildings to cater for its local demand. The school itself disagrees and has raised serious concerns that children entering the school will likely have to be accommodated in the hall. This would have a negative impact on the well-being and physical activity and the movement breaks of the children in the school's special classes. Therefore, can the Minister and her Department officials liaise with the school to see what can be done to ensure adequate space for Kilcredan pupils?

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  The Department funded a substantial extension and refurbishment in 2014 of this school. This included six new classrooms, special education rooms, a GP hall, a new basketball court and a new carpark. The existing building was also completely refurbished. The school was subsequently approved for a further extension under the ASA scheme in 2021, to provide a two SEN classroom unit and one additional mainstream classroom. This project is devolved to the school authority for delivery and is at stage 1 of architectural design and planning. As the Deputy knows, the school was also approved for an SEN repurposing project in 2024, to reconfigure an existing room to cater for a second special education class, pending the provision of that new permanent extension. A further application for rental of interim accommodation to cater for a mainstream class was refused in May of this year, on the grounds that there is already sufficient capacity in the area and the responsibility of the school to manage its enrolments to suit its capacity in that context. In the Youghal area, we have to look at the capacity within the planning school area as part of our prioritisation process.

Deputy Noel McCarthy  I thank the Minister for her response. There have been some positive developments recently with the approval of a safe routes to school programme application. This was good news for the school as it will greatly help its future expansion. However, the problem is the expansion and extra development within the parishes I was speaking about, and the need for local children to go to those schools. The Minister mentioned there is a space in Youghal but, as she knows, people like to attend the school they live close to. However, with legitimate space concerns and a steady increase in enrolment numbers, this case requires the particular attention of the Department in the short term. The school is understandably disappointed at the Department's position on providing additional accommodation as it awaits proposed expansion. I have written directly to the Minister to highlight this. With this in mind, I ask her to provide an update on the progress of the long-term proposal for Kilcredan National School, which would see the construction of one much-needed mainstream classroom and two SEN classes.

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  The information I have to date is the project is devolved to the school authority for delivery and it is currently at stage 1 of the architectural design and planning. I can give the Deputy more detail if he needs it. Since 2020, the Department has provided more than €796 million in capital funding for Cork schools. Over this period a total of 168 schools have been upgraded, either through the provision of a new school building, a large-scale extension or the provision of modular accommodation. Some 12 school projects to go to tender or construction this year or next were included in the NDP implementation plan. There are currently 18 school projects in Cork under construction. This summer we have 35 schools which were approved to undergo works as part of the climate action summer works programme. In addition, since 2020, 306 special classes have been sanctioned in Cork, and the Minister of State beside me is very aware of this. Some 66 were sanctioned for September 2026.
Question No. 8 taken with Written Answers.
School Accommodation

Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú  In relation to grants for assistive technology for students, are there plans to increase the funding for the scheme or to update or change its criteria? The Minister is aware of what brought this to my attention. It is a ten-year-old boy from north County Louth with dyslexia. Following assessment, it was found he would benefit from a computer and assistive technology but who is not eligible for the grant. I have discussed this with the Minister. We need to find a solution and to look at the overall criteria. There are wider issues as regards AAC also.

Minister of State at the Department of Education (Deputy Michael Moynihan)  I thank the Deputy for his engagement in relation to this issue. The assistive technology scheme supplements the overall funding provided to schools for digital technology and equipment. It supports children who require essential specialised equipment to access the school curriculum.  Assistive technology is a critical enabler for students with special educational needs, allowing them to benefit fully from the modern, technological-focused education system. The Department of Education and Youth recognises the significant benefits of assistive technology in school settings, particularly for students with more complex needs. It supports access to the curriculum and encourages classroom participation and positive educational outcomes. Under the current scheme, schools receive funding towards computers and specialised equipment required for educational purposes. To qualify, a student must have a diagnosis of a physical or commutative disability and a professional assessment confirming the equipment is essential to access the curriculum. The review of the assistive technology scheme is at its final stages and has culminated in a new circular which I expect to announce in September 2026.  A key outcome is a planned move from a diagnosis-based model to a needs-based approach. This will give schools greater autonomy to determine when assistive technology is required, reduce administrative burdens and improve timely access to supports. A streamlined application process is also being developed for implementation. These changes aim to deliver a more responsive, effective and child-centred scheme. The Department will continue to routinely examine the level of grant aid payable under the assistive technology scheme to ensure that the level remains appropriate and aligned with the needs of children who require assistance. Ultimately, any child who needs assistive technology to access the curriculum will receive it. In line with the policy and funding parameters of the scheme, promoting assistive technologies is a programme for Government commitment and a key ministerial priority.

Deputy Sorca Clarke  When DEIS plus schools were announced in May, St. Joseph's and St. Michael's in Longford town were rightly included. Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  Addressing educational disadvantage and ensuring that every child and young person can reach their full potential is a key priority for me as Minister for Education and Youth. The introduction of the DEIS plus scheme will provide enhanced supports to a small cohort of schools with the very highest concentration of students at risk of educational disadvantage.  Schools were identified for inclusion in DEIS plus through a nationally consistent, evidence-based identification model which drew on a range of indicators associated with persistent and intergenerational disadvantage. The model was applied uniformly across all eligible schools to ensure a fair and objective process.  Recognising the importance of accuracy and fairness, schools that were not satisfied with the outcome were afforded an opportunity to appeal in line with the arrangements set out by the Department. The appeal process allowed schools to correct inaccuracies in enrolment data or seek verification that the DEIS plus identification model had been correctly applied to their data. All appeals submitted by schools, including the one referred to by the Deputy, are undergoing a detailed technical review in accordance with the published criteria. The outcomes of the review are independently verified by an appeals panel with expertise in data analysis, education policy and educational disadvantage, providing an additional layer of assurance regarding the integrity and consistency of the process.  It would be inappropriate for me to comment on the result of any individual appeal in advance of the completion of that process. That process will be completed in the coming days and schools will be notified of the outcome of their appeal. I do also recognise however, that some schools are operating in the context of complex local pressures that cannot currently be fully reflected in the DEIS plus identification model. At present, the model must use data from the online enrolment databases and the HP index in order to be based on data that are available nationally and consistently for all schools. I will come back in again.

Deputy Hildegarde Naughton  The appeals process is underway at the moment. It will be announced shortly. I am not involved in that. It is independently being assessed. Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh  SNAs are very dedicated members of our school community who work very hard with our most vulnerable children. Deputy Michael Moynihan  I thank the Deputy. By way of background, the number of SNAs working within the education system has grown significantly to support the increasing number of students with special education needs, both in mainstream schools and in special schools and classes. By the end of this year, there will be approximately 26,000 SNAs in our education system.  In recognition of the importance of the SNA role, the Department established the SNA workforce development unit and on 3 June 2026 published the first SNA WDP. Built around five strategic pillars, the plan recognises the vital contribution SNAs make to supporting children and young people with additional educational needs and enabling their full participation in school life. It sets out a clear framework to strengthen and support SNAs through enhanced professional development, greater role clarity, workforce sustainability measures and stronger collaboration across all school communities. The actions set out in the SNA WDP were developed over a period of more than two years through extensive engagement between the Department of Education and Youth, Fórsa and other stakeholders. Direct stakeholder consultation on the plan included: focus groups with SNAs, teachers and school leaders; consultation with children and young people; a survey of SNAs with which more than 13,000 SNAs engaged; and a number of online webinars with SNAs and school leaders.  I note the outcome of the ballot by members of Fórsa to not accept the plan. While I am disappointed by this outcome, the Department remains committed to constructive engagement with Fórsa and available to engage in relation to these matters. The Department continues to work with all stakeholders to achieve sustainable improvements for the SNA workforce in pursuit of an education system that is of the highest quality and where every child and young person feels valued and is actively supported and nurtured to achieve his or her full potential.
